The large performance gap between BM25 (20.21 F1) and InLegalBERT (85.02 F1) shows that simple word matching is not enough to answer these legal questions. Performance also varies across the seven Acts, indicating substantial differences in answer-extraction performance.

title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: https://github.com/thefinnlab/low-rank-alignment

title: Discovering Interpretable Acoustic Features in Autoregressive Voice-Cloning TTS Models
abstract: Voice-cloning TTS models synthesize an unseen speaker's voice from brief speech prompts, but it remains unclear which acoustic properties they represent and use. We introduce a feature-based interpretability framework for autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models, analyzing features from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), PCA, and random directions via sparse probing, steering, and quantitative auto-interpretability. We focus on Qwen3-TTS and extend probing and steering to $5$ additional models to test generalization across architectures. These models encode concepts like pitch, energy, noise, and accent, but sparse prediction and steering are effective only for some concepts. Strong probing does not always translate to steering or vice-versa. SAEs are useful for sparse probing of human-labelled concepts and novel-concept discovery, while PCA is competitive for dense probing and steering. Auto-interpretability finds $684$ automatically validated SAE features in Qwen3-TTS covering speaker clusters, speaking style, and recording conditions beyond known concepts. Overall, we perform a comprehensive interpretability study of autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models.

title: Last-minute Halloween costumes for tech nerds
abstract: It happens to the best of us — you’ve completely dropped the ball on figuring out a Halloween costume. Naturally, you’ve decided to solve this problem by turning to… TechCrunch? Yeah, sure, why not. I’ve got some ideas. Here are some last-minute techy Halloween costumes. Effort levels vary. Recursive self-improvement AI leaders like Dario Amodei and Sam Altman have expressed their fears that AI is developing too quickly , but if AI models become capable of “recursive self-improvement,” they’ll be able to advance on their own without human intervention, rendering any efforts to “pace the frontier” futile. I’m not sure how to visually represent the idea of an AI building itself, but you could really lean into the “self-improvement” part and forget the “recursive” aspect — it’s a last-minute Halloween costume. You don’t need to try that hard. Dress as the version of yourself you imagine becoming every year when you make New Year’s resolutions. Carry around a self-help or productivity book like “Atomic Habits” or anything by Malcolm Gladwell, a yoga mat, and a huge bottle of water. Leave in the middle of the party to “go to therapy” when you actually just want to go home. Brag to people about how good your Oura Ring’s sleep score is. You are the embodiment of someone trying to better themselves. You are recursive self-improvement. Image Credits: aldomurillo / Getty Images A deceptively cute AI agent Meta and OpenAI both recently launched AI assistants with creepily cute avatars. It’s almost Elizabeth Holmes-esque — they look innocent, so you underestimate their potential to cause disaster. (While we’re talking about her, you’re only allowed to do the black turtleneck Holmes costume if you’re a natural blonde, or if you have a blonde wig.) What you’re going to do is make yourself look big and fluffy. Maybe you have a poofy puffer jacket, or maybe you can find some colorful feather boas to wrap yourself in. Add a distinctive hat, glasses, or other accessory to make yourself look more like a ChatGPT Dot. If you have a colorful shirt and matching bottoms, that also works. Throughout the night, ask people if you can obtain read/write access to their Gmail. Image Credits: OpenAI A guy who is actively recording you with Meta glasses Whether you call them “pervert glasses” or not, we should all be able to agree that it would be really spooky if someone just started recording you without your consent — perfectly in keeping with the Halloween spirit. Just grab a pair of glasses — or buy a cheap pair somewhere convenient — and attach a big red or white circle to one lens, mimicking the red recording light. If you want to make the costume extra creepy (or, if you can’t make a big circle sticker), you can just wear normal glasses and say that you’re ‘guy recording with the light covered up.’ Please, just don’t actually record people without their consent while you wear this costume. Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg Image Credits: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg Mark Zuckerberg wearing a vaguely unsettling T-shirt While we’re at it, Mark Zuckerberg’s fashion has been pretty recognizable lately. He’s been wearing a lot of slightly oversized, boxy black T-shirts. It may be hard to replicate the black-text-on-black-shirt style he gravitates toward, but you could attach a piece of paper to yourself that says “Building is my love language.” If you feel confident in your Latin pronunciation, you could go for something actually scary, like the time he wore a shirt that said “Aut Zuck aut nihil,” which means “Either Zuck or nothing.” It’s a little ominous. Photographer: Minh Connors/Bloomberg Image Credits: Minh Connors/Bloomberg / Getty Images An AI usage limit notification For some people, there’s nothing scarier than running out of Claude tokens. Grab a piece of cardboard, print out screenshots of notifications telling you that you’ve reached your usage limit, and go spook some vibe-coders. I’ve illustrated this idea using an edited stock photo. You don’t have to dress like you work at Hot Topic — that’s just the model in the image. Image Credits: 4×6 / Getty Images A PHP vulnerability The scary PHP-opocalypse is fresh in our memory — it was only last week that AI unearthed critical PHP flaws that could’ve been catastrophic for the internet. The fear that web developers felt is still palpable, making it a good Halloween costume: You are a PHP vulnerability. Here’s what you’re going to do. Buy a T-shirt and a sharpie, and write PHP on it. Keep it simple. What about the vulnerability part? You’re going to have to commit to the bit. All night, you’re going to talk to your friends about your feelings. Actually bare your emotions. Talk about how your recent loss of a loved one made you remember how fragile life can be. If making yourself vulnerable kills the vibe, just pretend it was part of the Halloween costume and that you’re really cool and fun and never feel sad ever. Image Credits: Tatsiana Volkava / Getty Images Bryan Johnson The costume explains itself. Bryan Johnson, a second time Couples costume alert! Maybe you have more than one Halloween party to go to this weekend, but you want your various costumes to stick to a specific theme. Once you’ve got your sleepy time getup sorted, it’s time to prep your second costume portraying the controversial biohacker : GLP-Bryan. Johnson wrote on X earlier this year: “I frequently lay on top of Kate with all of my bodyweight. The deep pressure calms her nervous system, quiets racing thoughts, and releases oxytocin which lowers cortisol. We call it GLP-Bryan.” Naturally, people were confused, so he shared an image to demonstrate. Yes, this will be hard to reproduce as a Halloween costume, but if you’ve run out of time to buy anything, this one will do. Just wear a T-shirt and jeans, which you probably already own. It will be weird to lie on top of your partner in the middle of a party. Really weird. But that’s what you get for waiting until now to figure out a costume. lmk if you want a video demo https://t.co/9g95g9y7D3 pic.twitter.com/FiYjSs86nm — Bryan Johnson (@bryan_johnson) September 24, 2026

title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom
abstract: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again. A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027. Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it. Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, revenue grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. Meta s also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank . It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. The Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

title: Zest’s new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text
abstract: Zest , the restaurant discovery app that launched earlier this year, is already thinking about a future where mobile apps are no longer the primary interface. On Thursday, the startup introduced a new feature: a personal AI-powered “restaurant concierge” that lives in your text messages, similar to other popular AI agents like Instinct or Poke. The launch reflects a broader shift in how startups are thinking about AI, as conversational AI agents take on tasks that had previously required users to launch stand-alone mobile apps. For Zest, that means bringing its restaurant recommendations into texts, then allowing users to immediately take the next step of booking a table. “The agent is the product now,” explains Zest founder and CEO Mario Gomez-Hall. “You text it, and it answers from your own history and your friends’. It doesn’t need weeks of conversation to learn you because it starts from where you’ve actually been,” he said. Image Credits: Zest Originally founded in November 2024, with $1.8 million in pre-seed backing from Alexis Ohanian at 776 and Steve Jang at Kindred Ventures, the app’s unique feature is that it links up with users’ credit cards to track where they’re actually eating out to get a sense of their tastes and interests. With this data on hand, Zest can make tailored suggestions of what places you might like to try next, whether that’s in your own city or suggestions of places to try when you’re traveling. The credit card data used by Zest’s app is imported via the financial services company Plaid , which is used by banks and other fintech and budgeting apps. Zest says it focuses only on those transactions in the food and drink categories when making its personalized map and lists. The startup’s latest idea is to tackle the same problem — where should I go to eat? — from a new angle. It will now make its suggestions from inside a text message thread and can turn to AI to do things like check availability and make the reservation for you through connected services like OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms. Image Credits: Zest To work, users will text the Zest concierge at (212) 470-6067. What’s even better is that Zest can be dropped into a group chat, where it can blend everyone’s tastes to find places the whole group will love. Here, it can also settle indecision with an in-thread voting feature and then can book a table for the group without leaving the conversation. Users can ask Zest for recommendations based on a number of factors, like cuisine, craving, occasion, dietary restrictions, or neighborhood, and can ask questions about the restaurants, like how busy the place may be, or whether it offers Wi-Fi, and more. Plus, you can ask Zest to send you the menu to help you make a decision. In TechCrunch’s tests, the AI worked fairly well, offering a list of suggestions for new places matched to our tastes that also fit particular conditions, like time of day, party size, location, and other factors. While finding an open table is something other apps have offered for years, there’s a convenience factor in being able to just text back and forth about the various options and have it tell you the available booking times. The company began testing the concierge last month, but decided to hold the launch until it could add the booking capabilities; over time, the startup is considering moving Zest beyond restaurants to offer recommendations for businesses, shopping, and more. By shifting to texts, Zest hopes the company can scale beyond its initial thousands of users and generate revenue. “Booking and ordering are the first revenue lines. Zest books your table through OpenTable or Resy today, with food ordering coming, and there are transactions there to participate in,” said Gomez-Hall. “The reason that gets interesting is that Zest learns your taste faster than a general assistant does, because it starts from where you’ve actually been instead of asking you questions. That’s worth something well beyond dinner,” he added.

title: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
abstract: Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications. After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite. A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally. The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools. Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation. If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links. Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites. Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable. In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles. Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth. Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.

title: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns that the AI boom is ‘a great opportunity to go deceive people’
abstract: “ You Can See Everything ,” the documentary capturing disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes’ final weeks before prison, is sparking national conversation as it becomes one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time. The film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, intentionally refuses to characterize Holmes as a master manipulator or victim, instead highlighting her uncanny, almost hypnotic knack for making people pity her, even when they’re well aware of her crimes . Tyler Shultz didn’t need to see “You Can See Everything” to make up his mind about Holmes. Shultz, whose first job out of college was at Theranos, was a key whistleblower who exposed the company’s dangerously inaccurate blood testing devices, which made their way into Walgreens stores and delivered faulty results to real patients. (Theranos reached a peak valuation of around $10 billion despite its technology never actually working — the company only used its own machines for a fraction of tests , instead outsourcing others to third-party equipment.) There is little reason to keep talking about Holmes — her case is closed, and she’s in federal prison — but her con-artistry has fascinated the media ( myself included ) for the last decade. In fact, as Shultz says in an interview with The San Francisco Standard, “the only reason we’re talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is because she wants us to be talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now.” But the cautionary tale of Theranos takes on a new significance as we enter the peak of the AI era, when companies that have never turned a profit are raising capital at trillion-dollar valuations. “I think the days of having a thirty-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over. Elizabeth took that model and scaled it to $100 million,” Shultz told SF Standard . His grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury George Shultz, was a notable investor and board member himself. “I believe that what [Holmes] did was raise the biggest angel round of funding of all time, but even at the smaller levels, I think investors need to recognize that when they put that type of money in someone’s hands, they are giving them tremendous power,” he added. Theranos’ funding often came from individual investors like the DeVos and Walton families, rather than venture firms. Theranos did not share scientific information or evidence that its machines worked with potential investors, citing concerns about revealing trade secrets, which warded off many top venture capitalists in Silicon Valley. At the time Theranos’ fraud was uncovered, it was seen as a shrill wake-up call for investors that they need to prioritize due diligence. But in the AI era, Shultz worries that investors may forget these lessons. “A huge danger with AI is that I think it is really hard to do due diligence on it,” he said. “It’s really hard to tell the difference between what is something truly unique and new versus like, a ChatGPT wrapper… If you want to deceive people, I think this is a great opportunity to go deceive people.” The first question posed by “You Can See Everything” lies in the premise of the movie itself. Why would a mother of two young children choose to invite a film crew to follow her final days with her family before surrendering to serve a prison sentence of over 11 years? The film poses questions that seem inscrutable, but this one seems pretty clear. She wants people to pity her, because this pity could be more useful for her future endeavors than hate or mockery. In the film, we see Holmes and her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, working on Haemanthus , a diagnostics company that they call “Theranos 2.0,” which has reportedly raised about $20 million in funding. “You Can See Everything” doesn’t make Holmes look good, but it also glosses over the more heinous crimes of Theranos, like giving dangerously faulty medical information to real patients, or even its targeted harassment of Shultz himself when he was attempting to sound the alarm about his former employer. In the cultural zeitgeist, Holmes remains more of a joke than a persona non grata. “I have this feeling of unease about what might come next,” Shultz said. “She’s certainly preparing and beginning her second act, and I don’t know exactly where it’s going to go.”

title: DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents
abstract: There’s a big uproar about AI agents taking over commerce and orders, but that might not be the case just yet. Delivery company DoorDash revealed during its third-quarter earnings call that it has only seen “several hundred” orders from third-party agents like Muse, Instinct, Fo, and others. For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily. “I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst’s questions about the topic. “What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents,” he said. Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash’s app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents. DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent it launched in September , a CLI agent introduced in July , and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched in June, which allows users to place orders through prompts and photos . The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering. The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors .

title: Can AI data centers be mass-produced like cars? This startup aims to find out
abstract: AI infrastructure company Runware is making news again, just months after unveiling the Sonic Inference Pod, a modular data center built in a factory and shipped to customers ready to install. Now the company has bigger plans. It told TechCrunch it wants to build a factory that assembles these pods on a production line, as if they were cars. The idea isn’t entirely new. Companies like Crusoe and Schneider Electric also sell prefabricated pods, but Runware says it can ship its pods faster. Flaviu Radulescu, co-founder and CEO of Runware, told TechCrunch that the company plans to scale production at its Romania-based factory to 30 megawatts of data center capacity per day by 2028, or nearly 1 gigawatt per month. That’s a whole lot of capacity: At that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year, about 10 gigawatts . But it also reflects an industrywide push to deploy data centers faster and more efficiently. Nvidia announced, for example, the Vera Rubin AI factories and the DSX POD earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one. Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year. Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said. The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.” Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion , which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December. “Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.” Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said. Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google. The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.” Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said. “Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added.

title: You don’t need to believe in a god to get a religious exemption from using AI at work
abstract: Pope Leo XIV has decried AI as a threat to human dignity , but it’s not just the devoutly faithful who might worry about how AI squares with their beliefs. David Durman, a nontheistic humanist, recently secured a religious exemption from using AI in the workplace. “Humanism is a collection of beliefs about the human experience and how humans interact with the world,” Durman, a University of Kentucky administrator, told TechCrunch. It centers on “human well-being and flourishing, both individually and collectively … and implores a person to try to improve both their well-being and their flourishing as well as the others around them.” As he watched AI grow more popular in daily life, Durman sought out the American Humanist Association (AHA) — a nonprofit advancing secular humanism — to investigate how he could gain legal protections against having to use AI at work. He believes that using the technology runs counter to his beliefs. “The way we become moral actors for ourselves and for others is through the active application of our minds, and the diminishing of that [through AI use] is going to necessarily have a negative impact on our ability to do so,” he said, reflecting on how overreliance on AI might affect critical thinking. In a statement published by the AHA earlier this week, Durman wrote, “AI is interfering with people’s ability to earn a living, the environmental costs spell disaster for humanity and our planet, and its supplanting and theft of human creativity threaten elements of our culture like art and literature that make society flourish.” Humanism is not anti-religious, but it tends to appeal to people who are skeptical of a god or other supernatural power yet still seek a scientific and moral framework to ground themselves in. “Concern about AI and human dignity can run through several different faiths and traditions, whether that’s Catholic teachings, or Universalism, or Humanism, and we want Humanists or nontheists to know that they fall into these categories — that they are also protected by the law at work,” Alexandria Huiskens, staff attorney at the AHA, told TechCrunch. Durman is the first humanist to secure workplace accommodations that allow him to abstain from AI use, and one of the first people to publicly discuss their pursuit of these protections. He was inspired to seek them when he read that Erin Maus , a Unitarian Universalist and software engineer, was able to secure similar protections for herself. “For me, this was about me and my convictions,” Durman said. “I’m obviously not trying to tell people how to think or feel … But I do hope that it encourages people who have similar concerns to pursue not necessarily religious exemption, but pursue their concerns to the best of their ability where they feel is the most appropriate.” University of Kentucky spokesperson Jay Blanton told TechCrunch that the institution reviews requests for religious accommodations on an individual basis, considering the employee’s job responsibilities and the circumstances of the request. “In this case, the university determined that an accommodation could be provided while allowing the employee to continue performing the essential functions of their position,” Blanton said in a statement. “As technology and job responsibilities evolve, accommodations may be reviewed to ensure they remain reasonable and workable.” Maus’ situation is especially unusual, since it has become rare for software engineers to write code without any AI assistance. But in Durman’s administrative role, in which he supports researchers applying for grants, he has not been required to use AI at work. Like many workers across fields, some of his colleagues and leadership have recommended that employees try out these tools, so he sought to secure his exemption now, in case the suggestion becomes a mandate in the future. “I hope that if [others] have similar feelings, that they feel encouraged to pursue some kind of resolution,” Durman said.

title: AWS will be a $1T business, Jassy says — but first, it will spend big
abstract: Andy Jassy has made it known that he believes AWS can be a trillion-dollar revenue business. During Amazon’s quarterly earnings call on Thursday, he repeated this ambition. “What we’re building at Amazon is unlike anything that’s ever been seen before. There has never been a business with a trillion dollars of annual revenue,” he said. However, before the cloud business gets there, Amazon is going to have to ramp up its capital expenditures to build out the infrastructure necessary to support that blossoming business. “We still expect 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion — the majority for AWS — and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027, with a clear line of sight to attract its financial returns,” Jassy revealed on Thursday. Amazon’s big spending on its AI infrastructure buildout has been an ongoing source of concern for investors this year. Indeed, during Thursday’s call, Wall Street analysts repeatedly asked Jassy to explain the spending, the signals that the growth really will come, and the profit margins expected. Jassy told them it was all money well spent because the e-commerce giant planned to capitalize on a historic moment in global cloud demand driven by AI. AWS revenue increased 39% from the year-ago quarter, a trend of steady growth for the sixth straight quarter . And the CEO forecast that it would increase by 40% not just next year, but in 2028, too. “AWS is a $184 billion annualized revenue run-rate business, and yet the opportunity remains extraordinary,” Jassy enthused. “With our continued pace of innovation, new core and AI functionality, enterprises wanting to run their core and AI workloads in AWS, and the amount of capacity that we’re adding each year, we believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each 2027 and in 2028, and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years.” Jassy added that the company was “in the very early days” of AI adoption by the enterprise and said that, so far, the “strategy is working.” Later, when questioned why the investment needed to grow AWS was so substantial, Jassy characterized the AI boom as a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity” that required, and was worth, such a big financial commitment now. “We’re going to invest to continue being the leader,” he said. “We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue.” Investors, however, remained concerned. Shares were down about 6% on Thursday in after-market trading. The AI boom has been a mixed blessing for the cloud industry, since the AI services that undergird the boom are supported by cloud infrastructure. Like Amazon, other cloud providers are spending big but also earning big. Microsoft, for instance, just posted yet more record-breaking revenue growth, driven largely by its cloud business. It, too, has spent a bundle .

title: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
abstract: AI News Tech Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.﻿ As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Oct 30, 2026, 8:48 PM UTC Image: Justin Sullivan / Getty Images Part Of RAM price hikes: the latest on the global memory shortage see all updates Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI’s impact on math , Altman said: “A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time. You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.” Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box or the new touchscreen MacBook Pro , the outcome is the same. Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years. And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are getting more expensive right now. title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
abstract: Tech AI News The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers. The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers. by Emma Roth Oct 30, 2026, 8:26 PM UTC Illustration by Cath Virginia / The Verge | Photos from Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable . With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually. The shared “policy token” signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website’s robots.txt file , which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training. Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company. The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models. Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default . OpenAI , Google , Microsoft , and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token. Microsoft, however, will offer more granular controls that will give publishers the ability to opt out of AI training or AI grounding , the process of pointing an AI model to a verified source of information to reduce hallucinations. Microsoft notes that websites will still appear in Bing’s search results regardless of their preferences. While Anthropic has already adopted the signal, Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year. OpenAI says it will implement it in the “coming months.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth
abstract: Tech AI News Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth The Project Suncatcher satellite generated a haiku about being in space. The Project Suncatcher satellite generated a haiku about being in space. by Emma Roth Oct 30, 2026, 6:21 PM UTC Image: Google Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Google’s AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space: Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Google says it tried out other space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts as well. The test is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google launched the satellite into orbit earlier this month . “Next, we will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit,” Google says. “Verifying our TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space paves the way for our next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
abstract: AI News Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru The coffee chain aims to ‘recognize’ customers as they arrive. The coffee chain aims to ‘recognize’ customers as they arrive. by Emma Roth Oct 30, 2026, 5:38 PM UTC Photo by: Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images﻿ Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Starbucks could eventually show you a personalized digital menu when you pull up to the drive-thru. During an earnings call on Thursday , Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said the company is going to explore “experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless,” as spotted earlier by More Perfect Union . It sounds similar to the technology that Taco Bell is experimenting with , which could change the layout, content, and visuals on a digital menu board “on a car-by-car basis.” McDonald’s also r ecently showed off an AI-powered feature it’s piloting at a handful of drive-thrus, allowing its “ArchIQ” chatbot to identify repeat customers and let them order their “usual.” Starting in 2027, Starbucks will also begin testing background AI models at the drive-thru to help baristas “input orders more accurately and efficiently,” according to Niccol. The company also plans to integrate AI into the Starbucks app’s search and discovery features, and may allow “conversational and agentic” ordering in the future. Starbucks has already started allowing customers to place orders through ChatGPT , and also rolled out an AI-powered Green Dot Assist that employees can use to ask questions about things like recipes and service standards. It’s still not clear how soon we can expect to see personalized digital menu boards at Starbucks, but Niccol says it’s still “early,” adding that “we’ll test, learn, and scale what works.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Pope Leo calls for the disarmament of AI: ‘Machines are tools, not persons’
abstract: AI News Policy Pope Leo calls for the disarmament of AI: ‘Machines are tools, not persons’ UN member states should take steps to ban ‘lethal autonomous weapons,’ Pope Leo says. UN member states should take steps to ban ‘lethal autonomous weapons,’ Pope Leo says. by Emma Roth Oct 30, 2026, 2:58 PM UTC Photo by Ernesto Ruscio/Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Pope Leo XIV says AI systems should be “disarmed,” adding that humans “have the responsibility to guide, change and, when necessary, reject its applications.” In Friday’s Papal Address , Pope Leo encourages United Nations member states to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons” during their meeting in Geneva next month. The address reflects many of the ideas Pope Leo laid out in his first major papal document in May, which highlighted “safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence.” In line with his encyclical, Pope Leo tells participants that “Machines are tools, not persons,” and warns about the dangers of granting AI systems rights or legal personhood. “Decisions affecting human life, freedom, and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed, and responsible human oversight,” Pope Leo says. In 2024, Pope Francis similarly called for a ban on autonomous weapons, saying, “No machine should ever choose to take the life of a human being.” AI has become a popular topic for Pope Leo, who suggests he chose his name because he must confront advances in the technology — similar to how Pope Leo XIII presided over the church at the forefront of the Industrial Revolution. Pope Leo closes out his address by calling for international institutions to safeguard the common good from AI-related risks, along with “shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability so that decisions concerning the development and use of AI can be examined, challenged when necessary, and accompanied by appropriate remedies for any harm caused.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Silicon Valley wants you to invest in miracles
abstract: AI Business Report Silicon Valley wants you to invest in miracles Anthropic’s S-1 is a new milestone in Big Tech’s sprawling and lofty promises to Wall Street. Anthropic’s S-1 is a new milestone in Big Tech’s sprawling and lofty promises to Wall Street. by Ellen Thomas Oct 30, 2026, 1:11 PM UTC Image: The Verge / Adobe Stock Part Of Fall 2026 earnings watch see all Investing in any stock is kind of like gambling in the sense that you’re betting your money on a company’s future performance. But how do you bet on a technology that could, in the worst-case scenario, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” or best case, “bring forth an age of miracles”? To some extent, Anthropic suggests in a letter at the top of its S-1 filing, you have to just believe. Anthropic’s 335-page S-1 prospectus, filed Monday, is part of a steady hype escalation in Silicon Valley’s interactions with Wall Street. In some ways, it’s not even that bizarre; SpaceX IPO’d in June after filing an S-1 that referenced dinosaurs and “colonizing Mars.” But its sweeping language and sheer volume — including 94 pages of risk factors — is a sometimes overwhelming collision of AI industry rhetoric and a hard financial pitch. Out-of-this-world promises are integral to Anthropic’s survival as a company . That doesn’t make reading the S-1 any less surreal. In the letter, Anthropic’s founders urge prospective stock owners “not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.” The march toward advanced AI “is one of the seminal moments in human history,” the letter says. “Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles.” But the S-1 warns that if things go wrong, the consequences could be disastrous — even an “existential” risk to humanity. Many dangers are laid out in exhaustive detail, including risks that models “behave in ways that no user or developer intended,” leading to “catastrophic” incidents that the entire insurance industry couldn’t afford to underwrite. Tech startups preparing to go public haven’t always used the information overload approach. “In 1980, a highly touted company called Apple Computer went public. Its prospectus, which I have, is 47 pages long with zero risk factors,” said Jay R. Ritter, a professor at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business. “If you go back and read it, it’s incredibly simple.” Ritter pointed to Facebook’s S-1 filing as a turning point. The company now known as Meta filed a 200-page prospectus with 22 pages of risk factors. CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s letter to investors was a manifesto on his move-fast-and-break-things approach to growth, which he dubbed “The Hacker Way.” While the idea might be to cover all possible bases, “a problem with this bloat is that it’s become more and more difficult to find the nuggets of what’s important,” Ritter said. “You know, I don’t know if you’re like me, but the longer it is, the less inclined I am to read it.” Anthropic’s founders explain in their investor letter that oversharing is part of their “anti-sell” strategy, designed to attract long-term investors who believe in their vision. “It is very dangerous when people buy your company’s stock based on expectations you cannot fulfill or on incorrect predictions about how you will behave. This is in fact very similar to one of Anthropic’s guiding principles: underpromise and overdeliver,” the founders’ letter says. Some of the statements in Anthropic’s S-1 read as surprising admissions. “We may make forward investments that may seem irresponsibly large,” for instance, or “model safety, interpretability, alignment, and welfare may lead us to limit or delay the deprecation of older models.” Maybe none of this should be surprising, considering the founders do warn readers about the company’s policy of practicing “radical honesty.” Anthropic’s ‘radical honesty’ includes being open about the prospects of human extinction This policy led to the biggest jumpscare of the whole filing, on page 46: “Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Followed quickly by: “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.” Anthropic has famously been a proponent of doomsday AI scenarios. CEO Dario Amodei has said there’s an up to 25 percent chance that further AI development could lead to human extinction. The heart of Anthropic’s pitch — or anti-sell — is that despite the risks, it is absolutely committed to developing safe and secure AI technology. After all, it will go public as a public benefit corporation, a type of business entity that, unlike C-corporations that are required to maximize shareholder value, must prioritize a social mission alongside shareholder interests. “Powerful AI” — Anthropic’s term for hypothetical future AI that surpasses collective human intelligence — is presented in the company’s S-1 as inevitable. If this technology is coming no matter what, then Anthropic, a public benefit corporation, should lead the charge. But Anthropic will need a lot of money, possibly an unlimited amount, to do this. And more practically, as Liz Lopatto has written , powerful AI (in the form of dramatic recursive self-improvement) might be about the only way Anthropic can stay ahead of the competition and survive. “All of us have a sincere conviction that the AI exponential will generate so much value, that, in the long run, it will far outweigh any shorter-term economic sacrifices we make as part of our mission,” the letter says. For all the information the company made available in its S-1, there are some gaps. Crucial information that could be used to assess profitability — third quarter results, for instance — is missing. Anthropic saw explosive revenue growth in the second quarter, but the second quarter was also the height of tokenmaxxing , which could have led to a surge in sales. Some corporate executives have warned that AI costs are surging out of control. While Anthropic’s operating losses narrowed in the second quarter, the S-1 also revealed hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations to secure the computing power it says it needs to keep growing. It also said it will start building its own data center infrastructure, a costly move that would eat into profit. Ritter thinks Anthropic will likely share its third quarter results the closer it gets to an IPO date. And besides, he added, “nobody knows” what will happen once a company goes public, including the company itself. It’s all a gamble in that sense. Anthropic isn’t WeWork… although never making money is on its list of risk factors, of course “For its first 22 years, Apple was largely a failure as far as investors were concerned,” Ritter said. “In its first three years, it greatly underperformed the market. And now it’s worth what, $5 trillion?” When WeWork filed its S-1 in 2019, it was skewered for using lofty rhetoric. A line about the company’s aim to “elevate the world’s consciousness” was especially roasted. That was different, Ritter said. WeWork was “a money-losing real estate company pretending to be a tech company at a ridiculously high valuation.” “There was no chance of ever making huge profits in the future.” Technically, that’s a risk for Anthropic too. It’s on page 63 of the S-1. “We have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.” Then again, this is the age of miracles.

title: Sam Altman sympathizes with mathematicians, but says OpenAI’s math onslaught won’t stop
abstract: AI News Science Sam Altman sympathizes with mathematicians, but says OpenAI’s math onslaught won’t stop Altman says OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions on math — and has more discoveries up its sleeve. Altman says OpenAI has spent hundreds of millions on math — and has more discoveries up its sleeve. by Robert Hart Oct 30, 2026, 1:01 PM UTC Image: The Verge Part Of All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics see all updates Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . After months of bombarding mathematicians with a relentless stream of AI-generated results, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he sympathizes with researchers struggling to make sense of it all. But he has no intention of stopping — and hints there could be much more to come from the company’s stockpile of discoveries. “I think, on net, the world deserves to understand how the universe works,” Altman said during an episode of the Cheeky Pint podcast released Thursday. “But I do have empathy for the method.” His comments mark one of the first times the OpenAI chief has directly acknowledged the company’s impact on mathematicians, following a string of genuinely impressive AI-generated results whose chaotic , poorly communicated rollouts have left researchers bewildered and struggling to keep up, even amid widespread excitement about AI’s potential as a tool for discovery. Altman argued that the public’s right to new scientific knowledge “outweighs” the disruption caused by OpenAI’s releases, though he acknowledged the company needs to improve how it communicates its findings. “I feel unequivocal on this point: Humanity deserves fundamental knowledge, and we should not be sitting on a major fundamental science discovery,” he said. “The world deserves that.” Mathematicians speaking to The Verge have repeatedly criticized OpenAI for how it announces its results, citing inadequate attribution, little context, and insufficient verification. Researchers say this has left them doing the painstaking work of checking and making sense of their findings even as the company presses ahead with more. This month alone, OpenAI has released hundreds of mathematical results , often with little more than brief writeups that researchers have described as poorly written and hard to follow. Yet OpenAI is now facing criticism for doing precisely what Altman says it should not be: sitting on potentially significant findings. Mathematicians and scientists speaking to The Verge this week said they are frustrated by what they see as OpenAI’s gatekeeping of research , following the announcement of three major breakthroughs in mathematics, physics, and computer science. Details for one of the claimed results — involving Yang-Mills theory, the mathematical foundations of modern particle physics — have not been released publicly. OpenAI says it is due to the recommendations of a hand-picked group of experts it consulted on how best to release it. The practice runs directly counter to the advice of a previous group of mathematicians the company consulted , but forms part of what the company says is a new approach to communicating its findings. On the podcast, Altman hints that OpenAI is sitting on many more mathematical discoveries than it has made public, too. Asked whether the company has more than the hundreds of proofs they have already released, Altman replied: “We do. Of course.” Altman also acknowledged that OpenAI’s pursuit of mathematical problems did “get out of control” for a short period of time, but said that was deliberate and necessary to probe the limits of its AI models. He described an internal Slack channel called “Model Name-Hold My Beer,” where employees “were just throwing that at the hardest problems they could” to see how the models would perform. Altman also estimated that OpenAI has spent in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars tackling mathematical problems, including around $10 million — “maybe a little more” — on its Navier-Stokes solution , one of mathematics’s legendary Millennium Prize problems. The spending offers a glimpse of the vast resources AI labs are bringing to bear on scientific problems, raising concerns among researchers that they may be priced out of their own fields . It looks like mathematicians and other researchers hoping for a breather may be out of luck. title: Maine’s data center revolt will decide who controls the Senate
abstract: Election 2026 AI Policy Report Maine’s data center revolt will decide who controls the Senate As tech billionaires pour record millions into Maine’s high-stakes Senate race, rural voters push back against the resource strain, rising utility costs, and phantom jobs of the AI data center boom.﻿ by Abigail Bassett Oct 30, 2026, 11:00 AM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Election 2026 AI Policy Report Maine’s data center revolt will decide who controls the Senate As tech billionaires pour record millions into Maine’s high-stakes Senate race, rural voters push back against the resource strain, rising utility costs, and phantom jobs of the AI data center boom.﻿ by Abigail Bassett Oct 30, 2026, 11:00 AM UTC Part Of All the latest updates on AI data centers see all updates Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, was midway through defending her record during the final debate of the midterms when an audience member cut her short. “I’m terrified,” a man shouted. “AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our water.” Collins brushed off the outburst, tying the man to her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. But the fear echoing through the auditorium wasn’t so easily dismissed. Just days before voters head to the polls, the rapid expansion of resource-hungry data centers has exploded into one of Maine’s most volatile campaign issues. Maine drew national headlines in April when the state Legislature passed what would have been the nation’s first statewide moratorium on large data centers — had Gov. Janet Mills not vetoed the bill 10 days later. But the fight hasn’t slowed down, with towns across the state adopting temporary moratoriums or putting the question of data center expansion to voters this November. In a September poll of Mainers by UMass Lowell and YouGov , 76 percent of respondents said they oppose building a data center in their community, with 58 percent strongly opposed. Maine’s hotly contested Senate race is set to be the most expensive Senate race per capita that the US has ever seen, with Democrats spending a projected $81 million and Republicans $114 million . Much of that campaign cash has come from the very industry Mainers and rural voters across the country have been fighting for more than a year. The outcome of the race will help determine which party controls the Senate and help shape federal data center and AI policy, impacting data center construction not just for Maine residents, but for the entire country. Cheap land, rich water Maine and other rural states are becoming prime targets for new data centers. While cities run short on land and power, Maine has abundant cheap land, vacant industrial mills and buildings, and ample access to water, thanks to its numerous rivers and waterways. Recognizing the high stakes, major tech companies and private equity firms tied to data centers and AI have invested millions in the midterms to win over skeptical locals. The issue has sparked fierce local debate, leading towns and cities across the state to enact temporary bans this summer. Molly White , the researcher, writer, and software engineer behind Tech Influence Watch , says that voters are paying a lot of attention to the issue because they connect data centers to rising costs for utilities. As White points out, many Mainers are also already feeling the pinch due to record-high heating oil costs this fall, and “they’re now looking at an election where the question is, is this candidate going to invite a data center to move in next door, and then my electricity prices go up, or the knock-on effects are going to hurt me even more when I’m already in very dire straits?” she said. White launched her site in 2024 to track crypto spending in political races, but has since expanded it to monitor AI and Big Tech investments. White says the playbook that AI and data center backers are using in the midterms is very similar to the one the cryptocurrency industry used in 2024. “There’s a lot going on in this election,” White says, “but I do think it has been a big issue in Maine and across the country, where you’ll go to a political event, you’ll see people asking questions of candidates, and AI keeps coming up. Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.” “Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.” — Molly White Data center developers and their political allies often sell rural Maine communities on long-term job creation — a promise economists say rarely materializes. In reality, economic research indicates that most data centers create virtually no net employment once construction is complete. Historically, Maine’s industry has centered around lumber and timber, shipbuilding, commercial fishing, textiles, and pulp and paper manufacturing. The timber industry contributed around $8.3 billion to Maine’s economy in 2024, but Donald Trump’s tariffs and rising operating costs have hit it hard, resulting in mill closures and layoffs. Mark Brewer , who chairs the political science department at the University of Maine, says Maine’s history complicates the debate. These former mill towns jump at the chance to rebuild their local tax bases and infrastructure, but past boom-and-bust cycles make residents cautious. “Maine has a long history of extractive industries providing jobs,” Brewer says, which allowed Mainers to tolerate these industries despite the state’s environmental focus. With data centers thus far, he says, “the jobs part of it’s not there. It’s one thing to put up with a paper mill that’s employing three shifts of 1,000 workers, right? Data centers aren’t doing that.” For many rural Mainers, the question is not only whether a data center will bring jobs back, but whether to trust the companies promising them or the government helping make the deal, said Nicholas Jacobs , the director of the Public Policy Lab at Colby College in Maine. These residents say they’re concerned about the opaque ownership of these data centers, limited long-term employment, and the risk of wealth being extracted from rural communities. Tech millions fuel Collins’ reelection war chest Tech and AI interests see an ally in Susan Collins, the 73-year-old Republican chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Like most congressional Republicans, she has largely supported data centers and AI, though she has said she believes data centers should be evaluated on an individual basis . Collins has even used her position as head of the Appropriations Committee to secure $6.2 million in federal funding for a high-performance computing hub data center in central Maine, which is designed to bolster localized AI and biotech research. Her stance has brought in a tremendous amount of campaign donations from Big Tech, AI, and data center donors for her reelection bid. Collins’ individual donors include Alex Karp, the cofounder and CEO of Palantir; Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz of VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, which heavily backs data centers; and others from Google, Meta, and Microsoft. According to White’s donation tracker , Collins has received $325,644 from AI and crypto donors. Nearly 100 billionaires have donated to Collins’ reelection bid in some form or another . “It’s one thing to put up with a paper mill that’s employing three shifts of 1,000 workers, right? Data centers aren’t doing that.” — Mark Brewer Super PACs like the Republican Senate Leadership Fund dumped nearly $42 million into ads across Maine. Elon Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund this summer , and has spent around $450 million of his own money to support Republicans in the midterms . Musk’s America PAC has spent around $2.1 million in Maine . Pine Tree Results PAC, to which Collins and her husband have personal ties, put $29.1 million into the race to support her.

title: Wikipedia’s operator says a bad AI copyright ruling could threaten the open web
abstract: Policy AI Tech Wikipedia’s operator says a bad AI copyright ruling could threaten the open web In the NYT’s case against OpenAI, the Wikimedia Foundation says training AI should be fair use — but regurgitating articles shouldn’t. In the NYT’s case against OpenAI, the Wikimedia Foundation says training AI should be fair use — but regurgitating articles shouldn’t. by Lauren Feiner Oct 30, 2026, 9:00 AM UTC Image: The Verge Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform. The Wikimedia Foundation is staking out a middle ground in a group of landmark AI copyright cases, pushing courts to legally protect large language models (LLMs) training on copyrighted work — but not chatbots regurgitating that work to users. An overly black-and-white ruling, it says, could either deprive Wikipedians of useful AI-based tools or endanger the open web. In an amicus brief filed Friday, the nonprofit behind Wikipedia weighed in on a set of lawsuits pitting publishers including The New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft, taking neither side. “Wikimedia is concerned that the parties’ positions in this case push for overbroad and simplified applications of the fair use doctrine” around AI, the organization says in its legal filing. A nuance-free victory for publishers, it fears, could let copyright holders “gatekeep” even innovative and transformative uses of their work. On the other hand, a victory for AI companies could constitute “a green light to snub licensing terms and fragment the flow of knowledge between human authors and audiences.” “Wikimedia is concerned that the parties’ positions in this case push for overbroad and simplified applications of the fair use doctrine” The ruling could be existential for Wikipedia. Wikimedia websites “have become one of the most critical sources of data for all artificial intelligence and machine learning training,” the company says in the filing. But these same systems siphon away visitors , undermining the communities that maintain these sites. Wikimedia argues that they’re also violating copyright: Services like ChatGPT reproduce text that’s licensed freely under Creative Commons, it says, but don’t adhere to the terms of that license. At the same time, it says, the LLMs that power these systems are useful to Wikipedia: They can help editors fight vandalism, detect copyright violations and doxxing, and look for articles that need improvement, among other uses. “A ruling that does not apply fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge, and stifle the development of open source technologies, ultimately impacting access to information for everyone in both cases,” Wikimedia Foundation general counsel Stephen LaPorte says in a statement. “The court needs to understand that Wikipedia is created through a collaborative process that requires a strong foundation of open and accessible human knowledge to thrive.” “A ruling that does not apply fair use principles carefully could threaten the sustainability of free knowledge” The Times argues for a more expansive definition of fair use as it applies to LLMs. It alleges , for example, that OpenAI infringed on its copyright by scraping its website to build training datasets. OpenAI and Microsoft both contend that using LLMs constitutes fair use. OpenAI has said that regurgitating work “is a rare bug.” Microsoft, in a September filing , says that expert analysis found that Copilot rarely reproduces full sentences from news content used to ground the model, which it said, “hardly undermines the transformative purpose of LLM training.” Wikimedia proposes a compromise. Scraping websites shouldn’t be considered copyright infringement, it argues, and using copyrighted works to pre-train LLMs without a license should constitute fair use when they provide “something new and different from the original sources,” according to a blog post. But if these models pull copies of material in response to user queries, then deliver it to users “while supplanting readers’ engagement with those original works,” that should require a license. The key difference is that in the latter case, AI output is simply substituting for the original work, and doesn’t transform it enough to qualify as fair use. In those cases, Wikimedia says that AI companies should respect licensing requirements to use such information. For Wikipedia, this would mean crediting the original source of information under its Creative Commons license, which also requires “any remix or adaptations” to remain under that same license. “We are taking a position in this case to defend the free and open human knowledge that Wikipedia depends on,” Wikimedia CEO Bernadette Meehan says in a statement. “Expanding access to knowledge through AI is a powerful goal, but it must respect the people, contributors, and communities that make reliable knowledge possible. Finding this balance is both a mutual benefit and a shared responsibility for the entire information ecosystem.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.
