title: nemotron-halloween
abstract:
Back to Articles nemotron-halloween Enterprise + Article Published October 30, 2026 Upvote 3 Rick Grandy rgrandy Follow nvidia Maryam Motamedi maryameee Follow nvidia Building a Haunted House with NVIDIA Nemotron Open Models Or rather… Boo! Now Get Off My Lawn! TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR , Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB , Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D , and he runs on a single workstation. I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain. That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk. How Monster House works Listening: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 ASR turns visitor speech into text. [CONFIRMED: nemotron-speech-streaming-en-0.6b.q8_0.gguf ] Thinking: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB , an open small language model for conversational agents, writes each reply. A LoRA adapter supplies the personality. Speaking: NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot voices each reply from a short reference sample of the character. Animating: NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D turns clean speech into mouth animation in Unreal Engine 5. Seeing: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni describes costumes, while YOLO and ByteTrack count and track visitors. Running it: NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent coordinates everything on one workstation with an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q and an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. A grin full of splinters The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors. A few expressions from a house with plenty to say. Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster. While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about. Teaching bad manners The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it. The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice. Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget. The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline. After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on Bolt E4B to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the BF16 checkpoint available for comparison. If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B. It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply. Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship. Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job. With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not. A voice worth waiting for Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects. A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing. median end-of-speech-to-audio with Bolt Q4 & TTS = 1.70 seconds
median end-of-speech-to-audio cached responses = 0.72 seconds
(note: speech-end detection currently waits for 300 ms of silence ) NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice” block on the UI’s tool tab. I could then read and record a sample line of text in my best happy pirate or angry pirate voice. When it’s “Go” time, Bolt E4B decides what to say, and Magpie turns that text into speech with the proper delight or despair. Next down the pipe is Audio2Face-3D and the 3d character scene I created in Epic’s Unreal Engine. The default model weights work best with a clean neutral male or female voice, not too deep, not too high (choose the appropriate gendered model for your use case). I wanted the house to have a very deep and demonic voice with echo and chamber.

title: Meet TokenEconomizer: Microsoft’s Plugin That Cuts Coding Agent Costs by Up to 30.9%
abstract: A team of researchers from Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley have released TokenEconomizer , an open-source cost controller for coding agents. TokenEconomizer is a plugin that learns from past sessions in a repository to cut waste in later ones. It works with Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI and Pi. It does not touch model weights or agent code. On 277 SWE-Bench tasks, it lowered mean cost by 18.4% to 30.9% across 5 agent-model settings. Every agent turn re-bills the system prompt, every loaded tool schema and the full history. The research team profiled 60 SWE-Bench tasks across 6 repositories using Claude Code with Opus 4.8. They found 3 recurring sources of waste: They also tested 3 fixed open-source strategies: RTK , Serena and Aider’s RepoMap . None was cheaper everywhere. All 3 cut cost on Django and raised it on SymPy. TokenEconomizer is an external controller that treats the agent as a black box. It keeps a state per repository, built from completed traces. Before each task, it sets 3 policies through the prompt, the tool settings and the event stream. An LLM proposer turns trace digests into 1-line facts, such as the working test command. Each fact carries regex detectors that check later traces without a model call. A fact enters the prompt after 3 confirmations on tasks with non-overlapping edited files. Its need rate must also stay at or above 0.4. One contradiction counts as 5 confirmations, so wrong facts retire quickly. Shell, read, write and edit tools are always kept. Other tools are masked after 3 consecutive unused tasks, or when an LLM judge marks them irrelevant. The full catalog returns every 5 tasks for a re-audit. On Django with Claude Code, the first request on task 2 fell from 43,351 to 16,295 prompt tokens. The controller learns a turn budget: 1.25 times the 90th percentile of successful run lengths. Cheap rule checks flag repeated failures or dense errors. An LLM judge then decides if the agent is stuck, at 0.7 confidence or higher. A stuck agent gets 1 redirect, then a stop if the loop recurs. Source: arXiv 2610.22732 , Table 1. Costs include all controller calls. 3 seeds per setting. Pass@1 improved in 4 of 5 settings. Lower reasoning effort saved cost but cut Pass@1 by 1.8 to 10.3 points. RTK alone raised cost in 12 of 30 repository-setting cells, and RepoMap in 15. Savings build over time. Most repositories cost more at first, but all were cheaper by the sixth task. Alone on Claude Code, tool pruning saved 13.2% to 17.7%, micro-skills 11.8% to 14.3%, and the loop guard 5.4% to 7.1%. Results also held outside SWE-Bench. Costs fell 16.0% to 21.2% on Web-Bench and 16.5% to 19.6% on CredData. ReposVul saw only 6.4% to 9.3%, because shorter runs leave less to remove. Cost rows: TokenEconomizer paper. Licenses and claims: each project’s repository or docs. The plugin needs one of the 4 agents and Python 3.10 or newer. On Claude Code, clone the repo, add it as a marketplace, then run claude plugin install tokeneconomizer@tokeneconomizer . Learned data stays local in ~/.tokeneconomizer . Tool pruning and the loop guard are on by default. Micro-skills are off by default, because the proposer adds model calls. Check out the Paper , GitHub Repo and Project Page . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Need to partner with us for promoting your GitHub Repo OR Hugging Face Page OR Product Release OR Webinar etc.? Connect with us The post Meet TokenEconomizer: Microsoft’s Plugin That Cuts Coding Agent Costs by Up to 30.9% appeared first on MarkTechPost .

title: AI Security Agents Compared: Claude, Codex, Mantis, Cloudflare
abstract: Anthropic, OpenAI, Cloudflare and Google now each ship an AI agent that hunts security bugs in source code. We checked the repos, docs and technical details behind each one. The key finding: all 4 tools converge on one design. One agent finds a bug, a separate agent tries to disprove it, and only survivors get a patch. The differences are in where they run, who can use them and how much proof they demand. The problem every one of them is solving is noise. Google’s security team writes that sloppy AI code scanning produces hallucinated bugs and true-positive rates under 7% . A scanner that is wrong 93% of the time costs reviewers more than it saves. The shared fix is separation of duties. The agent that reports a finding never gets to confirm it. Cloudflare states the rule directly in its README: the verifier is never the agent that found the bug. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google each describe a similar validation step before anything reaches a report. The second driver is offense. Anthropic team states that it built its scanner partly because attackers were already using AI models to find exploitable flaws, per The Hacker News . Google opens its Mantis post by noting that models can now discover and exploit bugs with little human help. What it is: A multi-agent vulnerability scanner that runs inside a Claude Code session. It is the local version of Anthropic’s hosted Claude Security product, per the plugin README . How it works: Agents map the architecture, build a threat model, hunt across every component and verify each finding independently. The plugin offers 3 jobs from one menu: scan the codebase, scan changes, or suggest patches, per Claude Code docs . Output: A Markdown report along with a SARIF 2.1.0 file for GitHub code scanning. Each finding carries severity, a CWE category, impact and reproduction steps. Patches are drafted in a scratch copy and land as F<n>.patch files. The plugin never commits, pushes or opens a pull request on its own. Cost and access: It makes no model calls of its own, so there is no separate API key. Scans count against your Claude plan’s usage limits. Timeline: Anthropic opened a limited preview called Claude Code Security in February 2026. The hosted product reached public beta for Enterprise customers on Claude Opus 4.7 . The Claude Code plugin entered beta on July 22, 2026, per Cybersecurity News . In August, the hosted scanner moved to Claude Mythos 5, per Dataconomy . Where it fits: Anthropic positions it as one layer. The security-guidance plugin checks code as Claude writes it, and /security-review does a single pass on a branch. Claude Security is the on-demand deep scan. What it is: A CLI and TypeScript SDK, published as @openai/codex-security, for finding, validating and fixing vulnerabilities. How it works: It scans a whole repo, selected paths, or a Git diff. A –mode deep flag runs parallel discovery workers. It validates candidate findings, generates patches and can verify existing fixes. A cs policy command drafts a SECURITY.md that tells future scans what counts as a vulnerability in your project. Output: Threat models, SARIF, JSON or CSV exports, plus publishing to Linear. It can import GitHub code-scanning alerts and suggest owners from Git history. A GitHub Action runs scheduled or pull-request scans; findings are report-only by default. Cost and access: The client is Apache-2.0, but the scanner behind it is not. DevOps.com notes the CLI and SDK stay in limited beta for approved customers. The README lists OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, OpenRouter and Fireworks AI as providers. Requires Node.js 22.13+ and Python 3.10+. What it is: An MIT-licensed skill that turns any capable coding agent into a security auditor. How it works: A 6-phase audit: Requirements: A coding agent that supports tool use and parallel sub-agents, plus Node.js for the validators. It also wants an OS-enforced sandbox with no external network. Without one, leads stay needs_validation instead of being executed. npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill –skill security-audit Then ask the agent: “security audit this codebase.” Output defaults to ~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>, outside your repo. The data behind it: Cloudflare published the skill on June 18, 2026, with its post Build your own vulnerability harness . The roughly 450-line skill seeded an internal harness that now scans 128 repos. Cloudflare reports these lifetime numbers: Better recon context cut the first-pass rejection rate from 40% to 11%. Cloudflare also uses one model for discovery and a different model for triage, so models check each other. What it is: An Apache-2.0 set of security-review skills plus an ADK reference harness for AI coding agents. Google team states that it is part of how it finds and fixes bugs internally. How it works: Mantis reads the repo’s history to learn from past security fixes. It builds a hierarchical summary tree, condensing files into directory and root summaries. Google team states that this cut token overhead by over 85% . It then generates a threat model and hypotheses, hunts, deduplicates and critiques findings. What sets it apart: Reproduction and patch verification. Mantis tries to reproduce each bug, from a static exploit sketch up to a unit test or mock server. It patches with an adversarial loop that attacks the fix. It also calibrates severity against a rubric to stop “thousands of criticals.” A mantis-advise skill then feeds what it learned back into code generation. Setup: Clone the repo and point any coding agent at it, or run the ADK harness directly. The harness supports a –focus prompt such as “look for IDOR” and a –max-tokens spend ceiling. At least 12 more agent-based vulnerability tools shipped or went public in 2026. Almost all repeat the same find-then-independently-verify loop. They split into free harnesses you run yourself and commercial or internal platforms. AppSec Santa also tracks harnesses from Anthropic (defending-code-reference-harness), Trail of Bits, Capital One (vulnhunter) and Cisco (ai-deep-sast). Cisco’s runs fully local on Foundation-Sec-8B, so no code leaves the machine. The pattern holds across vendors: deterministic engines or validators do the proving, models do the reasoning, and a human approves every fix. Cloudflare’s own architecture suggests a practical combination. Run discovery with one tool or model, then validate with a different one. Different models surface different shares of the bugs. The post AI Security Agents Compared: Claude, Codex, Mantis, Cloudflare appeared first on MarkTechPost .

title: Samaya AI Releases Sterling: A 3B-Active Finance Research Agent Model that Beats Claude Fable 5.1 on FrontierFinance at 11x Lower Cost
abstract: Samaya AI has released Samaya Sterling , a post-trained model for agentic financial research. Sterling is built on NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning , a 30B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. On Samaya’s FrontierFinance benchmark , it scores 58.9%. Claude Fable 5.1 scores 55.9%. Each Sterling question costs $0.61, against $6.89 for Fable 5.1. For developers, the takeaway is a concrete recipe: co-train a small model with its harness, and it can win in a narrow domain. Samaya Sterling is a LoRA post-trained version of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, tuned to work as a financial research agent. It plans research, calls finance tools, gathers evidence and hands findings to a separate report writer. According to Maithra Raghu’s X announcement , it started as a 2-person effort on agentic orchestration efficiency. Samaya team adapted its production finance harness for a small model. Detailed guidance was stripped from the system prompt and tool descriptions. Tools were merged to shorten the prompt. Two helper models manage context. A condenser shortens long tool results. A compactor summarizes the trace as it grows. A research budget caps how long the agent works. After that, the report writer answers from what was found. Training used LoRA on Tinker , Thinking Machines Lab’s training API. It ran in 4 stages: FrontierFinance has 220 public queries scored against expert-written rubrics. The grader uses a 3-model judge panel. Samaya team states that no benchmark question was used in training. Checkpoints were chosen on 100 internal validation questions. Sterling scores 58.9% at $0.61 and 282 s per question. Fable 5.1 scores 55.9% at $6.89 and 268 s. Samaya’s own high-effort system scores 2.9 points lower at $1.81. Every stage added quality: 42.5% (base), 51.4%, 54.8%, 57.5%, then 58.9%. Median tool calls rose from 3 to 17. In high-effort mode, Sterling reaches 60.6% at $1.83 and 372 s. On the hardest third, it rose from 31.8% to 45.2%. The model itself costs $0.04 per question. Tools and helper models make up the rest of the $0.61. FrontierFinance figures for all columns come from the Samaya blog and are self-reported. Check out the technical blog , the FrontierFinance benchmark , the dataset and the grader repo . title: Edge0 Releases Audio8-TTS-Realistic, a 0.6B Voice Cloning TTS Model
abstract: Edge0 has released Audio8-TTS-Realistic , an open-weight text-to-speech model for zero-shot voice cloning. Audio8-TTS-Realistic is a 0.6B-parameter model that clones a voice from 1 reference clip and transcript. It supports 23 languages, 12 more than its predecessor. The weights and code ship under Apache 2.0 . For developers, the catch is competitive multilingual accuracy at a size that is cheap to fine-tune and serve. It is the second 0.6B release in Edge0’s Audio8 TTS family. It builds on Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b and keeps the same Transformers inference interface. The repository bundles the checkpoint, a 44.1 kHz neural audio codec, tokenizer, processor and custom code. It can also generate speech without a reference voice. New languages are Arabic, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Malay, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Thai, Turkish and Vietnamese. The model uses a dual-autoregressive (DualAR) design inspired by Fish Audio S2 Pro . According to the technical research report , the slow branch is built on Qwen2.5 0.5B. It has 24 layers at width 896 and runs at about 21.5 frames per second. Each step predicts text tokens plus the first audio codebook. A shallow 4-layer fast branch then predicts the remaining 9 codebooks in parallel. Sequential compute therefore happens only at the frame level. The team argues that word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) miss rhythm, pauses and timing. A model can score well on both and still sound synthetic. The critic scores each output against a matched human recording of the same sentence. It was trained on a quality ladder built from 6 open-source TTS systems. These were ranked in a private blind listening study, with human recordings at the top. Synthetic pause compression adds finer rungs to the ladder. An identity-erasure loss stops the critic from rewarding generator fingerprints. The critic head has about 3M parameters on top of a frozen WavLM-large encoder. A duration penalty also kicks in beyond 1.35x the reference length. This blocks the policy from gaming the critic with slower speech. The final stage used only Chinese and English prompts. It still improved both aggregate metrics on the 13 lower-resource languages. Their error fell from 22.53% to 20.77%, and SIM rose from 0.637 to 0.679. All numbers below are self-reported error rates, where lower is better. On CV3, Audio8 beats VoxCPM2 (5.35%), CosyVoice3-1.5B (6.89%) and Qwen3-TTS-1.7B (7.73%). On MiniMax, Qwen3-TTS-1.7B scores 27.41%, but it officially supports only 10 of the 24 test languages. Larger models still lead elsewhere. Higgs TTS 3 reports 4.41% on CV3 and 2.74% on MiniMax. Qwen3-TTS-1.7B averages 1.01% on Seed-TTS. Edge0 itself calls its table a reference comparison, since evaluation pipelines and text normalization differ. VoxCPM2’s CV3 average is computed from its per-language table. Install PyTorch 2.5+ and Transformers 4.57+, then load with trust_remote_code=True . Voice cloning needs a clean reference clip and its exact transcript. The GitHub repo adds a CLI, batching and supervised fine-tuning scripts. For GPU serving, an SGLang Omni adapter provides paged attention, dynamic batching and an OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech API. Edge0 notes throughput and streaming were not benchmarked. A free Playground runs on Hugging Face ZeroGPU. Check out the Paper , Model Weights , Repo and Samples . title: Baseten Releases joey-1, a 2B Decision Model at $0.01 per 1M Tokens
abstract: Baseten has released joey-1 , a 2B model from its in-house research lab, Base Labs. The joey-1 decision model returns a label and a calibrated probability instead of generated text. It targets high-volume routing, classification and guardrail checks. Baseten prices it at $0.01 per million input tokens , with open weights on Hugging Face under MIT. joey-1 is a 2B decision model from Baseten’s Base Labs that answers typed questions in 1 forward pass. You send a state (text or images) and 1 or more questions. The model returns a probability for every option of every question. It does not write free-form text that your application must parse. joey-1 is the third member of a family. Baseten shipped mammoth-1 (27B) and elephant-1 (9B) last week. All 3 share training data and the /v1/systemone API, so switching is a 1-line change. Base Labs post-trained Qwen3.5-2B with a full fine-tune of the language model. The vision encoder stays frozen. Full-attention layers use a block-bidirectional mask. All questions are answered from 1 shared-prefix prefill, so extra questions add little cost. Training details from the model card : Calibration lets you set a confidence threshold. Uncertain answers can escalate to elephant-1, mammoth-1 or a human. Baseten reports a P50 end-to-end latency of 20 ms for an average 2,000-token request. That is about 2.5x faster than elephant-1 (49 ms). The blog’s TL;DR also claims 5x faster than comparable decision models, without naming them. Model APIs charge $0.01 per 1M input tokens; output and cached input are listed at $0.00. elephant-1 costs $0.035 and mammoth-1 costs $0.10. Baseten’s example: 10M support tickets a month at about 500 tokens each is 5B tokens. That is about $50 on joey-1, versus $500 on mammoth-1. All scores below are self-reported on Baseten’s model card . On the Jev Decision Index 0.4 public split, joey-1 scores 63.30. That ranks #37 of 230 models and is the top score under 4B. The Jev Decision Index is a community leaderboard on Hugging Face. On the same split, Cloudflare’s 27B Clef scores 61.71 and Jev 1.14 scores 60.70. joey-1 trails elephant-1 in every area. It beats Jev 1.14 in 4 of 5 areas, including language, tools and retrieval. On Baseten’s replica of the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, joey-1 scores 62.9, versus 65.9 for mammoth-1. *Jev 0.4 scores for all models come from Baseten’s joey-1 model card . **Latency figures are not comparable. Baseten measures end-to-end on its platform; Cloudflare reports its own Decision Index 0.2.1 run. You can fine-tune joey-1 on Baseten Training Jobs using the fine-tuning cookbook . joey-1 is also listed on OpenRouter at $0.01 per 1M input tokens. title: Vibe Coding a Classic Game: Building Breakout Step by Step with an AI Assistant
abstract:
Vibe Coding a Classic Game: Building Breakout Step by Step with an AI Assistant Vibe coding is a workflow where you describe what you want in natural language and let an AI agent handle code generation, execution, and iteration rather than typing every line yourself. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on October 30, 2026 in Programming Vibe coding is a genuinely new way of building software, not a rebrand of an old one, and it deserves a real definition before this tutorial uses it a hundred more times. The term was coined by Andrej Karpathy in early 2025 to describe a workflow where you describe what you want in natural language and let an AI agent handle code generation, execution, and iteration rather than typing every line yourself. It caught on fast enough that Collins English Dictionary named it their Word of the Year for 2025 , and by 2026 it's not a novelty; it's a standard way real software gets built. This article is a genuine, start-to-finish vibe coding project: building the classic arcade game Breakout , using an AI coding assistant to generate every piece, with every prompt shown, every resulting code block explained in real detail, and the complete, tested game assembled at the end. This isn't a toy example. Every line of code in this article was actually written and verified before publication; the collision physics, the win and loss conditions, all of it, ran through real automated tests rather than being assumed to work. What Is Vibe Coding? The mechanical description is simple: you describe a goal, an AI agent generates code toward it, you review and iterate, and you repeat until it does what you need. What's changed since the term appeared is the sophistication of the agents doing the generating; current tools don't just autocomplete a line, they can read an entire project, edit multiple files, run the code, and fix what breaks, all from a natural-language instruction. Airbnb, for example, reports that AI now writes around 60% of its new code . The current tool landscape is worth knowing before picking one: Claude Code is a terminal-native agent well suited to exactly this kind of project: describe a feature, and watch it write and test the code directly in your project folder Cursor is an AI-native code editor for people who want that same power inside a familiar IDE Replit Agent is built with beginners specifically in mind, and it walks through a visible plan before writing code, which is genuinely useful for understanding the "why" behind each step, not just the "what" Bolt.new and v0 are faster paths to a working prototype for people who don't want to touch a terminal at all The Game We're Building: Breakout Breakout is one of the most influential arcade games ever made, and its backstory matters because it explains why the game is structured the way it is. Atari released Breakout on May 13, 1976 , conceptualized by Nolan Bushnell and Steve Bristow as a single-player evolution of Pong, and built by a young engineer named Steve Wozniak, working alongside his friend Steve Jobs. Wozniak's design was so aggressively minimized in its chip count that Atari's own manufacturing line reportedly couldn't replicate it and had to ship a version with more components instead. The two Steves would go on to found Apple together that same year, and Breakout's hardware logic directly influenced parts of the original Apple II's design. The rules are simple enough, which is exactly why it's a good vibe coding project: complex enough to need real logic, simple enough to fully understand end to end. A wall of bricks lines the top of the screen. A ball bounces around the play area, and you control a paddle at the bottom, moving it left and right to keep the ball in play. Every time the ball hits a brick, the brick is destroyed and you score points. If the ball gets past your paddle and falls off the bottom of the screen, you lose a life. Destroy every brick, and you win; run out of lives, and the game ends. Prerequisites You need less than you'd think: a modern web browser (Chrome, Firefox, or Safari all work fine), a text editor, and one AI coding assistant. This tutorial has zero build tools, zero frameworks, and zero dependencies to install; the entire game is one HTML file that runs by opening it in a browser. Setting up Claude Code: install it with npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code , then run claude from inside an empty project folder to start a session. If you'd rather use Cursor, Replit, or another tool from the list above, every prompt below works identically; just paste it into whichever assistant you've chosen. Here's the actual build, broken into the same stages you'd naturally prompt an AI assistant through, one real capability at a time rather than asking for the whole game in one shot, which tends to produce something harder to debug when it doesn't quite work. You can find the full code in this repo . Step 1: The Canvas and Game Skeleton Prompt : "Create a single HTML file for a Breakout game. Set up an HTML5 canvas 480 pixels wide and 400 pixels tall, centered on the page, with a dark background. Add a heading, and placeholder text elements for score and lives above the canvas. Don't add any game logic yet, just the skeleton."
Score: 0 Lives: 3
What this does: the canvas element is where every visual frame of the game gets drawn; it's a blank rectangle you control at the pixel level through JavaScript. Starting with just the skeleton, no logic, is deliberate: it lets you confirm the page structure actually renders correctly before adding anything that could break. That matters more with AI-generated code than hand-written code, since it's easier to spot exactly where something went wrong when you're only checking one small piece at a time. Step 2: The Paddle Prompt : "Add a paddle: an 80x10 pixel rectangle near the bottom of the canvas. Make it move left and right with the arrow keys, and keep it from moving off either edge of the canvas." const paddle = { width: 80, height: 10, x: (canvas.width - 80) / 2, y: canvas.height - 20, speed: 7, dx: 0 }; const keys = { left: false, right: false }; document.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => { if (e.key === "ArrowLeft") keys.left = true; if (e.key === "ArrowRight") keys.right = true; }); document.addEventListener("keyup", (e) => { if (e.key === "ArrowLeft") keys.left = false; if (e.key === "ArrowRight") keys.right = false; }); function updatePaddle() { if (keys.left) paddle.dx = -paddle.speed; else if (keys.right) paddle.dx = paddle.speed; else paddle.dx = 0; paddle.x += paddle.dx; paddle.x = Math.max(0, Math.min(canvas.width - paddle.width, paddle.x)); } What this does : keydown and keyup listeners track which arrow keys are currently held, rather than reacting once per press, which is what makes the paddle move smoothly while a key is held down instead of jumping once per keystroke. The last line of updatePaddle is the boundary check; Math.max and Math.min together clamp the paddle's position so it can never move past either edge of the canvas, a one-line fix for a bug that's easy to forget entirely until you watch the paddle vanish off-screen. Step 3: The Ball and Its Physics Prompt : "Add a ball: a small circle that starts near the bottom center of the canvas and moves diagonally. Make it bounce off the left, right, and top walls." const ball = { x: canvas.width / 2, y: canvas.height - 30, radius: 6, speed: 4, dx: 3, dy: -3 }; function updateBall() { ball.x += ball.dx; ball.y += ball.dy; if (ball.x + ball.radius > canvas.width || ball.x - ball.radius < 0) ball.dx *= -1; if (ball.y - ball.radius < 0) ball.dy *= -1; } What this does : dx and dy are the ball's velocity, how far it moves on each axis every frame, and updating position by simply adding them each frame is the entire basis of the game's motion.

title: Silent Data Errors That Survive Every Cleaning Pipeline
abstract: Silent Data Errors That Survive Every Cleaning Pipeline 4 bugs that pass every null check, duplicate check, and schema test. By Nate Rosidi , KDnuggets Market Trends & SQL Content Specialist on October 30, 2026 in Data Science A quarter of organizations say poor data quality costs them more than \$5 million a year , and 7% put that number above \$25 million, a Forrester finding IBM cites in its own data quality research. Most of that damage never shows up on a dashboard. Standard cleaning catches nulls, duplicate rows, and type mismatches. Those checks run fast and catch real problems, then stop looking the moment every column passes. Four bugs clear those checks anyway and still break the model, the dashboard, or the finance report downstream: entities duplicated without ever looking identical, values that sit inside range but make no sense in context, timestamps that leak information from the future, and denominators that drop the people who would have changed the answer. Each one shows up in a real interview question on StrataScratch . Here's what we'd miss on a naive read of each question, and what to check for instead. The Syntax, Semantics, and Pragmatics Gap We can split data quality tests into three layers, borrowed from linguistics. Syntax asks whether a value is well-formed: is the zip code 5 digits, does the date parse, is the column non-null. Semantics asks whether the value makes sense for what it represents: is a 214-year-old customer possible, is a 3 am login from a store that closes at 10 pm believable. Pragmatics asks whether the same kind of value needs a different test depending on who's using it: for example, a pharma company where a drug discovery team and a manufacturing team look at the same kind of record and don't agree on what counts as valid. We see most production pipelines stop at syntax. Pandera and dbt tests (SQL queries that check data quality) default to type, null, and range checks, the ones a generic library can write without knowing the business. Semantic checks need someone who understands what the data means. That gap is where the 4 bugs below live. Silent Data Error #1: Duplicated Entities A duplicate check tests whether 2 rows are byte-for-byte identical. drop_duplicates() catches "John Smith, 123 Main St" twice, but not "John Smith, 123 Main St" and "J. Smith, 123 Main Street": 2 differently written rows for the same customer that a lifetime-value model still counts as 2 different people. The check passes because the row isn't duplicated. The entity is. This Amazon interview question asks you to do the opposite on purpose: given a worker table, output every HR employee's first name and department twice. Data: the worker table has 13 employees across HR, Admin, and Account. Code: SELECT first_name, department FROM worker WHERE department LIKE 'HR' UNION ALL SELECT first_name, department FROM worker WHERE department LIKE 'HR'; Output: The official answer is a UNION ALL . That's also what happens, unintentionally, when 2 source systems ship the same table into a warehouse with no dedup step before the join. Every SUM or COUNT downstream doubles, and no null check flags it. The same failure shows up 2 more ways on the platform, and between them the 3 examples in this section cover how duplication enters downstream metrics: duplicate rows, an entity double-counted under a coarser grain, and rows over-matched by a loose join. A Microsoft, Apple, and Dell question needs COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) for monthly active users: swap in COUNT(*) over the same table and the number changes, because 1 user firing 10 events looks like 10. The Fix to This Error The fix runs in both directions: canonicalize the string (lowercase it, strip punctuation, normalize the address), score similarity instead of testing equality, and route anything in between to a review queue. Silent Data Error #2: Impossible but Valid Values A value can sit inside its column's type, inside its declared range, and still be wrong for the row it's in. A 214-year-old customer passes an integer check; a negative delivered quantity passes a numeric check. Catching either takes a rule that knows what the number means, not its type. This Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy question asks for every manager whose salary is less than twice the average salary of the employees reporting to them, and shows how that error hides inside a normal aggregation. Data: dim_employee holds 9 employees, and map_employee_hierarchy pairs each manager_empl_id with the empl_id of a direct report. Here, we are only using some of the data from dim_employee : Code: SELECT h.manager_empl_id, managers.salary AS manager_salary, AVG(employees.salary) AS avg_employee_salary FROM map_employee_hierarchy h JOIN dim_employee managers ON h.manager_empl_id = managers.empl_id JOIN dim_employee employees ON h.empl_id = employees.empl_id GROUP BY 1, 2 HAVING managers.salary < 2 * AVG(employees.salary); Output: Nothing about this query is wrong. A single bad salary in dim_employee — zero, negative, or typed in cents instead of dollars — shifts the average and silently drops managers from the result or adds them to it. The query passed every syntax check on the way in. The bug sits in a single cell. The Fix to This Error The fix is business-aware constraints and peer-group plausibility checks, applied at ingestion. Age between 0 and 120 and order quantity greater than 0 are business constraints: they encode what's possible for the business, not just what fits the data type. Salary compared against the distribution for the same level and location, not just against 0, is the stronger check: it catches a value that's plausible on its own but wrong for the row it's in. Silent Data Error #3: Timestamp Leakage Leakage happens when a feature carries information from after the moment it's supposed to describe. Wikipedia 's definition is the cleanest one: information that would not actually be available at prediction time ends up in the training row anyway. This Microsoft question asks you to find each employee's current salary from a table with no timestamp at all, only repeated salary rows per employee, so "current salary" has to be inferred by assuming salary only goes up: the purest version of the problem. Data: ms_employee_salary has 98 rows for 76 employees, several with more than one salary on file and nothing to say which came first. Code: SELECT id, first_name, last_name, department_id, salary FROM ( SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER ( PARTITION BY id ORDER BY salary DESC, department_id DESC ) AS rn FROM ms_employee_salary ) s WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY id ASC; Output: That ROW_NUMBER() trick is the right answer here. It's also what a warehouse does when ingesting a slowly changing dimension with no effective-dated column: "most recent" becomes a guess, and any feature joined on employee_id downstream inherits it. Use that inferred "current" salary to recreate a prediction made 6 months earlier, and the historical row gets information from its own future. That's the leak. A related Amazon question is a time-window bug, not a leakage bug: users with a second purchase 1 to 7 days after their first, ignoring same-day purchases. Swap that strict BETWEEN 1 AND 7 for a loose <= 7 , and same-day, multi-item baskets start counting as returning users, a retention number inflated by rows that were never a second visit. The query sets its own definition of "return visit" here; no future information reaches the model. The Fix to This Error The fix is structural: store both when an event happened and when the row was written, and join features with a strict event_time <= feature_time inequality, never a bare MAX() . Silent Data Error #4: Survivorship Bias Survivorship bias is a denominator problem: the rows that would tell you the truth were removed before your query ran. The classic case is hedge fund index returns calculated only over funds still trading, dropping every fund that closed.

title: The AI Skills That Actually Show Up in Job Postings Right Now
abstract: The AI Skills That Actually Show Up in Job Postings Right Now Which AI skills appear most often in job postings right now, and what do they mean for your career? By Vinod Chugani on October 29, 2026 in Career Advice Spend any time on a job board right now and you'll see AI mentioned everywhere. But there's a gap between what shows up as a vague requirement and what employers are actually screening for, and that gap matters if you're trying to build marketable skills rather than just adding buzzwords to your resume. This article draws on data from several large-scale analyses of job postings in 2025 and 2026 to show which AI skills appear most consistently, how demand breaks down by role type, and what that means for where you should focus your time. Why the Numbers Are Moving So Fast Here's the number to start with: an analysis of more than 360,000 job postings collected between late 2025 and mid-2026 found that AI is now the second most requested skill across all roles, appearing in roughly one in five postings. It ranked behind only communication, and ahead of Python, SQL, and cloud platforms like AWS. That alone would be notable. What makes the pattern more striking is the rate of change. Dice analyzed seven million U.S. tech job postings and found that AI skill requirements jumped from 15% of postings in January 2024 to 75% by mid-2026. Lightcast data cited by the Bipartisan Policy Center found that postings explicitly requiring AI-related skills increased 144% year over year. In data and analytics roles specifically, AI appears in close to 45% of postings. The takeaway: AI fluency is moving from a differentiator to a baseline expectation, and it's moving faster than most people's skill-building timelines. The Skills Employers Are Naming, by Category Not all AI skills carry equal weight, and demand isn't uniform across role types. Looking at the data, four broad categories emerge. AI Literacy and Prompt Engineering AI literacy is the most widely requested category and covers the broadest population of workers. It means a general understanding of what AI tools can and cannot do, how to use them effectively at work, and how to evaluate their outputs critically rather than just accepting them. Prompt engineering sits within this category and has seen dramatic growth. Dice found it among the fastest-growing AI skills by year-over-year demand, at 253% growth. LinkedIn 's 2026 labor market report showed that U.S. jobs requiring AI literacy skills, including prompt engineering, grew 70% year over year. Across the broader job posting dataset, prompt engineering shows up in 7% of all postings, ChatGPT proficiency in 6%, and large language model familiarity in 4%. One caveat: employers aren't hiring standalone prompt engineers. The skill appears most often as one component within a broader role — the same way Excel proficiency or internet research became baseline expectations rather than job titles. The most valuable position in most fields is what some workforce analysts call "prompting plus something," where the AI skill amplifies domain expertise rather than replacing it. Agentic AI and Workflow Automation This is the fastest-growing category by rate of change, though it's still concentrated in technical roles. Stanford's 2026 AI Index found that the share of AI job postings mentioning agentic AI rose from 0.69% to 18.9% in a single year. Dice's analysis of seven million postings shows that demand for agentic AI grew 587% year over year, with AI agents themselves growing 503%. What this looks like in practice: employers are increasingly looking for people who understand how AI systems can be configured to take sequences of actions autonomously, often using tools like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector databases, and agent orchestration frameworks. A 2026 analysis of 390 AI engineer postings found that 56% mentioned AI evaluation, 50% mentioned AI agents, and 26% required experience with RAG specifically. For non-technical professionals, the relevant takeaway isn't that you need to build these systems. It's that familiarity with what agentic workflows are and what they can accomplish has become expected in roles that work alongside engineering teams. Machine Learning Foundations Machine learning remains the most consistently requested foundational technical skill across the full history of AI hiring, even as newer categories grow faster from a smaller base. Roles requiring machine learning knowledge are concentrated in engineering, data science, and research, but the terminology appears far more broadly. What's shifted in 2026 is the specificity of requests. Earlier postings often listed machine learning as a general requirement. Current postings more frequently ask for experience with particular parts of the machine learning lifecycle: model evaluation, fine-tuning, and machine learning operations (MLOps) — the infrastructure and processes needed to move machine learning systems from experimentation into production. Data engineering, which involves building the pipelines and storage systems that feed machine learning models, currently tops recruiter search data from platforms like SignalHire , ahead of both AI engineering and data science roles. This demand reflects a practical constraint: companies that have invested in AI capabilities often hit bottlenecks at the data layer before they ever get to the modeling layer. AI Governance, Ethics, and Responsible AI This category sits in a complicated place in the data. On one hand, it appears in LinkedIn's 2026 Skills on the Rise report as a top priority for business-side hiring. Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index found that nearly half of corporate interactions with AI assistants are now focused on cognitive work like analysis, evaluation, and strategic thinking, which raises the stakes around governance frameworks for those outputs. On the other hand, actual job posting data tells a quieter story: AI governance and responsible AI terms each appear in only around 1.5% of postings, and employer adoption has been slower than you might expect given how broadly AI is now deployed. The World Economic Forum estimates that 22% of current jobs will shift structurally by 2030, which raises compliance and ethics questions that most organizations haven't yet built systematic hiring pipelines to address. Practically speaking, governance skills are unlikely to be why someone gets hired initially, but they're increasingly what separates candidates at senior and principal-level roles. Qarera 's analysis found that AI skill requirements appear in 39.5% of principal-level postings, roughly double the overall average. How Demand Differs Across Functions One of the more important shifts in the 2026 data is where AI skill requirements are showing up outside of technical roles. Lightcast found that 51% of job postings requiring AI skills sit outside IT and computer science, across sectors including healthcare, finance, marketing, and human resources. In product management roles specifically, AI appeared as a required skill in 37% of postings in Qarera's dataset. For design roles, the figure was 23.1%, and for business analyst roles, 19.1%. These aren't engineering roles, and the AI skills being requested aren't engineering skills. They reflect an expectation that professionals in these functions can work effectively alongside AI systems, make sense of their outputs, and judge when and where to apply them. LinkedIn's 2026 report captured this direction clearly: employers are looking for professionals who can define AI value propositions, not only build systems. That framing matters for how non-technical professionals think about positioning their skills. What the Pay Data Suggests Salary data is an imperfect signal, but the direction in the current market is consistent. Postings that mention AI skills pay roughly 28% more than equivalent roles that don't, according to analysis from multiple hiring platforms.

title: 5 Docker Containers You Need for a Home AI Lab
abstract: 5 Docker Containers You Need for a Home AI Lab Learn which five Docker containers make a reliable home AI lab, from Ollama and Open WebUI to Qdrant, n8n and Portainer CE, what job each one does, and the first mistake to avoid with each. By Nahla Davies , KDnuggets on October 29, 2026 in Data Engineering The first weekend goes well. A model runs locally, a chat window answers questions, and the laptop fan finally has a reason to exist. The third weekend is where home AI labs die. Three containers sit on ports nobody wrote down. A folder of PDFs never got indexed, a cron job lives in someone's shell history, and an update wiped the models because they were stored inside the container. Not one of those failures is an AI problem; every one of them is a lab problem. A useful home lab is a small set of containers with clear jobs, not one giant AI box. KDnuggets took the same layered view in its look at the local AI stack . Model serving, an interface, retrieval memory, automation and management are separate layers, and each one is a container you can replace without touching the others. The five below are picked for the friction they remove rather than for how much AI is in the name. Two of them have no AI in them at all. Container Job in the stack First caution Ollama Serve: runs local models, exposes port 11434 Models kept inside the container vanish on recreate; use a named volume Open WebUI Talk: browser chat, users, files, provider links A regenerated WEBUI_SECRET_KEY logs everyone out; set it once Qdrant Remember: vector search over your own documents Not needed for casual chat; add it when retrieval matters n8n Automate: scheduled ingestion, webhooks, glue jobs Holds credentials; back up its volume and keep the port private Portainer CE Manage: restarts, logs, volumes, updates, cleanup Docker socket access controls the host; trusted network only Table 1. The five containers, the job each one does in the stack, and the first thing that goes wrong with each. Original reference table for this article. Sources: Ollama Docker Hub, Open WebUI quick start, Qdrant quick start, n8n Docker Compose docs, Portainer CE install docs. Original reference table. 1. Ollama: The Model Runtime Ollama is the engine room. It pulls and runs local models and exposes an HTTP endpoint on port 11434. Every other container in the lab talks to that endpoint, so nothing else needs to know how a model is loaded. The official Docker Hub image ships three routes: CPU only, NVIDIA GPUs through the NVIDIA Container Toolkit with --gpus=all , and AMD GPUs through the rocm tag. The install detail that matters most is the volume. Models are large, and a container recreated without a named volume downloads them all again. Worse, it can lose a model you pulled from a tag that has since moved. The documented run command is: docker run -d --gpus=all -v ollama:/root/.ollama -p 11434:11434 --name ollama ollama/ollama Drop --gpus=all for the CPU route. One honest caveat: GPU pass-through depends on the host, not on Ollama. The documented Docker GPU routes are Linux and Windows with WSL2. Docker Desktop on macOS does not hand containers an NVIDIA GPU, so a Mac lab either runs Ollama natively for speed or accepts CPU inference inside Docker. 2. Open WebUI: The Interface Layer A terminal is fine for testing a model and useless for living with one. Open WebUI puts a browser interface on the lab: chats, users, file uploads, and connections to Ollama and to any other provider you add. Docker is the officially recommended install , and the quick start is one command: docker run -d -p 3000:8080 --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway -v open-webui:/app/backend/data -e WEBUI_SECRET_KEY=your-secret-key --name open-webui --restart always ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main Two of those flags earn their place. The volume at /app/backend/data holds users, chats and uploaded files. Without it, every recreate starts the lab from a blank login page. WEBUI_SECRET_KEY signs sessions, so set it once with something like openssl rand -hex 32 and keep it, because a container that regenerates the key logs everyone out. The :cuda and :ollama image variants exist for GPU acceleration and for bundling Ollama inside the same container. Both are options rather than the default, since a separate Ollama container is easier to upgrade and to share between tools. 3. Qdrant: Retrieval Memory for the Lab Do you need a vector database at all? For casual chat, no, and skipping it is a legitimate decision. The moment the lab is supposed to answer questions from your own documents, notes or project files, those files have to be embedded and searched. That is what Qdrant does: it stores vectors and finds the nearest ones. It is the memory the AI consults, which is a different thing from the AI itself. The local quick start runs Qdrant with two ports, 6333 for the REST API and dashboard and 6334 for gRPC. The quick start also mounts a storage path so collections survive restarts. The dashboard at localhost:6333/dashboard is worth opening once, because seeing a collection fill up is the fastest way to confirm an ingestion pipeline is doing anything. A model alone is not a useful system, a point the earlier KDnuggets piece on self-hosted LLMs in the real world makes at length. Retrieval is usually the layer that turns a demo into something you reach for. 4. n8n: The Automation Spine Every lab eventually needs glue. Files land in a folder and need embedding, model endpoints need calling on a schedule, and summaries need pushing somewhere a human will read them. n8n is a workflow tool that runs those jobs visually. Its Docker Compose install is the sensible route for a lab, because Compose is how the rest of the stack should be described anyway. It serves on localhost:5678 and defaults to SQLite, with Postgres as the option once workflows multiply. Three workflows show what it is for: Nightly ingestion. A scheduled job watches a folder, chunks new files and writes them into Qdrant. Summarize on demand. A webhook takes a URL or a PDF, sends it through Ollama for a summary and posts the result to a notes file. Weekly review. A job asks the model to read the week's lab notes and flag anything unfinished. The caution is the obvious one. n8n holds credentials and workflow definitions, so its volume needs a backup, and its port has no business being exposed beyond the home network. 5. Portainer CE: The Control Panel After four containers, the boring work becomes the work: restarts, logs, volume checks, spotting an image with an update, cleaning up the six stopped containers from last month. Portainer CE gives all of that a browser UI. The official install runs on HTTPS port 9443 and keeps its own state in a portainer_data volume. The install also mounts the Docker socket at /var/run/docker.sock . The socket mount is the part to respect. Whatever can talk to the Docker socket can control every container on the host. That is what makes Portainer useful, and it is also why it belongs on a trusted machine behind a home network, never on a public port. Treat it as the admin console it is. The lab won't need it on day one; it will need it the first time someone asks why the chat interface stopped answering and nobody can remember which container to restart. Starting With Two Containers and Adding the Rest When the Lab Demands Them The five jobs are serve, talk, remember, automate and manage. Ollama and Open WebUI cover the first two and make a working lab in an afternoon. Add Qdrant when you catch yourself pasting the same document into a chat for the third time. Add n8n when a manual step has happened often enough to be annoying. Add Portainer before the stack becomes opaque, which is usually the week after n8n arrives. Describe all of it in one Compose file from the start. Compose gives every service a name the others can use as a hostname, so Open WebUI reaches the model at http://ollama:11434 with no IP addresses involved.

title: Run AI Models for Edge Application Development with Just a Few Commands
abstract:
AI is expanding beyond the data center as developers build a new generation of agents to act at the edge: monitoring driver attention and cabin conditions, helping robots understand their surroundings and plan tasks, and coordinating fleets of machines on production lines. These physical AI applications rely on models that perceive, reason, and act within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. But getting a model ready to run can involve substantial setup. NVIDIA DGX Spark, now available in a 64GB configuration , gives embedded developers a platform to prototype, fine-tune, and test models and agents. NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM provides a lightweight C++ inference runtime designed for embedded workloads, bringing the same inference framework to development on Spark and deployment on platforms such as NVIDIA Jetson Thor , NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor , and NVIDIA IGX Thor . You can get started in just a few commands with the trtedge command-line interface (CLI). It downloads your selected model and builds TensorRT engines optimized for inference on Spark. In this tutorial, you’ll run NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning , a text-only model, on Spark using TensorRT Edge-LLM. You’ll test prompts in your terminal and serve the model through an API for application prototyping. You’ll also enable DSpark speculative decoding to accelerate generation. Prerequisites: Set up your development environment To get started, you’ll need a DGX Spark with a supported NVIDIA software stack, NVIDIA CUDA 13, TensorRT 10.16.1.11 or newer within the 10.x series, and Python 3.10 to 3.12. The examples below were tested with TensorRT Edge-LLM 0.11.1 and TensorRT 10.16.1.11. Open a terminal on your DGX Spark, create and activate a virtual environment, and install TensorRT Edge-LLM: python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv-edgellm
source .venv-edgellm/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install "tensorrt-edgellm[server]==0.11.1" Note: The virtual environment keeps newly installed packages separate while allowing access to all system Python packages, including TensorRT. Check the TensorRT version and confirm that the TensorRT Edge-LLM runtime loads: python -c "import tensorrt as trt; v = tuple(map(int, trt.__version__.split('.'))); assert (10, 16, 1, 11) <= v < (11,), f'TensorRT >=10.16.1.11 and <11 required; found {trt.__version__}'; from tensorrt_edgellm import runtime; runtime.load()" Note: If compatible system TensorRT bindings are unavailable, follow the NVIDIA TensorRT pip installation instructions to install a compatible TensorRT 10.x version in the activated environment, then rerun the verification command. With the virtual environment still active, start a chat with Nemotron-3.5 Lightning: trtedge chat nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 On your first launch, wait for the model download (approximately 21GB) and engine build to finish. Files are stored in ~/.cache/tensorrt-edgellm by default, so allow space for both the model and engines. Later launches reuse matching cached engines. Once the chat prompt appears, enter: Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence. Example response: 25°C is equal to 77°F. Continue the conversation with follow-up questions, or type /exit to end the session. Serve your model Serve your model through a local OpenAI-compatible API on Spark for application development and testing. With your virtual environment active, start the server: trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8000 The server builds or reuses an engine for this configuration. Once startup completes, open a second terminal on your DGX Spark and check that it is ready: curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready A response containing "status":"ready" confirms that the server is ready. Send your first prompt to the chat completions endpoint: curl -fsS -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4", "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": "Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence." } ], "stream": true, "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 128
}' The response streams as JSON events. Keep the server running for more requests, or press Ctrl+C in the server terminal to stop it. Optional: Enable speculative decoding You can speed up generation with DSpark speculative decoding , which uses a draft model to propose several tokens for the main model to verify in a single pass. To enable it with three draft tokens, press Ctrl+C in the server terminal, then restart the server with DSpark enabled: trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8000 \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dspark", "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4-DSpark", "num_speculative_tokens": 3 }' Once the server is ready, send another prompt to the chat completions endpoint to try DSpark-enabled generation. You can experiment with num_speculative_tokens and other settings to tune generation speed for your workload. See the speculative decoding documentation to learn more . Performance on DGX Spark 64GB TensorRT Edge-LLM delivers low response latency and fast token generation with NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning on DGX Spark 64GB. The table below reports time to first token (TTFT) and generation speed with and without DSpark speculative decoding. Decoding Workload Median TTFT (ms) Mean generation speed (tokens/s) DSpark OFF SpeedBench 1K 201.0 73.3 DSpark OFF SpeedBench 2K 329.5 72.8 DSpark OFF HumanEval prompts 98.1 73.4 DSpark ON SpeedBench 1K 203.0 108.5 DSpark ON SpeedBench 2K 331.6 105.3 DSpark ON HumanEval prompts 98.7 126.9 Table 1. Nemotron-3.5 Lightning performance on DGX Spark 64GB with and without DSpark speculative decoding. Generation speed is the average token generation rate per request, excluding time to first token. DSpark uses three draft tokens. Peak total system memory use during inference with DSpark was 27.9GB, including the OS. Measured on DGX Spark 64GB running DGX OS 7.6.0 (Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS), using NVFP4 with thinking enabled, batch size one, one concurrent streaming request, and a 128-token output limit. Average input lengths were 1,153 tokens for SpeedBench 1K, 2,247 for SpeedBench 2K, and 139 for HumanEval. Next steps Try another model from the supported models list and continue developing your application on Spark. Options include vision-language models that interpret images and video, as well as speech recognition and text-to-speech models. Explore the TensorRT Edge-LLM documentation for model-specific workflows and requirements on your target embedded platform. And visit the Nemotron developer page for resources to get started. Explore open Nemotron models and datasets on Hugging Face and Blueprints on build.nvidia.com .

title: Build Specialized Agents on a Stack You Control with NVIDIA NemoClaw
abstract: Building an autonomous agent requires a model, a harness, and domain-specific tools. To deploy an agent more securely, developers need a runtime that enforces policies, along with optimization and observability tools for reliable execution. For production agents, the challenge lies in making these agents capable and safe to operate with access to real enterprise systems and data. This post explains how these components work together, with a focus on how NVIDIA NemoClaw open blueprints enable developers to build specialized agents on a stack they can own, customize, and run. This post provides criteria to help developers integrate NemoClaw with a harness they already use: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or LangChain Deep Agents. What an agent harness provides An agent requires four things: A model that reasons . A harness that defines how the agent operates. Tools and skills that extend its capabilities. A runtime that governs what the agent can access and do in production. NemoClaw works with agent harnesses NemoClaw open blueprints currently support three harnesses: OpenClaw can access files and applications, write code, spawn sub-agents, and maintain context across sessions. It runs on your own machine or server and supports long-running sessions, memory, and scheduled tasks. Hermes Agent , from Nous Research, is designed to get better with use. As teams correct the agents’ approach and repeat workflows, Hermes captures those patterns as durable skills that can be reused in future work. LangChain Deep Agents provides a customizable harness for complex, multistep tasks. It combines planning, file-based context management, memory, and delegation to specialized subagents. Each harness gives an agent skills, tools, orchestration, and memory. Using NemoClaw for full-stack production agents NemoClaw is not a competing harness, and it is not a runtime. It is a collection of blueprints that assembles an open agent stack on top of the harness selected by the developer. The stack combines model and harness optimization with runtime governance. Each NemoClaw blueprint brings together four components: A tuned open harness, such as Hermes Agent, LangChain Deep Agents, or OpenClaw, optimized to work with NVIDIA Nemotron. Nemotron open models . NVIDIA NeMo tools for optimization, including NVIDIA NeMo Relay for observing and improving agent execution, plus routing capabilities that can help improve throughput, cost, and reliability. NVIDIA OpenShell is the secure runtime that governs agent access to files, networks, credentials, and tools. If you are already building with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or LangChain Deep Agents, a NemoClaw blueprint can assemble the surrounding stack without requiring you to rewrite the agent. Figure 1. NemoClaw is an open blueprint that works with several agent harnesses Why co-optimizing the model and harness matters An agent combines a model and a harness. The model thinks, while the harness provides the environment in which it operates. When the two are matched, the model can focus on the task. When they aren’t, it may ask for context again, stop early, or loop without progress. For example, LangChain tuned its Deep Agents harness for Nemotron 3 Ultra by adjusting prompts, tools, and middleware without retraining the model. Starting from an already strong baseline, the harness tuning brought Nemotron 3 Ultra to near-frontier performance at approximately 10x lower cost per run compared with leading closed models. The NemoClaw blueprint for LangChain Deep Agents packages these optimizations directly. Every developer using LangChain Deep Agents with Nemotron 3 Ultra can access these optimizations without reproducing the tuning work. The tuned Nemotron 3 Ultra model profile is available through LangChain on GitHub . When to use each Use a harness such as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, or LangChain Deep Agents to build and experiment with the agent’s skills, tools, memory, and orchestration logic. Use a NemoClaw blueprint to assemble and run a specialized agent on an open stack that combines a tuned harness, models, optimization, telemetry, and OpenShell runtime controls. Question Agent harness NemoClaw blueprint What it is Software that manages how an agent uses tools, maintains context, and carries out tasks A reference stack that combines a supported harness with models, optimization tools, and a runtime What it provides Tools, skills, memory, and orchestration A tuned harness, models, optimization tools, and OpenShell runtime controls How they work together Provides the agent’s execution logic within the stack Combines the harness with the other stack components When to use it To build and customize an agent’s behavior To assemble and run an agent with model and harness optimization and runtime controls Table 1. Roles and capabilities of an agent harness and a NemoClaw blueprint A harness helps you build a capable agent. A NemoClaw blueprint helps you run that agent on an open stack with model and harness optimization, telemetry, and runtime governance. Example: A memory-driven Chief of Staff, built on Hermes The NemoClaw community repository includes a memory-driven Chief of Staff recipe. The agent maintains a persistent, human-readable model of the people, projects, priorities, and working patterns it encounters, so it doesn’t have to reconstruct context from scratch on every task. It is built as a deployable Hermes profile for NemoClaw, as outlined in the technical design walkthrough. The recipe shows the stack working together rather than in isolation. OpenShell governs the agent’s file system, process, and network access, and keeps credentials for managed inference and Model Context Protocol (MCP) connections outside the sandbox. This helps keep the agent bound by policy even when its memory or retrieved context leads it toward an unintended action. NeMo Relay is integrated natively into the Hermes session. It closes trace spans at real session boundaries, including a new session, reset, or expiry, and exports the resulting trajectories for audit and further optimization. Importance of agent governance Every NemoClaw reference includes OpenShell, the runtime that adds security and policy enforcement around the agent harness and tools, governing the actions a model can take. The OpenShell tutorial covers how to create your first policy to prevent data exfiltration to GitHub. NemoClaw references include more sophisticated OpenShell policies that govern agent connections across many different internal tools, sites, and communication channels. Deploy across cloud, data center, and local systems NemoClaw agents can run in the cloud, in data centers, on NVIDIA DGX Spark, and on NVIDIA RTX PCs and workstations. A NemoClaw clinical agent for a hospital and a NemoClaw simulation agent for electronic design automation can run on the same stack while using entirely different tools and skills. NemoClaw agents can also work alongside frontier agents. Claude, Codex, or Cursor agents can delegate domain-specific subtasks to NemoClaw-powered specialists running on open models and owned infrastructure. Get started Choose a NemoClaw blueprint for your harness, then customize its tools, models, and runtime policies for your workflow. Take the Deploy Secure Agents with NemoClaw DLI course —a 101-level introduction to the stack. Follow the NemoClaw quickstart to deploy an agent through a NemoClaw blueprint. Explore the NemoClaw GitHub repository for the full example and additional blueprints. Learn how to deploy self-evolving agents for faster, more secure research with Hermes Agent and NemoClaw. Stay up to date on NVIDIA AI by subscribing to NVIDIA news and following NVIDIA AI on LinkedIn , X , Discord , and YouTube . Visit the developer page for resources to get started. Explore open Nemotron models and datasets on Hugging Face and NVIDIA Blueprints on build.nvidia.com.

title: How to Check and Configure NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage for Your Platform
abstract: NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage (GDS) accelerates GPU storage access in on-premises and cloud environments. It provides a robust, portable, and efficient data path between NVIDIA GPUs and storage targets to increase bandwidth, minimize latency, and reduce CPU and memory utilization across a broad range of platforms, application frameworks, and workload patterns . Configuring NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage starts with understanding your environment. Which settings and storage paths are appropriate for your platform and workload? Extensive documentation describes how to configure and troubleshoot supported architectures and storage solutions, but you must navigate this information and optimize your deployment. Figure 1. High-level diagram of the GPUDirect Storage data path with gds-diag The gds-diag tool was developed by the GPUDirect Storage team to simplify optimization and configuration of GPUDirect Storage. gds-diag is a simple, open-source command-line utility that assesses environments, identifies problems, and suggests improvements to help you make the most of your GDS deployment. It is also bundled with an optional agent skill that adds a natural-language interface and orchestration layer. The skill interprets your intent, selects and invokes the appropriate subcommands, and coordinates multi-step diagnostic workflows. Beyond command selection and routing, the skill extends gds-diag with model-guided reasoning. It can interpret diagnostic results, apply relevant system context, and propose or carry out appropriate remediation. This post shows you how to get started with gds-diag using either the command-line interface or the agent skill. Download and installation To use gds-diag , you need a Linux system with Python 3.8 or newer. GPUDirect Storage requires an NVIDIA datacenter-class GPU and NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit 12.2 or newer, but these are not dependencies of gds-diag itself. gds-diag is distributed as part of the NVIDIA Magnum IO GitHub repository with no other dependencies to install. Clone the repository on the machine where you plan to run it with git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/MagnumIO.git and select one of the following usage models: Command-line tool: This provides a deterministic, minimal-dependency path to diagnose GDS deployments. Go to the gds-diag directory, run gds-diag.py --help , and follow the Command-line usage guidance. AI agent: This provides the most intuitive, flexible, interactive, natural-language mechanism to diagnose GDS deployments while still retaining the reliable determinism of the underlying command-line tool. Open the gds-diag directory in your preferred AI coding assistant and follow the Agent skill usage guidance. Quick tip: The AI agent mode is recommended if this option is available in your environment. gds-diag is validated with both Claude and Codex, though it may work with other tools as well. Command-line usage The gds-diag command-line tool is a single Python script with multiple subcommands to focus on different diagnostic tasks. You can browse available subcommands by running ./gds-diag.py --help . For more information about a specific subcommand, run ./gds-diag.py <subcommand> --help . Quick tip: Not sure where to start? Just run ./gds-diag.py all /path/to/check , and gds-diag will automatically run a complete sequence of diagnostics for that path. This works in bare-metal, virtual machine, and container environments. Figure 2 groups the available subcommands into four categories. Figure 2. Table of gds-diag subcommands, grouped into categories Choose a diagnostic category based on your stage of deployment or the problem you need to investigate. End-to-end checks: Use all to automatically select appropriate diagnostics for your environment and run them in sequence. Preparing for installation: Use pre-install to check GPU support and CUDA Toolkit installation. Use support-matrix to view supported storage targets and plan your deployment. Validating an installation: Use post-install to check whether GDS is installed correctly and identify blockers. Use config-audit to review configuration files and environment variables that influence GDS behavior. Deep diagnostics: Use container-check to assess GDS support in container environments, including containerd, Docker, Enroot, and Kubernetes. Use mount-check to diagnose a specific mount point or directory. The anatomy of a gds-diag finding The output of most gds-diag subcommands is presented as a set of findings grouped into sections, as Figure 3 shows. Figure 3. Screenshot of an example gds-diag finding with annotations Each finding and each section has a status badge. “FAIL” indicates a hard blocker. “WARN” indicates a potential blocker. “INFO” communicates notable information. “PASS” indicates a nominal finding and is shown only when you use the --verbose option. Each finding includes an explanation followed by a mitigation plan. gds-diag will not implement the mitigation plan or otherwise modify the system on its own . Its role is to identify problems and optimization opportunities and help you or your administrator make improvements. Multiple sections (and findings within those sections) may be shown. Quick tip: You can also emit all diagnostic reports as structured JSON data with the --json command-line option. This could be useful if you plan to ingest findings into another tool or archive them for future reference. Most subcommands follow the same structure. The gds-diag.py support-matrix command is a notable exception: it emits output in the form of a table with footnotes. This subcommand shows which platform combinations GDS supports.
