title: Wealth Management Client Onboarding Needs More Than AI
abstract: Wealth Management client onboarding can stall even when every system has done its job. The document is collected, the screening result is back, and the workflow task is complete. Yet the case is still waiting because someone has to determine what changed, which evidence is current, and who owns the exception. For the client, those boundaries are invisible. They experience one journey and expect their information and progress to move with them. Inside the firm, however, that journey crosses customer relationship management (CRM), document, know your customer (KYC) , screening, custody, and workflow systems, each holding a different part of the case. Firms have invested in making those individual steps faster, and AI is accelerating them further. But a quicker extraction, screening summary, or routing decision does little if the next team must still reconstruct the case, reconcile the evidence, and reopen work that appeared complete. Onboarding still loses time at these handoffs. A modern platform has to connect the case across systems, coordinate work as conditions change, and preserve the controls and human judgment that the process depends on. When it doesn't, the cost accumulates between systems. The first cost is what clients feel most directly: time . In Singapore, opening a private banking account takes about 6 weeks, with complex cases taking longer. In May 2026, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said initiatives from an account-opening workgroup co-led by MAS and industry were expected to bring that median within one month. Inside the firm, it shows up in staff time. The Capgemini World Wealth Report 2026 found that 60% of 144 wealth executives lacked a unified client view. The same report found that 1,317 relationship managers across 16 markets said operational work consumed 41% of their time. That figure covers wealth operations broadly, not onboarding alone, but it shows how much capacity routine coordination can absorb . The onboarding journey itself spans many teams. A 2024 EY report of more than a dozen global asset managers found that more than half involved at least 10 teams in onboarding. Yet only 15% reported strong integration with their CRM systems. A 2024 KPMG and Private Wealth Management Association study of 35 Hong Kong private wealth institutions cited onboarding demands as a factor in rising costs and deteriorating client experience. The findings span markets, populations, and supervisory regimes, and each needs to be read in context. Across them, the pattern is consistent - fragmented client information, with many teams stitching the journey together. Firms absorb that coordination through staff hours, repeated evidence searches, manual reconciliation, exception handling, and control-history preparation. Integration, maintenance, and change testing add more cost while account opening and funding wait. Faster tasks do not always produce a faster onboarding journey. A system can finish its work on time and still leave the case stalled at the next handoff. AI can accelerate each task further, but it does not automatically remove friction between systems. AI is already moving into wealth and asset management. In a 2025 EY survey of 100 decision-makers , split evenly between wealth and asset management firms, 95% of firms reported scaling generative AI across multiple use cases, while 78% were exploring agentic AI. Yet translating this momentum into measurable business value remains a challenge, with only 27% of executives reporting substantial business impact from GenAI. Looking at the work itself explains the gap. AI can extract document fields, summarize a screening result, or recommend the next workflow action. Each capability may improve a task within a single application, yet the handoff still depends on current evidence and a clear record of what changed. Teams also need to know whether earlier work must be revisited. AI agents make that dependency more important because routing work across specialist agents and approved tools requires a shared case state. That state must show what is complete, what has gone stale, and which exception blocks the next step. Without it, faster orchestration can reproduce the same fragmentation it was meant to reduce. Governed case context is a current, versioned, source-linked view of each client onboarding case. It brings together the evidence, case state, completed controls, open exceptions, agent activity, and decision history. Because the context is versioned, teams can see what changed, what the change affected and whether earlier work needs to be revisited. Different parts of onboarding can live in different places. Core client and custody records may remain in their assigned systems, while evidence processing, controls, models, and case workflows can run on the Databricks Data + AI Platform. Governed case context connects that work in one governed view, as the diagram below illustrates, while preserving record ownership and decision authority. On Databricks, Unity Catalog centralizes access controls, lineage and auditability for this context, while open table formats such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg support reliable data management and interoperability across systems. Governed case context is useful only when it helps the next agent or reviewer understand and advance the case. A practical test is whether they can answer four questions without reconstructing its history: With those answers in one place, a governed supervisor agent can resume work from the current case state. It can assign independent tasks to specialist agents, call approved tools, and bring in a reviewer when judgment is required. It can also flag conflicting evidence and assemble a complete package for review, while the evidence, changes, and actions behind that package remain attached to the case. The value comes from putting this context to work across the journey. A modern platform must keep it current, coordinate agents and people around it, and preserve visibility and governance from the first piece of evidence through the final decision. Putting governed case context to work requires four platform capabilities. Together, they address the friction identified earlier: rebuilding the case at each handoff, coordinating work manually, governing access to sensitive data, and measuring tasks without seeing the whole journey. Together, these capabilities turn governed case context into an operating model. The architecture below shows how the context, supervised agents, and human review work together in practice. The architecture puts the four capabilities into a recurring operating loop around each case. Information can arrive from source systems, while evidence processing, controls, risk models, and onboarding workflows run on the platform. Each result returns to governed case context with its source references and history attached, giving the next agent or reviewer the current state of the case. A governed supervisor agent reads that context and selects the next permitted action. Depending on the case, it can call an approved tool, assign work to a specialist agent, or involve a reviewer. When new evidence makes an earlier result stale, it can reopen the affected work instead of restarting the entire case. It also monitors completion and freshness, flagging missing or conflicting control results before the case moves forward. A simple example shows how the loop works. Consider a case waiting on a required document. The supervisor can identify the gap, prepare a client outreach email for review and pause any work that depends on the missing evidence. Once a reviewer approves the outreach and the document arrives through the designated channel, the case context updates. The supervisor can then trigger document processing, rerun only the affected checks and route the case to its next permitted step.

title: Deliberate decisions and enterprise AI value
abstract: AI progress is moving quickly. Expectations are rising, experimentation is spreading and organizations are under pressure to show meaningful returns. But the decisions that matter most are rarely about whether AI is possible. They are about where to commit, what to prioritize and how to move forward when the evidence is still incomplete. That is the focus of Deliberate Decisions: How Grounded Leadership Is Advancing the Path to Enterprise AI Value , a report produced by DataIQ in partnership with Databricks. The report brings together perspectives from senior data and AI leaders who are making these choices in real organizations. The report draws on open peer discussions at DataIQ Guild 2026, an invite-only think tank for senior data and AI leaders. Across industries, leaders described a similar challenge: they are expected to maintain momentum while technology, operating models, workforce impact and business cases continue to evolve. Early AI success can raise expectations faster than an organization can absorb. Pilots and proofs of concept can multiply before teams have the capacity to assess, govern and support them. Ownership can become unclear as AI crosses functions, while roles and workflows change faster than organizations can define them. The answer is not to slow down until everything is certain. Nor is it to commit to every promising use case. The report points toward a more grounded form of leadership: making deliberate, evidence-based choices while preserving the ability to adapt. Download the report now: Deliberate Decisions: How Grounded Leadership Is Advancing the Path to Enterprise AI Value Five leadership disciplines emerged from the discussions at DataIQ Guild 2026: To lead data and AI today is to navigate a constant tension between commitment and flexibility. Every investment, architecture and operating model decision requires leaders to balance confidence in what they know today with openness to what may change tomorrow. The Databricks perspective in the report identifies four foundations for navigating that tension: These foundations are reflected in Databricks capabilities such as Lakebase , a governed transactional foundation for building and running data and AI applications and agents, and Genie , which helps people and AI agents access organizational context responsibly and efficiently. Together, they reinforce the report’s central message: progress does not require waiting for certainty. It requires making informed decisions, knowing where to commit and preserving choice. A successful pilot is not the same as an AI capability that is ready for production. The report explores the difference between early results and sustainable adoption, including the operational support, governance, skills, monitoring and cost model that become visible once AI enters a live workflow. As Thomas Gebetsroither, Data & Analytics Operations Lead, Axpo Trading & Sales, mentioned: Leaders will find a practical way to test whether an AI initiative can remain useful, reliable and affordable beyond the conditions of a bounded experiment. AI demand can come from the board, business functions, employees and vendors. But demand alone cannot determine the agenda. The report looks at how leaders start with a well-defined business problem, make trade-offs visible and prioritize work with enterprise-scale potential. It also examines why AI investment may be better managed as a portfolio. Organizations can make a range of initial bets, increase investment as evidence strengthens and stop or redirect work that does not justify further commitment. AI adoption is not owned by one team. Business outcomes, workflow change, risk, adoption and ongoing costs are distributed across the organization. You will learn why clear decision rights are not enough unless a business owner is also prepared to own the outcome and its consequences. This matters because an approved use case without committed ownership can create a new problem rather than solve an existing one. As AI handles more execution, people spend more time framing problems, interpreting results and deciding what happens next. The report examines why human authority must be explicit, how organizations can build role-appropriate AI fluency and why automating away opportunities to develop expertise can create long-term risk. The central question is not whether humans remain somewhere in the process. It is whether they still have the authority, context and time to challenge an output when it matters. Organizations need enough continuity to know where accountability sits and which principles apply. At the same time, technology choices, roles and operating models need room to evolve. As the report delineates, the challenge for leaders is not to protect people from automation. It is to avoid automating away capabilities the organisation cannot replace. The report offers a way to identify the fixed points that matter — purpose, decision rights, standards, human authority and business ownership — while keeping other decisions flexible and, where possible, reversible. Deliberate Decisions does not predict which technology will win. It focuses on the judgment calls leaders are making now: what to commit to, where to push back, how to move forward responsibly and how to preserve choice as conditions change. For leaders moving from experimentation toward enterprise AI value, the report provides a practical framework and shared language for making trade-offs visible. Rather than presenting a use case as an isolated technical project, connect it to the business outcome it should change, the evidence supporting the next investment and the ownership required to sustain it. That creates more useful conversations with executive sponsors and business teams. It also makes it easier to assess readiness, stop, redirect, or redesign work when the evidence changes, treating course correction as disciplined leadership rather than failure. Before approving the next use case, ask: These questions will not remove uncertainty. They can improve the quality of the decisions made in its presence. The full report develops these ideas through five leadership disciplines and perspectives from the DataIQ Guild community. It is designed to help leaders compare their own decisions with the choices other organizations are making as AI becomes more consequential. Download the full Deliberate Decisions report to explore the leadership model and the practical actions behind it. Look beyond pilot results. AI is ready to scale when the organization can support, govern, adopt and afford it in a live workflow. Start with a clearly defined business problem and enterprise value. Manage initiatives as a portfolio, increasing investment as evidence strengthens. A business owner should be accountable for the outcome, adoption, operating consequences and ongoing costs, with clear decision rights across teams. Define which decisions remain human-owned and give people the authority, context and time to challenge, override or stop an AI system. Set fixed points for purpose, standards, ownership and human authority, while keeping roles, operating models and technology choices open to review. title: Announcing General Availability of Real-Time Mode for Spark Declarative Pipelines on Databricks
abstract: We introduced Real-Time Mode (RTM) last year which enabled customers to build low-latency, operational use cases. This was a game changer because it allowed customers to process streaming data in milliseconds, up to 100x faster than traditional micro-batch architecture. Furthermore, they no longer needed to maintain separate, specialized engines like Flink alongside Spark, eliminating duplicate codebases, fragmented governance models, and operational overhead. Today, we are announcing RTM in Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP) is now Genearally Available. SDP has become the standard way to build streaming and ETL pipelines on Databricks, automatically handling dependency resolution, incremental processing, orchestration, failure recovery, and data quality enforcement. With RTM, customers can build operational, low-latency pipelines while retaining all of those SDP benefits. Whether for fraud scoring, real-time alerting, or pushing fresh features to operational stores, you can now use SDP across all of these use cases. RTM is an evolution of the Spark Structured Streaming engine that achieves end-to-end latencies in the millisecond range. It does this by streaming data continuously, running all query stages simultaneously, and passing data between stages as soon as it is produced. For the full architecture deep dive, read the blog, “ Breaking the microbatch barrier: The architecture of Apache Spark Real-Time Mode .” RTM can support any workload that benefits from turning data into decisions in milliseconds. Some example use cases include fraud detection, live personalization, real-time recommendation systems, and real-time feature computation. We benchmarked RTM against Apache Flink on actual customer workloads performing feature computation, and RTM is up to 92% faster than specialized engines like Flink. Below are the benchmarks. For more information on the datasets and queries referenced, see this GitHub repository . Customers are increasingly defaulting to SDP for their ETL workloads. With RTM, SDP now supports all streaming workloads, including operational low-latency streaming, enabling customers to use a single framework across all pipelines. One framework means one observability stack, one billing model, and no fragmentation across different APIs. SDP serverless takes it further. There is no compute to choose and no cluster to size. You get sub-second latency, without any complex infra tuning, while paying only for the cores your query uses. RTM flows also get SDP features such as versionless upgrades and low-downtime maintenance, which reduce both the operational work and the disruption of upgrades. One use case where RTM on SDP has immediate impact is real-time feature computation. ML models for fraud detection or personalization depend on fresh signals, such as a user's total transaction amount over the last 10 minutes, to make accurate predictions. Computing these rolling-window aggregations and landing them in an online store within milliseconds is where RTM on SDP closes the gap. The Databricks Feature Store uses this exact architecture to deliver end-to-end p99 latency of 200ms from Kafka to the online feature store . Real-Time Mode requires the pipeline mode to be continuous and spark.databricks.streaming.realTimeMode.enabled set to true takes over. Real-time mode requires an update flow. Use dp.create_sink() to define the output target, then use the @dp.update_flow decorator with pipelines.trigger set to "RealTime" and target pointing to the sink. For supported sources and sinks, see the documentation . Use cases like fraud detection or real-time personalization require not only that features be computed in real time but also that they land in a queryable, low-latency store. A fraud model needs a customer's latest transaction before it clears, and a personalization engine needs to read what a user just browsed. Today, you can write to any custom sink like Lakebase , Redis, or any other OLTP store from SDP using a ForEach sink . Define the writer, register it as a foreach_sink , and wire it to an update_flow . Features land in your operational store within milliseconds of being produced, with no offline-to-online sync in between. Applications and models can query them at ultra-low latency. What’s next for RTM on serverless? RTM extends Spark Declarative Pipelines into a new class of workloads, operational, latency-sensitive applications that demand immediate response to streaming data. By bringing sub-second latency to the SDP APIs your team already uses, it eliminates the need to operate a separate framework or engine for your most time-critical pipelines. Whether you're building fraud detection pipelines, personalization engines, or ML feature computation systems, real-time mode gives you the latency your application demands with the simplicity of SDP. Real-Time Mode on Spark Declarative Pipelines is now Generally Available. Check out the following resources to get started with RTM on SDP: What is Real-Time Mode (RTM) in Spark Declarative Pipelines? Real-time mode (RTM) lets Spark Declarative Pipelines (SDP) process streaming data with end-to-end latency in the millisecond range. It streams data continuously, runs all query stages at the same time and passes data between stages as soon as it's produced. Real-time pipelines benefit from SDP's orchestration and automatic failure recovery. Is Real-Time Mode available in Spark Declarative Pipelines? Yes. Real-time mode on Spark Declarative Pipelines is now generally available. It brings the real-time mode already available in Spark Structured Streaming to SDP pipelines. How do I turn on real-time mode in a pipeline? Set the pipeline to continuous mode and set spark.databricks.streaming.realTimeMode.enabled to true . Then define an update flow with pipelines.trigger set to "RealTime" and a target that points to a sink. Can a real-time pipeline write to Lakebase or another OLTP store? Yes. Define a ForEach sink with a writer that implements open , process and close , then point a real-time flow at it. This works for Lakebase, Redis or any other OLTP store. What use cases is Real-Time Mode in Spark Declarative Pipelines built for? Real-Time Mode is built for operational workloads that turn streaming data into decisions in milliseconds. Examples include fraud detection, live personalization, real-time recommendations and real-time feature computation. The Databricks feature store uses this architecture to reach a p99 latency of 200 ms from Apache Kafka to the online feature store. title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
abstract: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account. “It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here .

title: Dartmouth's provost warned us about AI cheating—but his own AI use cost him his job
abstract: On August 9, 2026, Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell wrote a Washington Post op-ed called "Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem." This week, Schnell discovered the depths of the problem himself as he resigned from the university after an advisory committee found that he failed to disclose significant AI use in an academic paper and in the Washington Post op-ed, even though publishers required such disclosure. Schnell didn't make it especially easy for the committee to investigate his AI use; the report uses the term "insufficient cooperation." He did turn over his Dartmouth laptop, but he did not turn over logs from his personal LLM accounts related to the writings in question. Nor did he agree to meet with the committee. The committee did get access to the Claude enterprise account Schnell had used through Dartmouth, though. This shows him using the LLM as a tool for revising his papers, finding and fixing bugs in code, and editing or generating figures.
