title: Crosstalk-Solutions/project-nomad
abstract:
Project NOMAD Knowledge That Never Goes Offline Project NOMAD is a self-contained, offline-first knowledge and education server packed with critical tools, knowledge, and AI to keep you informed and empowered — anytime, anywhere. Installation & Quickstart Project NOMAD can be installed on any Debian-based operating system (we recommend Ubuntu 26.04 LTS; 24.04 LTS and Debian 12 are also supported). Installation is completely terminal-based, and all tools and resources are designed to be accessed through the browser, so there's no need for a desktop environment if you'd rather setup NOMAD as a "server" and access it through other clients. Before you start: NOMAD itself needs about 5 GB of disk and under 1 GB of RAM . The offline content you add afterwards is what actually fills a drive, and the AI Assistant is what drives the memory requirement up. See Device Requirements for both, and the FAQ for individual content sizes. Note: sudo/root privileges are required to run the install script Quick Install (Debian-based OS Only) sudo apt-get update && \
sudo apt-get install -y curl && \
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Crosstalk-Solutions/project-nomad/refs/heads/main/install/install_nomad.sh \
  -o install_nomad.sh && \
sudo bash install_nomad.sh Project NOMAD is now installed on your device! Open a browser and navigate to http://localhost:8080 (or http://DEVICE_IP:8080 ) to start exploring! For a complete step-by-step walkthrough (including Ubuntu installation), see the Installation Guide . For Windows users, see the WSL2 install guide — community-supported path covering native Docker and Docker Desktop install routes. Advanced Installation For more control over the installation process, copy and paste the Docker Compose template into a docker-compose.yml file and customize it to your liking (be sure to replace any placeholders with your actual values). Then, run docker compose up -d to start the Command Center and its dependencies. Note: this method is recommended for advanced users only, as it requires familiarity with Docker and manual configuration before starting. How It Works NOMAD is a management UI ("Command Center") and API that orchestrates a collection of containerized tools and resources via Docker . It handles installation, configuration, and updates for everything — so you don't have to. Built-in capabilities include: AI Chat with Knowledge Base — local AI chat powered by Ollama or you can use OpenAI API compatible software such as LM Studio or llama.cpp, with document upload and semantic search (RAG via Qdrant ) Information Library — offline Wikipedia, medical references, ebooks, and more via Kiwix Education Platform — Khan Academy courses with progress tracking via Kolibri Offline Maps — downloadable regional maps via ProtoMaps Data Tools — encryption, encoding, and analysis via CyberChef Notes — local note-taking via FlatNotes System Benchmark — hardware scoring with a community leaderboard Supply Depot — a one-click app catalog (PDF tools, file browser, e-book library, password manager, and more) plus the ability to run your own custom Docker containers Automatic Updates — opt-in, hands-off updates for the core software, installed apps, and offline content, on a schedule you control Easy Setup Wizard — guided first-time configuration with curated content collections NOMAD also includes built-in tools like a Wikipedia content selector, ZIM library manager, and content explorer. What's Included Capability Powered By What You Get Information Library Kiwix Offline Wikipedia, medical references, survival guides, ebooks AI Assistant Ollama + Qdrant Built-in chat with document upload and semantic search Education Platform Kolibri Khan Academy courses, progress tracking, multi-user support Offline Maps ProtoMaps Downloadable regional maps for offline viewing and search Data Tools CyberChef Encryption, encoding, hashing, and data analysis Notes FlatNotes Local note-taking with markdown support System Benchmark Built-in Hardware scoring, Builder Tags, and community leaderboard Supply Depot Built-in One-click app catalog + bring-your-own custom Docker containers Device Requirements While many similar offline survival computers are designed to be run on bare-minimum, lightweight hardware, Project NOMAD is quite the opposite. To install and run the
available AI tools, we highly encourage the use of a beefy, GPU-backed device to make the most of your install. At its core, however, NOMAD is still very lightweight. For a barebones installation of the management application itself, the following minimal specs are required: Note: Project NOMAD is not sponsored by any hardware manufacturer and is designed to be as hardware-agnostic as possible. The hardware listed below is for example/comparison use only Minimum Specs Processor: 2 GHz dual-core processor or better RAM: 4GB system memory (the whole stack without AI runs in under 1 GB) Storage: At least 5 GB free disk space (plan for 10 GB to install comfortably) OS: Debian-based (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS recommended) Stable internet connection (required during install only) Adding the AI Assistant brings the install to roughly 25 GB , because Ollama and a general-purpose model are both large, and a model needs about its download size in memory while it answers. That memory comes from VRAM if you have a discrete GPU and from system RAM if you do not, which is the single biggest reason the figures below are so much higher. To run LLMs and other included AI tools: Optimal Specs Processor: AMD Ryzen 7 or Intel Core i7 or better RAM: 32 GB system memory Graphics: NVIDIA RTX 3060 or AMD equivalent or better (more VRAM = run larger models) Storage: At least 250 GB free disk space (preferably on SSD) OS: Debian-based (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS recommended) Stable internet connection (required during install only) For detailed build recommendations at three price points ($150–$1,000+), see the Hardware Guide . Again, Project NOMAD itself is quite lightweight — it's the tools and resources you choose to install with NOMAD that will determine the specs required for your unique deployment Running AI models on a different host By default, NOMAD's installer will attempt to setup Ollama on the host when the AI Assistant is installed. However, if you would like to run the AI model on a different host, you can go to the settings of the AI assistant and input a URL for either an ollama or OpenAI-compatible API server (such as LM Studio). Note that if you use Ollama on a different host, you must start the server with this option: OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0 . Ollama is the preferred way to use the AI assistant, as it has features such as model download that OpenAI API does not support. So when using LM Studio, for example, you will have to use LM Studio to download models.
You are responsible for the setup of Ollama/OpenAI server on the other host. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) For answers to common questions about Project NOMAD, please see our FAQ page. About Internet Usage & Privacy Project NOMAD is designed for offline usage. An internet connection is only required during the initial installation (to download dependencies) and if you (the user) decide to download additional tools and resources at a later time. Otherwise, NOMAD does not require an internet connection and has ZERO built-in telemetry. To test internet connectivity, NOMAD first attempts to make a request to Cloudflare's utility endpoint, https://1.1.1.1/cdn-cgi/trace . If that endpoint is unreachable (for example, because your network blocks 1.1.1.1 ), it falls back to other endpoints the application already contacts (the GitHub API and the Project NOMAD API) and considers the connection online if any of them respond. You can override the endpoint used for this check in two ways. The connectivity test URL can be configured from the UI under Settings → Advanced (stored locally on your instance), or you can set the INTERNET_STATUS_TEST_URL environment variable.

title: openclaw/openclaw
abstract:
OpenClaw 🦞 — Your assistant, on your devices, in your chats OpenClaw is an open-source AI assistant that runs on your own computer and meets you in the channels you already use: Discord, iMessage, Slack, Teams, Telegram, WhatsApp, and 20+ more, plus native apps for macOS, iOS, Android, Windows, and Linux. One Gateway runs it as a personal assistant on a laptop or as a shared team deployment ; configuration is the only difference. Yours, with no catch. State, memory, and credentials live on your hardware. Models and agent harnesses (Claude, Codex, local models) are plugins you can swap without changing anything else. Your prompts go to the model provider and chat platforms you configure, plus any diagnostics export you enable yourself; by default OpenClaw itself phones home for nothing but a daily version check, anonymous feature statistics are opt-in, and update.checkOnStart: false disables both ( what OpenClaw sends ). OpenClaw is stewarded by the OpenClaw Foundation , an independent 501(c)(3), and has no paid tier, hosted service, or token. The architecture case — trusted gateway, untrusted execution, policy enforced by code — is in Why OpenClaw . Website · Docs · Getting started · Why OpenClaw · FAQ · Vision · DeepWiki Install The installer supports macOS, Linux, and Windows. It provisions a supported Node.js runtime when needed. # macOS / Linux / WSL2 curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash # Windows PowerShell iwr - useb https: // openclaw.ai / install.ps1 | iex Already manage Node.js? Install the published package instead (Node 24.22.1+ or 26.12.1+; Node 26 recommended): npm install -g openclaw@latest --allow-scripts=openclaw That command is for npm 12 or npm 11.16+. On npm 11.15 and earlier, omit --allow-scripts=openclaw . See the installation guide for the lifecycle script
contract, Docker, Nix, and other deployment paths. Quick start On a fresh install, the installer scripts start onboarding automatically.
Complete the wizard they open. If you installed the package directly with npm,
pnpm, or Bun, run: openclaw onboard --install-daemon After onboarding: openclaw gateway status
openclaw dashboard Onboarding verifies model access, creates the workspace, and configures the Gateway. The last command opens the Control UI; send a message there to confirm the assistant is working. See the getting started guide for channel setup and troubleshooting. How it fits together The Gateway is the local control plane for sessions, tools, events, and channel connections. The Control UI , CLI, and TUI connect to the Gateway. Channels bring the assistant to WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Google Chat, Signal, iMessage, and other messaging services. Companion apps and nodes add voice, Canvas, camera, screen, and device-local actions on supported platforms. OpenClaw works with hosted and local model providers . Its tools , skills , and plugins extend what an assistant can do. Security Treat inbound messages as untrusted input. DM-capable channels pair unknown senders by default; approve a pairing request with openclaw pairing approve <channel> <code> . Tools run on the host for the main session unless you configure sandboxing. Read the security guide , exposure runbook , and sandboxing guide before connecting other users or exposing the Gateway remotely. Documentation Goal Start here Configure models and auth Models · Model providers Connect a messaging service Channels Add tools, skills, and plugins Tools · Skills · Plugins · ClawHub Run apps and device nodes Platforms · Nodes Use the CLI and chat commands CLI reference · Slash commands Configure or operate the Gateway Configuration · Architecture · Updating · Release channels Development The repository is a pnpm workspace. Plain npm install at the repository root is not supported. git clone https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw.git cd openclaw
pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm ui:build See CONTRIBUTING.md for the contribution workflow and the source setup guide for the development loop. Governance OpenClaw is developed in the open by the OpenClaw Foundation , an independent 501(c)(3). The Foundation employs the core team and signs releases. Donors and infrastructure sponsors support the Foundation; none of them own or direct the project. OpenAI is a donor, not an owner. Community See CONTRIBUTING.md for maintainers and contribution guidelines; AI-assisted PRs are welcome. Use the issue chooser for bugs and feature requests, get official OpenClaw support at community.openclaw.ai , and report vulnerabilities through SECURITY.md . New capabilities usually belong in plugins built on the plugin SDK and shared through ClawHub . OpenClaw was built for Molty , a space lobster AI assistant, by Peter Steinberger and the community. Explore the project lore , soul.md , Peter's site , Star History , and @openclaw . Special thanks to Mario Zechner for his support and for pi , and to Adam Doppelt for the lobster.bot domain. Donors and sponsors The Foundation is funded by donors including Amazon, Lobster Computer Company, Offline Holdings, OpenAI, Red Hat, and the University of Michigan, with infrastructure support from Blacksmith, Convex, GitHub, NVIDIA, and Vercel. Contributors Thanks to all clawtributors: License MIT © OpenClaw Foundation. See THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for incorporated or adapted code.

title: infosave2007/aivpn
abstract:
Experimental Project. AIVPN is an engineering research project exploring network protocols and methods of protecting data in transit. It does not guarantee the ability to bypass network restrictions, anonymity, or protection against detection and blocking. The project has no political objectives. The project is not intended for unlawful use. Users must comply with the laws applicable where they are located and use the software at their own risk. The author does not endorse unlawful use of the project. Third-party claims about the project's guaranteed effectiveness or political purpose do not represent the author's position. 🌐 Русский | 中文 AIVPN Overview AIVPN combines UDP tunnel encryption with traffic masking. Masks define the outer protocol, packet sizes and send intervals. Being recognized as STUN or QUIC does not by itself prove statistical indistinguishability from a specific application. Key technical properties: InitialV2 and PFS - the initial exchange confirms a fresh server key; data and management commands travel only after PFS. Bound and privileged devices must also prove their persistent key and, when mTLS is required, present a valid certificate. O(1) session lookup — no session ID is transmitted in the clear. Every packet carries an 8-byte resonance tag derived from a timestamp and a per-session secret. The server resolves the session in constant time via a DashMap . Perfect Forward Secrecy — in-flight session key rotation via X25519 ratchet. Compromising the server key does not expose past traffic. Neural Resonance module — per-mask micro-MLP (~66 KB) monitors live traffic statistics; high reconstruction error triggers automatic mask rotation without disconnecting clients. Generative mask distributions - profiles support multimodal packet-size and inter-arrival models fitted from captured traffic with a BIC-selected Gaussian mixture. Clients sample the stored model; its presence does not establish similarity to a named application. Written in Rust — memory-safe, no GC pauses. Client binary ≈ 2.5 MB. Runs on a $5 VPS. Architecture Workspace layout crates/aivpn-common/     — shared crypto, protocol, mask profiles (no I/O)
crates/aivpn-server/     — Linux-only VPN gateway and management CLI
crates/aivpn-client/     — cross-platform VPN client (Linux / macOS / Windows)
crates/aivpn-android-core/ — JNI bridge for Android (Rust → Kotlin via C FFI)
crates/aivpn-ios-core/   — iOS Rust staticlib (C FFI), linked by PacketTunnelProvider
crates/aivpn-windows/    — Windows GUI (egui/eframe 0.31, manages aivpn-client.exe subprocess)
crates/aivpn-linux/      - Linux GUI (Iced 0.14, wraps aivpn-client subprocess)
platforms/android/       — Android Kotlin app (MVVM: MainViewModel + RecyclerView)
platforms/ios/           — iOS SwiftUI app + NetworkExtension PacketTunnelProvider
platforms/macos/         — macOS SwiftUI menu bar app + privileged helper daemon
platforms/aivpn-web/     — Web management panel (Hono 4 + SvelteKit 2, SQLite/PostgreSQL)
platforms/linux/         — Linux desktop packaging (AppImage, .desktop)
platforms/linux-kernel/  — optional in-kernel data-path module (out-of-tree)
platforms/openwrt/       — OpenWrt package
platforms/mikrotik/      — MikroTik RouterOS container
assets/masks/            — bundled traffic mimicry JSON profiles
assets/brand/            — icons and brand material
deploy/                  — server installer, systemd unit, Dockerfiles
deploy/ci/               — CI gates run by the Makefile (see `make help`) Key modules Module Location Purpose crypto.rs aivpn-common X25519 key exchange, ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD, BLAKE3/HMAC, resonance tag generation protocol.rs aivpn-common Wire format: [8-byte tag][pad_len][inner_header][encrypted payload][poly1305 tag] mask.rs aivpn-common MaskProfile — traffic shaping: header templates, FSM states, IAT distributions gateway.rs aivpn-server Central event loop: UDP receive, session dispatch, NAT forwarding, neural checks session.rs aivpn-server SessionManager — DashMap -based O(1) tag lookup, 256-entry replay window, 500-session cap neural.rs aivpn-server Neural Resonance: per-mask MLP 64→16→64 / fallback 64→128→64, MSE threshold 0.35, auto mask rotation client.rs aivpn-client State machine: Unprovisioned → Connecting → Connected, key exchange, reconnection tunnel.rs aivpn-client Cross-platform TUN: /dev/net/tun (Linux), utun (macOS), Wintun (Windows) mimicry.rs aivpn-client MimicryEngine — applies MaskProfile to outbound packets Initial exchange and accelerator compatibility Starting with 1.2.0, the initial exchange uses InitialV2. It is incompatible with 1.1.0 and earlier 1.2.0 development builds. Update servers, pool/site/chain nodes and all clients together, including embedded mobile cores. The connection key format and the inter-server management protocol are unchanged. The initial AEAD uses XChaCha20-Poly1305 with a random 24-byte nonce and the connection context in the AAD; the established channel keeps the existing ChaCha20-Poly1305 format and kernel ABI 7. The Linux module requires compatible Rust-for-Linux APIs, kernel headers built with CONFIG_RUST=y and the matching Rust toolchain. A kernel version number alone does not guarantee support. Before registering /dev/aivpn , the module checks file_operations.owner in the real miscdevice vtable and fails with ENODEV if the API does not pin the module code to the open descriptor. This check cannot be bypassed; without the accelerator, userspace TUN is used. Mask state and outer traffic validation The QUIC mask runs bidirectional QUIC v1/TLS 1.3: it keeps CIDs and packet numbers and handles ACKs, loss, timers and connection close. The engine runs inside the shared mask layer on top of the existing UDP/DatagramTransport. A cold Initial carries an empty Token. The initial AIVPN packet travels inside an encrypted HTTP DATAGRAM after TLS, HTTP/3 SETTINGS and CONNECT-UDP; until then payload data waits in a bounded queue. When the local buffer is full, the client waits for free space while it keeps processing ACKs and control messages. The logical UDP peer terminates inside the mask; no proxy sockets are opened. A plain GET and an unrelated CONNECT-UDP receive HTTP 403. CONNECT-UDP is not equivalent to ordinary HTTP/3 requests to Avito or VK Video and does not by itself prove similarity to them. Before inner authentication the server keeps a separate bounded TLS state that grants no VPN access and cannot replace an active session. Up to 128 such states are allowed globally, at most two per UDP peer, with at most ten seconds to complete setup; processing is charged to a shared CPU budget. Until the address is validated, responses are limited to three times the received traffic. TLS verifies the handshake signature and possession of the certificate key, but not the public PKI: trust in the server comes from the inner signed AIVPN exchange. 0-RTT and connection migration are disabled. The pre-authentication inbound packet limit is set by the server's --per-ip-pps-limit / AIVPN_PER_IP_PPS_LIMIT , 5000 packets per second per IP by default. The current QUIC generation with an admitted PFS session has a separate finite limit, --per-ip-authenticated-pps-limit / AIVPN_PER_IP_AUTHENTICATED_PPS_LIMIT , 100000 by default. Queues and counters for the two classes are bounded independently; pending TLS, plain and RTC traffic keep the first limit. The CID selects the route and quota but does not authenticate the packet: Quinn AEAD and the inner AIVPN checks remain mandatory, including for a known CID. Seven profiles open the exchange with an aligned optional STUN Binding Indication attribute. After PFS, the protected MaskState message binds the outer protocol parameters to the profile and connection generation. Zoom and webrtc_yandex_telemost_v1 use ICE/DTLS/SRTP; SberJazz and Telegram calls add TURN Allocate, Permission, ChannelBind and ChannelData. WhatsApp uses ICE/SRTP without DTLS, with separate per-direction keys from the protected exchange.

title: rivet-dev/rivet
abstract: Fast, high-density, scalable orchestration for agentic workloads. Rivet Actors are durable processes for agents, workflows, and sandboxes. 6.9 ms cold starts, 72 KB per Actor, billions on one control plane. One Rust binary and a bucket. No database, no message bus. Open source and self-hostable. Quickstart • Documentation • Changelog • Discord • X Getting Started Use with Your Coding Agent Give your coding agent the Rivet skills to create examples or integrate into existing projects: npx skills add rivet-dev/skills Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and other AI coding tools. Start From Scratch Node.js & Bun React Next.js Rust Effect View documentation → What is Rivet? Rivet is an orchestrator for agentic workloads. Where Kubernetes schedules pods, Rivet schedules Actors: long-lived processes with durable state, a SQLite database, a queue, realtime connections, and scheduling, each addressed by key. Create one Actor per agent, per session, per user, or per tenant. Run it on plain Node.js, Bun, or Rust. Open source and self-hostable. 72 KB per Actor : An Actor lives inside a node process you already run, not in its own container or VM. A server that held hundreds of pods holds hundreds of thousands of Actors. 6.9 ms cold starts : A cold start includes scheduling the Actor, creating its storage, and serving the first request. No image pull, no container boot. Billions of Actors on one control plane : Actors are scheduled independently, so adding capacity means adding machines. The same control plane runs a thousand Actors or a billion. Hibernates when idle, wakes on demand : An idle Actor writes its state and unloads. The next request brings it back in 4.4 ms with nothing lost. Keep state with each Actor : Every Actor gets its own SQLite database and key-value storage. The control plane replicates writes to the disks of several instances before acknowledging them, then moves data to object storage in the background. Storage never runs out and the bucket never sits on the write path. One Rust binary and a bucket : There is no database to run and no message bus. Control plane instances are identical, run every service, and find each other through the bucket. Run code agents generate at runtime : Each piece of new, untrusted code gets an Actor of its own, with its own database and filesystem and no reach into anyone else's. Works with the tools you already use : Typed SDKs for your backend and React hooks for your frontend. No custom runtime, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged. Backend import { actor } from "rivetkit" ; import { db } from "rivetkit/db" ; const agent = actor ( { // Per-Actor SQLite database, persisted across restarts and hibernation db : db ( { onMigrate : async ( db ) => { // Apply the SQLite schema await db . execute ( `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (role TEXT, content TEXT)` ) ; } , } ) , actions : { chat : async ( c , text : string ) => { // Durably save the message await c . db . execute ( "INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)" , "user" , text ) ; const messages = await c . db . execute ( "SELECT role, content FROM messages" ) ; const response = streamText ( { model : openai ( "gpt-5" ) , messages } ) ; // Stream tokens to every connected client for multiplayer for await ( const delta of response . textStream ) { c . broadcast ( "token" , delta ) ; } // Durably save the response await c . db . execute ( "INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)" , "assistant" , await response . text ) ; } , } , } ) ; Client (frontend or backend) // Connect to an Actor const agent = client . agent . getOrCreate ( "agent-123" ) . connect ( ) ; // Listen for realtime events agent . on ( "token" , delta => process . stdout . write ( delta ) ) ; // Call an action on the Actor await agent . chat ( "how many r's in strawberry?" ) ; Actor types Every product Rivet ships is an Actor, scheduled by the same control plane. Actors : Long-lived processes with state, realtime, and scheduling built in. Agents : A durable process per agent, with memory that survives restarts. Workflows : Multi-step operations that replay instead of starting over. Sandboxes (agentOS) : A filesystem, shell, and network for code you did not write. Dynamic Apps (preview): A backend per user, deployed the moment it is generated. Built for everything agents need Coding agents : One Actor per agent with a durable process, a sandbox, and state that survives restarts. Agent app builders : Your product generates a whole backend for a user; each one deploys as its own Actor that scales to zero. Company-specific agents : Run agents inside your VPC next to Postgres, your APIs, and your helpdesk, so no data leaves your cloud. Personal agents : A long-lived Actor per user with memory, scheduling, and reminders, online for months. Realtime apps : One Actor per document, room, or channel broadcasting changes to every connected client. How Actors compare to Kubernetes Rivet Actor Kubernetes pod Cold start 6.92 ms ~6 s Wake from hibernation 4.37 ms ~6 s (new pod) Memory per instance 72.4 KB ~200 MB Memory while idle 0 MB (hibernates) Always resident Scale Billions of Actors on one control plane ~5k nodes per cluster Storage Bottomless SQLite, replicated and moved to your bucket Persistent volume per pod Benchmark details & methodology Cold start (6.92 ms): Client send to full first reply from a newly created keyed Actor, including scheduling, storage creation, and framework startup: 6.92 ms p50, 8.11 ms p99 over 1,500 samples. Wake (4.37 ms): Client send to full reply from an Actor asleep for at least 10 seconds: 4.37 ms p50, 6.80 ms p99 over 1,200 samples. Setup: Measured October 25, 2026 on Azure eastus2 across three availability zones. Three control plane instances ( Standard_L8as_v5 , local NVMe), one per zone, with every write acknowledged by 2 of 3 instances. One node VM running Node.js 24 in the first zone. Full method and reproduction steps at rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking . Memory per instance (72.4 KB): RSS increase per running Actor. Measured with the Rust rivetkit SDK. Kubernetes figures are typical published values, not a matched benchmark. ~6 s cold start assumes a pre-provisioned node; ~200 MB is a typical idle Node.js pod; ~5k nodes is the documented cluster limit. Features Routing, scheduling, types, and telemetry, built in. Fault tolerance by design : A node going down reschedules its Actors elsewhere with their state intact. No replay harness or checkpointing of your own. Keep state with each Actor : Every Actor gets its own SQLite database and key-value storage. The control plane replicates writes and moves data to object storage, so you never size a disk for an Actor. Multi-region : Place Actors near the users and data they serve, and route requests to wherever each one currently lives. HTTP & WebSocket networking : Address an Actor directly over HTTP or hold a live WebSocket to it. No queue or broker in between. End-to-end type safety : Actor definitions generate their own client types, so a signature change breaks the build rather than production. React SDK : First-party hooks that subscribe a component to an Actor's state and keep it live as the Actor updates. OpenTelemetry & observability : Traces, metrics, and structured logs emitted in OTel format, into the collector you already run. Single Rust binary : The control plane ships as one static binary. Run a few identical instances behind a load balancer with an object storage bucket: no database and no message bus to stand up first. Cron & scheduling : Wake an Actor on a schedule or at a timestamp it sets for itself, without a separate scheduler. Sleeps when idle : Idle Actors release their resources and wake with durable state intact when the next request arrives. Actor-to-Actor calls : Actors address each other by key and call across the cluster as if the other one were local. No Kubernetes operator : One control plane behind a load balancer, speaking plain HTTP inside your VPC.

title: janhq/jan
abstract:
Jan - Open-source ChatGPT replacement English · 中文 · 日本語 Getting Started - Community - Changelog - Bug reports Jan is bringing the best of open-source AI in an easy-to-use product. title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
abstract:
Note: We're running a new Minecraft colony with 25 GPT-6.1 Terra agents. Follow on Twitch Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice). We teamed up with Olam Labs , which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry. Minecraft Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon . We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game. github.com/yc-software/minecraft-agent-harness Civ50 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs. The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages. At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access. plans/settlement.md Download Settlement coordination (Ada)

The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned. Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him. While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. title: Building an AI-native engineering org
abstract:
Last week Will Larson ( @Lethain ) asked how leaders are evaluating engineering managers for AI skills. My reply , a list of questions to think about, got a lot of bookmarks. More broadly, I've been thinking about how to build an AI-native engineering org for a while. Sharing some lessons from the last nine months of building at FurtherAI. Since January, the number of code changes each engineer merges a day has grown about 5x, while our revert rate has stayed under half a percent. But giving engineers coding agents didn't get us there on its own. Every time we sped up one step, work piled up at the next. So we started going through the entire process of shipping software, one step at a time, and figuring out what we could optimize. We also use our in-house Poirot and Sherlock agents to investigate and resolve issues across production and staging. They have all the tools and context they need across logs, metrics, trace and read-only database access Some of the best moments are when agents work together. Claude Tag triages a request, Devin does the work, and Poirot pulls the internal data it needs. It's fun to watch them talk to each other and pass information along. One interesting side effect is that non-engineers have started shipping code too. Our designer has merged about 50 changes since August, including the ones that built our design system. People in deployment and customer-facing roles can also make UI tweaks themselves right from slack None of this was free. Through the summer, much of our engineering effort went into tests and tooling, and customer-facing changes per engineer stayed between 17 and 30 a month. In September, that jumped to 45. October is on pace for 48. As engineering got faster, we started noticing a different problem. We got much faster at writing code, but not nearly as fast at deciding what to build. Say a feature used to take ten days: three to plan, six to build, and one to review. If agents make building 3.5× faster, but planning and review stay the same, the overall feature only gets 1.75× faster. Planning and review now account for 70% of the time, up from 40%. Traditionally, a lot of these decisions flow through engineering managers, PMs, and designers. That becomes increasingly difficult as engineers get faster. How do you organize a team where engineers can build much faster, without creating bottlenecks around decisions and reviews? Our bet is to push more ownership to engineers. Rather than adding more layers of management, we want engineers to handle more of the planning, execution, and review themselves. That changes what we expect from engineers and managers. I'm starting to think of engineering seniority in terms of how much of a problem someone can own end to end. Roughly: It also means engineers need to be closer to customers. We're empowering engineers to own more of the process end-end, from understanding the customer problem to shipping a solution to verifying success and owning regressions in production. This also changes what we expect from engineering managers. Managers need to understand what's being built, why, and whether it's the right solution. I want managers trying features on staging as an end user would, not just checking that the code was reviewed. You catch a different class of problems when you actually use the product. But the goal isn't just to review more. As always, it's to develop engineers who can make the right decisions themselves, so managers only step in on the ones that need their judgment. When writing code becomes cheaper, deciding what to build matters a lot more. I want engineering managers who understand customers, have strong product opinions, and are comfortable making product decisions, not just technical ones. They should also help engineers develop that judgment. We shouldn't need a PM or designer to make every small product decision. We spent most of this year figuring out how to make engineers faster. Now we're trying to figure out how to make the entire organization move at that speed. I suspect this will be a harder problem than automating code, tests, and reviews. We're still early, and there's a lot we haven't figured out. But it's one of the most interesting engineering challenges I've worked on. I'm curious what other teams are seeing. What broke first as your engineers started shipping faster? We're hiring Engineering Manager / Director at @furtheraicom to solve the next wave of challenges. If this sounds interesting, reach out! title: Google value plunges by $500B as AI fears rattle Wall Street
abstract:
Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales 9 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Kali Hays , Technology reporter and Mitchell Labiak , Business reporter EPA Google CEO Sundar Pichai has backed the company's massive spending on AI. Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hitting search advertising revenue. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said Google's "AI mode", where it answers questions conversationally, was eating into the money it makes from ads which appear next to results to traditional search questions. Yet, Schindler said he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine. Google's role in answering the world's questions has been challenged by the AI boom, with millions of people using programs such as ChatGPT and Claude instead. Kim Scott, who formerly led Google's advertising business, told the BBC's Today programme that the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch" by having its own AI summaries hit its search revenue. She said that Google was founded on the idea of making long-term bets on technology – even if they hurt the firm in the short term. "I think they're making a long-term bet on AI," she said. In its results published on Wednesday, Alphabet revealed that total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn. However, the firm did not make as much money as analysts had predicted, particularly in its advertising arm, which spooked many investors. Shares in the company plummeted over 12% to a six-month low following the release of the results. By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before. Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing Search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses." Investors not buying Amazon's trillion-dollar business hopes Microsoft and Amazon also issued updates this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending huge sums of cash in the ongoing AI race. But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business. Amazon's stock took a hit on Thursday , with its shares falling 6% in after-hours trading. Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn. That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months. Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future. Jassy noted that Amazon's cloud services business, as well as retail stores, may be those businesses. During a call with financial analysts he also repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools. "One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true." As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added. "We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon." Microsoft begs the question of AI's real value Wall Street's reaction to Microsoft's update was more muted, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday. The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers , which will further reduce the company's costs. Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn. Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago. Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors. But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI. "Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said. title: Cisco gives engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite 98% of the company's code
abstract:
(Image credit: Getty Images) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 16 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Subscribe to our newsletter In a world where youth unemployment is growing as AI replaces more and more entry-level jobs, Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel is going for a different approach. According to a report by Fortune , he's given a 27-year-old ex-startup founder — brought into the company by an earlier acquisition, and previously languishing in a role five levels below — a new job to refactor 98% of the company's legacy code within 24 months. The employee, Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, joined Cisco after it acquired EzDubs, a translation startup that Krishnamurthy helped build in 2023. While having executive experience, Patel found that "Paddy" was left "buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic." According to the report, Patel spoke to Krishnamurthy in Cisco's office in San Francisco, where Krishnamurthy told him that he could rewrite Cisco's legacy code in a team of just two people, and that "even the most AI-forward people on [Patel's] own team weren't thinking that way." Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here: As a result, he's now been tasked with rewriting 98% of Cisco's legacy code within 24 months, with four weeks as a proof of concept. "I've given him unlimited tokens because he's going to refactor code," according to Patel, telling him "you can go nuts." AI coding has skyrocketed in recent months, with GitHub forced to deploy 4 million extra CPU cores and 160 petabytes of storage to cope . However, the practice is not without its pitfalls, with rogue AI agents notorious for taking unsolicited actions including deleting entire company databases, TV show edits , and production setups . Patel hopes that there are more young hires in the Krishnamurthy mould that he can find, both in the company and externally to hire. He's looking for hires to "challenge the system and the status quo," to be "an energizer bunny that just goes and kind of revs everyone up." Patel believes that current corporate structures work against this kind of thinking. "If you don't hire the early-in-career [workers], and you just let your workforce continue the way that they were, where do fresh ideas get injected? How do you challenge the status quo?" He acknowledges that this will create friction, putting Gen Z employees among decades-old employees. "Tension is good.... I actually try to create tension in the teams because you want to have enough friction on the ideas. You don't want to have friction with the people and personalities." Patel believes that a combination of experienced, scale operators at Cisco, alongside external hires and "entrepreneurial founders, CEOs and engineers who are AI-native" will bring results. "Either of these groups by themselves aren't nearly as potent as when all three work together. It's what creates magic." title: The importance of communities around software
abstract:
lumi's code spelunking adventures The importance of communities around software As usual, the people are the important thing. Who could've guessed? :3 I've done a lot of activism for software freedom, over the years. At first it was
purely for software freedom and related topics, (such as security, autonomy and
privacy) but eventually this has evolved into something more holistic. I believe
that the software I use should be held to higher ethical standards than only being
free software. My activism used to focus on strong copyleft licenses, these are licenses which
require that the project stay free; that no-one can take the project and make it
proprietary. This has taken a backseat, as I now believe that there is something
more important than license: community . The community around a software project
is what dictates the values of the project. A strong copyleft license does still
signal that the project cares about software freedom, but, by itself it is not
enough. Copyright has always been a system that upholds the hegemony of the powerful,
it enriches corporations at the expense of the working class. Copyleft licenses
do use copyright against them, but can only do so much. We are using an abusive
system against itself, which is not sustainable or desirable in the long term. Software being free also states nothing about other ethical values of the project,
such as whether it is inclusive and whether it is run by its own community, or by
a corporation. It also states nothing about whether the project endorses extractive
technologies such as generative models. As an example of a project which is technically free software, but does not value
software freedom at all, consider an AGPL-3.0 project that is dual-licensed under
a commercial license and forces a contributor license agreement on its contributors.
This project is not community-run at all and is only free software in a narrow
sense of the word. This is why I don't care as much anymore about a project being under a copyleft
free software license or a non-copyleft free software license. It is still true
that the software being available under a strong copyleft license sends a signal
that the project cares about software freedom, but it is not a guarantee. So, if the license is not the (only) thing we need to look at, what do we also
need to look at? This depends on your own priorities, of course, but there are a
few things I could mention: Does the project have an inclusive code of conduct? Does the code of conduct or contribution policy ban generative models? Is the project completely in the hands of a corporation? Is there a contributor license agreement? Does it endorse proprietary and/or centralized platforms such as Discord and GitHub? What are the values of the lead developers of the project? Do they care about ethics in software? Try to join the communities of free software projects you use and care about,
eventually maybe even try to contribute. Even if you can't code, there are many
other tasks that need to be done: community management, documentation, artwork,
triage, outreach, and many other tasks. In the end, it's the community around a
project that shapes its values, so be a part of that community and push against
anything unethical. Speak up, if you can. For every person speaking up, there
will be many that can't or won't speak up; be their voice. Getting together to build software is important. Like stated before, this can
mean joining an existing project, but it can also mean creating a new one. It
can also mean joining or creating a software cooperative. These are communities
of people that develop software together. One community can span multiple
projects and we can all help one-another out. Examples include The Starlight Network and Polyphony . Meow. :333

abstract: Hi everyone! I had the idea for catcopter on my mind for a long time (got the domain ~13 years ago). It's a web multiplayer game where you can fly a dangerous cat and engage in competition with other players and critters (pterodactyls, chickens and angry penguins). I made it initially for me and my friends but it was quite fun so I thought I'll share it here too. The game is intentionally dorky and it was fun to develop. The tools I used were mostly Opus 5.5 (objects / rigging / motion), Tripo3d for some elements I struggled with and Fable for optimisation (cpu / networking). Backend physics are done with Rapier. Luckily I had a lot of elements / game dynamics done before from another project of mine ( https://flat.social ) so the actual iteration here took me around a week.

title: Herdr has released native app
abstract:
Herdr Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window. Install Linux and macOS curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source . Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64. The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin .
Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks.
On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app .
For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications. Windows Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer): irm https: // releases.herdr.dev / app / install.ps1 | iex Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up. Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer.
They also install herdr-core if it is missing.
The app can help install or update a core it cannot use. Find your work A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs . Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other. An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays.
New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder. The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent.
Agents that report status show as: Working: still busy. Blocked: waiting for you. Done: finished while you were looking elsewhere. Idle: not working, or a finished agent you have looked at. Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek , over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work.
Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS.
An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine. The window arranges terminals. The core runs them.
Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals.
After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs. Work on another machine Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action.
Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it.
Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer. Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom.
Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up. Make it yours Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences.
The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98.
A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs. Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start.
Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it.
A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error. Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json ; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format. Layouts and mods · Commands Updates and privacy Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core.
Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette.
Builds from source do not update themselves. Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy.
Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod. For agents herdr-app --skill This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here.
Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see. herdr-app ls
herdr-app status
herdr-app commands The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one.
See the command reference for arguments. Build from source For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing . Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI .
Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow. git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app.git cd herdr-app
just build
just test just install Install just to use these recipes.
The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop.
On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place.
Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build. Documentation checks also need Bun : just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages. To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build: python scripts/bench.py --bin < app executable > --set spinners --seconds 20 The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS. python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root <artifact folder> reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py .

title: A tiny world model running games on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W
abstract:
Using 2 small neural networks to generate and play the game at the same time on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W. The first one creates the game: given the current frame and the action, it predicts the next frame and the reward. The second one plays that game: it uses the generated frame and picks an action. Every frame above was sampled by the world model network, and the actions were taken by the actor network. Why I got interested in looped transformers, where one transformer block is applied several times with the same weights instead of stacking different layers. Reusing weights is cheap on memory, so I wanted to see if a looped world model could be small enough to run on a microcontroller. I picked the Pico 2 W because it is cheap and has an FPU, and small games because I could write the real versions directly into numpy and check every generated frame against them. Later I added a streaming RL agent so the board could also learn to play inside its own dream. Contents: the two networks · the games · the world model · the agents · quantization · on the chip · flashing · browser · reproduce · code layout The world model and the actor network 1: the world model network 2: the actor job frame + action → next frame + reward frame → action architecture looped transformer, q int8 MLP with two hidden layers, float32 size 26k–131k parameters 9k–16k parameters cost per frame 2–8M multiply-adds 9k–16k multiply-adds trained on recorded real games ( how ) with stream-x, in the real game or inside the dream ( how ) The size depends on the game, some games require more parameters to learn them to be playable, we tried to get to keep the number of the parameters small enough. On the chip neither network ever uses the real game: the actor only sees frames the world model, and the world model only gets actions from the actor. Both run on core 1 of the RP2350, while core 0 handles USB and the display. The pretrained actor can be swapped for a fresh stream-x agent that learns from scratch on the board. And any button press hands control to you, so you can play the dream yourself. The games Each game is a few hundred lines of numpy in src/tinyworldformer/games/ . It renders to a small grid of token ids, and one frame always holds the whole game state, so hidden state has to be drawn into the frame: the ball's heading is part of its token, and Doom-lite has a minimap. game frame rules random event world model exact frames, 2 loops Breakout 20×16 paddle, ball, 56 bricks, 5 lives the serve after a miss 26k params, 4.3M MACs 99.99% Doom-lite 32×32 raycast first-person view of an 8×8 maze; an enemy walks shortest paths to you; you shoot the enemy's respawn 55k params, 4.2M MACs 83.6% (see below) Flappy Bird 24×24 gravity, flaps, scrolling pipes the next gap height 46k params, 2.0M MACs 100% Pong 20×32 you against a CPU paddle that reacts late, first to 5 the serve after a point 46k params, 2.3M MACs 99.45% Pac-Man lite 48×48 23×21 maze, 249 pellets, two ghosts on shortest paths, 3 lives the ghosts' respawn 131k params, 8.2M MACs 86.4% "Exact frames" is the share of held-out transitions where every cell of the predicted frame matches the real game. Frames right after a random event are left out, since those can only be sampled, not predicted. Doom-lite's 3D view has 768 cells and a single shaded wall pixel off counts the whole frame as wrong, so its number looks worse than it plays; the game state is almost always right (see checking the dream ). You can play the real games in a terminal: uv run python -m tinyworldformer.games.play --game pacman (or breakout , doomlite , flappy , pong ). How the world model works Frames split into tokens The frame is cut into square patches: 2×2 cells in Breakout, 4×4 in Doom-lite, Flappy Bird and Pong, 6×6 in Pac-Man. That gives 36 to 80 tokens per game. A patch's embedding is the sum of one learned vector per cell, with a separate table for each position inside the patch so the cell order isn't lost. Every token also gets a position vector and the action's vector. Looped Transformer The model is a single transformer block (attention plus a ReLU MLP) with one set of weights, applied 1 to 4 times, with the input added back before every pass. The output after every pass is trained against the next frame, so at run time the loop count trades speed for accuracy. On the Pico to keep a decent frame rate we use uses two loops. The animation shows one held-out Doom-lite step. After one pass the model draws an enemy that isn't there, and each further pass removes part of it: 92, 35, 12, then 0 wrong cells. The bars on the right are the share of held-out frames each loop count gets exactly right. Here is a dreamed Doom-lite step decoded after 1, 2, 3 and 4 loops, with red boxes on cells that differ from the real rules: Exact held-out frames by loop count: loops Breakout Doom-lite Flappy Bird Pong Pac-Man 1 99.68% 59.8% 99.99% 98.47% 79.6% 2 99.99% 83.6% 100% 99.45% 86.4% 3 100% 85.9% 100% 99.60% 85.7% 4 99.96% 84.7% 100% 99.53% 84.4% Decoding The model outputs a score for every cell and every token. Turning those scores into a frame turned out to matter almost as much as the model, and it ended up as three rules (shown above on Pong): Background cells (walls, bricks, pellets, floor) each take their most likely token independently. Singletons (the ball, the player, each ghost) are placed with one choice over all (cell, token) pairs, so there is always exactly one of each. After a random event the choice is sampled among candidates within 2.2 logits of the best, so the world model samples a new serve or respawn instead of averaging them. Pac-Man and the ghosts are 2×2 sprites, but only one cell of each carries state (the mouth holds the heading; the ghost's lower-left cell holds whether a pellet is underneath). The other three cells are stamped from it instead of predicted. We implemented Rule 2 because the first Breakout model drew two balls at once; one global choice took exact frames from 91.6% to 99.7%. Checking the world model Accuracy on recorded data wasn't enough. An agent drives the dream into states the data never had, and any mistake there is something it can exploit. So the main check runs while an agent plays: read the game state back off the dreamed frame ( games/<game>.py: read ), apply the real rules to that state and the agent's action, and compare the result with the next dreamed frame and reward. 5,000 dreamed steps per game at 2 loops, with the shipped agent ( training/evalwm.py --agent ): game wrong game states wrong rewards wrong cells per step Breakout not read back; 0 frames with impossible tokens 6 (paid without a brick breaking) – Doom-lite 1 0 1.50 Flappy Bird 0 0 0.00 Pong 1 0 0.00 Pac-Man 742 38 0.39 Training First, agents play the real game and every step is recorded as one example (frame, action, next frame, reward), 1–3 million per game. Some episodes start from unusual states, like bricks with holes or random positions, so the data covers more of the game. Then the world model learns to predict the next frame with a per-cell cross-entropy loss: 30k steps, with the first 3–4k steps run in float, then int8 rounding switches on ( QAT ). The int8 weights are written into Rust source with every float stored as its exact bits. We check them with cargo test to reproduces the Python integer spec bit for bit, and then the firmware runs on the Pico. An agent trained in the world model reaches states the recorded data never had, so record real games with that agent and fine-tune the world model on everything. The agent in different games stated exploiting them so those are some fixes to it: Weighting the loss by "this cell changed" biased the model toward predicting change, so it drew two balls and broke two bricks. Weighting by where things can happen in the input frame, plus the global singleton choice, fixed it.

title: Pico CSS is no longer maintained
abstract:
This repository was archived by the owner on Oct 4, 2026. It is now read-only. Pico CSS is no longer maintained #754 lucaslarroche announced in Announcements Pico CSS is no longer maintained #754 lucaslarroche Oct 4, 2026 · 0 comments Return to top Discussion options Uh oh! There was an error while loading. Please reload this page . Quote reply lucaslarroche Oct 4, 2026 Maintainer v2.1.1 is the final release. Why Today, AI can generate lightweight, standalone, accessible HTML with just the CSS it needs, so a Minimal CSS Framework for Semantic HTML matters less than it used to. To stay relevant, Pico CSS would need a full rewrite: plain modern CSS instead of Sass, built on features it doesn't use today (OKLCH colors, cascade layers, Popover, anchor positioning) with fallbacks for older browsers, and a native compiler that strips unused CSS and makes customization easy. That would be a different project. Pico CSS stays as it is. What this means Nothing breaks. npm , the jsDelivr CDN and picocss.com stay online for the long term. The repositories are archived. No new issues, PRs or releases. Pico CSS is MIT licensed . You're free to fork it and take it further. See community forks . The Pico CSS name and logo are not covered by the MIT license. Please give your fork its own name, so users don't confuse it with the original. Thank you What started as a small side project ended up powering thousands of websites. Thank you to everyone who used it, opened issues, sent pull requests and wrote kind messages over the years. title: Florilegium: Procedural Flowers in LaTeX
abstract:
florilegium Origin The Reddit post asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made, and
this project doesn't try to reproduce it. It is one possible way, and the way I did it:
hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua, placed by a procedural
layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature.
It gets a similar look. What it is Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported
paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua
while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the
PDF. Every page gets its own garden. Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills
whatever space the text leaves free. Two documents share one package, and a third shows what else it does: florilegium.tex florilegium-grow.tex composition authored : stems, leaves and flowers placed by hand, every parameter sampled grown : a plant grown to fit the page by a greedy space-filling loop adapts to nothing (tuned for A4, 68 mm margin) the page layout, and the free space below the text on the last page preview Both PDFs are self-describing: the body text is the write-up of how the margin is drawn. Last page of the grown document: the text ends early, so branches arch into the space below. 300 dpi crop. Mottled washes with white streaks lifted out, lobed leaves with white veins,
forget-me-not cymes, a pale ghost flower behind the stems. Watch it grow as it grows with the free space it fills Seed 6, from an empty margin to the finished page. The stems rise first, leaves open as
the tips pass their nodes, and each stem ends in a flower. Then the greedy loop takes over:
on the right, each dashed circle is the largest free disc it found, just before a branch
grows to it. Big holes come first and slowly, small ones last and fast. The butterflies and
bees fly in, the bird glides onto its twig, and the snail crawls up its stem until the last
frame, which is exactly the page this seed always gives. The growth is recorded once, while the page is laid out: each stem is also drawn as
prefixes of increasing length and each motif at a few smaller scales, replaying the same
random draws. A frame then writes the pieces whose time has come, in their original
painting order. make grow-6 renders one seed this way ( build/grow-6.gif and .mp4 , about
45 seconds); add EXPLAIN=1 for the dashed circles. The margin reads the text showcase.tex , "A year in the margin": spring on the first page, summer, autumn on the
last. Each section describes the feature it shows. The grown margin can respond to the document around it: Initials. \florilegiuminitial[5]{E} sets the first letter of a paragraph in a tile
five lines tall. The outline of the letter is read from an OpenType font (Latin Modern
Bold by default) and painted like a petal; a vine passes over and under its strokes in
turn, with leaves where they fit and flowers in the gaps, often in the letter's counters.
The letter is also typeset invisibly, so the paragraph still copies as "Every". Flowers at the headings. With the option sections , every numbered section and
subsection gets a flower in the margin beside its heading, painted in the copper of the
accents, the way headings were once picked out in red. A flower where the text asks. \florilegiumbloom puts a flower beside the line it
stands in; \florilegiumbloom[lily] asks for any motif of the garden. The marks are found
in the page box when the page is shipped out, so this works in one run. Seasons. With the option aging , the garden ages from spring on the first page
(mostly in bud, small pale leaves) to autumn on the last (seed heads, falling petals, a
few copper leaves). It needs two runs, for the page count; \florilegiumage{0.8} sets an
age by hand instead. One seed in spring, early summer, late summer and autumn. The seasons change what grows,
not where. Visitors Most pages have visitors: a butterfly or two and bees in the open spaces, a snail crawling
up one of the main stems, and on about one page in five a bird perched on a twig of its own.
They come from a random stream of their own, so a page without them is exactly the page it
would have been; the option novisitors leaves them out. Any ink The whole palette comes from one color, ink : Delft blue, sepia, green, crimson, violet,
teal. The ramp from the darkest stroke to the palest wash is computed from that hue in
OKLCH, so the light end never turns gray. In PostScript postscript/florilegium.ps : the grown margin in pure PostScript, one self-contained file.
Ghostscript, or a printer, computes every petal while it interprets the page, and the
two pages of text explain how. The drawing core, every primitive and the growth loop are ported from ink.lua , flora.lua and grow.lua , procedure for procedure. It needs no TeX and no other file: gs -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dSeed=7 -o garden.pdf postscript/florilegium.ps
make postscript # the same -> build/postscript-7.pdf; SEED=12 for another garden -dSeed=N picks the garden; without it the clock picks one, so every print is new. -dAge=0 to 1 sets the season, and -dNoVisitors leaves out the butterflies, bees, snail
and bird. Two pages take about 2.5 seconds. Much of the Lua maps directly: PostScript's own
transformation matrix places each primitive (translate, rotate, scale), paths and Bézier
curves are native, and procedures built at run time stand in for Lua's closures (a petal's
half-width is a procedure handed to the outline builder). Four things don't map: Layers. The garden grows in one order but is painted back to front, so every fill and
stroke is captured with pathforall into a list per layer, and the lists are played back
at the end. Transparency. PostScript has none. Ghostscript provides it with -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY .
Without that flag, or on a printer, each translucent fill is mixed with the color it is
likely to land on and painted opaque. The result is flatter, but it's the same garden. Randomness. The generator is Park-Miller in 32-bit integer arithmetic, and PostScript
reals are single precision, so seed 7 here is a different garden from seed 7 in LaTeX. Text. The file typesets its own two pages in Times. It knows where its headings are and
where its text ends, so the copper flowers at the headings and the garden under the last
line work as they do in LaTeX. It has no initials, animation or authored composition. The file sent twice to an Epson inkjet with lp postscript/florilegium.ps , with no seed
given. The computer's print system runs the program again for each job, so each print takes
its seed from the clock and grows a different garden. A printer gets the opaque version, as
it has no transparency. Build LuaLaTeX, one pass, about a second a page (two passes for showcase.tex , whose seasons need
the page count). make # the three PDFs make seed-7 # one page from seed 7 -> build/seed-7.pdf make gallery # gallery/seeds.png + seeds.gif, inks.png, seasons.png (python3, Pillow, pdftoppm) make grow-6 # growth animation of seed 6 -> build/grow-6.gif + .mp4 (ffmpeg) make grow-6 EXPLAIN=1 # the same with the free discs marked -> build/grow-6-explain.* No TeX installed? Build the image once and run everything in it: docker build -t florilegium-tex tools
make RUN=tools/in-docker Or paste florilegium.sty , the six .lua files and one of the .tex files into an Overleaf project and set the compiler to LuaLaTeX. Use it in your own document: \usepackage [ grown ]{ florilegium } % or plain \usepackage{florilegium} for the authored one % options for the grown one: sections (flowers at the headings), aging (two runs), % novisitors (no butterflies, bees, snails or birds) \definecolor {ink}{HTML}{5B2A1F} % optional: the hue of the whole palette (this is sepia) \definecolor {accent}{HTML}{B4662F} % optional: the copper of the hairlines ...
