title: Show HN: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer
abstract: Instead of trying to run DOOM on things, I have instead decided to use DOOM (many, many, many doom games actually) to create a transformer. For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do : It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map! It can talk(kinda) You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4. If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

title: The Great American Rascal: Tom Sawyer at 150
abstract:
Books Reviewed The Adventures of Tom Sawyer Buy The Adventures of Tom Sawyer marks its 150th anniversary this year. It was first published in 1876, the centennial year of the American Founding. The novel itself marked its own kind of founding moment for American literature, which had been laboring—to borrow a phrase from The Federalist —under the “arrogant pretensions of the European.” America may have broken free of Great Britain in 1776, but we remained enthralled to Europe culturally for much longer. In his 1837 essay “The American Scholar,” Ralph Waldo Emerson lamented that American writers had “listened too long to the courtly muses of Europe” and scraped by on the “sere remains of foreign harvests.” Emerson then issued what Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr. dubbed an “Intellectual Declaration of Independence.” For Emerson, “genius looks forward.” He wanted to find, as he put it in his 1844 essay “The Poet,” the Homer of America—a bard “with a tyrannous eye” who “knew the value of our incomparable materials, and saw, in the barbarism and materialism of the times, another carnival of the same gods whose picture [one] so much admires in Homer.” In much the same spirit, Walt Whitman longed for a “democratic literature” filled with “archetypal poems” that could thicken America’s cultural “marrow.” American men of letters such as James Fenimore Cooper, Edgar Allan Poe, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville, and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow each made their contributions in the struggle to pull away culturally from Europe. But it was Samuel Clemens—Mark Twain—who made the decisive revolutionary break. In the words of the critic William Dean Howells, “I knew them all…our sages, poets, seers, critics, humorists; they were like one another and like other literary men; but Clemens was sole, incomparable, the Lincoln of our literature.” With The Adventures of Tom Sawyer , his first novel, Twain offered a new archetypal hero for democracy. He replaced the squeaky-clean “model boys” that tended to star in mid-19th century serials like McGuffey’s Eclectic Readers and Peter Parley’s Magazine , to which Twain’s father had subscribed. Tom is an altogether more vivid, more fully realized kind of boy. He leaps off the page from the very first word of the novel, which is his name, printed in huge capital letters: “‘TOM!’” yells his Aunt Polly. “‘What’s gone with that boy, I wonder? You, TOM!” An early review from England criticized the “queer Americanizing of the language.” The frontier vernacular was part of the point, however, as distinctive as the behavior of the boy hero. In the first chapter, on day one alone, Tom hides in a closet gorging on forbidden jam, runs away from Aunt Polly’s whipping, plays hooky from school to go swimming, opportunistically steals sugar at the dinner table, lies to his aunt about being in school, and gets into a fight with a new boy in town because he is well-dressed and wearing shoes. Twain announces outright that Tom “was not the Model Boy of the village.” He reinforces this theme so well throughout the novel that the Brooklyn Public Library excluded The Adventures of Tom Sawyer from their reading room upon its publication. Other reactions were more appreciative and far-seeing. Moncure Conway, Twain’s friend and literary agent in London, observed: “The book will no doubt be a favorite with boys, for whom it must in good part have been intended; but next to boys we should say that it might be most prized by philosophers and poets!” Conway was among the few (even to this day) to grasp the deeper import of the novel, which is often wrongfully dismissed as simply a humorously nostalgic tale for children. But one philosopher who seems to have appreciated Tom Sawyer ’s many subtleties was Friedrich Nietzsche. He wrote to his friend Franz Overbeck in 1879 that his mother had been reading it to him so he could rest his strained eyes. In another letter, this one to the novelist Paul Rée, he declared that he preferred Mark Twain’s American “silliness” to German “cleverness.” The Mischief-Maker of Missouri Perhaps there is a Nietzschean streak to Tom. He certainly delights in upending the staid morality of St. Petersburg, Missouri, whose inhabitants Twain describes as “grave, unromantic men.” They are locked into the drab ritual formalities of what Leo Strauss called the joyless pursuit of joy: grinding labor without much delight in profit; dutiful rote piety without genuine religious passion. Tom shocks and offends the sensibilities of almost everyone around him, but he also enlivens their world and broadens their horizons, turning the dour solemnities of the town into a backdrop for his playfully mischievous imagination. The most famous scene in the book is the one in which Aunt Polly punishes Tom for playing hooky by making him whitewash her fence on a Saturday morning. In late edits, Twain enhanced the fence from four feet high to mythic proportions—a forbidding structure nine feet tall and 30 yards wide. Yet Tom somehow convinces the other boys in town that whitewashing may not be work after all. “What do you call work?” Tom asks his peer Ben Rogers. “Why ain’t that work?” replies Ben. “Well, maybe it is, and maybe it ain’t,” says Tom. “All I know, is, it suits Tom Sawyer.” Tom neither denies nor affirms that whitewashing is work, shrouding the act in an air of mystery and bending reality by the sheer force of his will until his friends look with envy at a dull chore. An engrossed Tom refuses Ben’s initial pleas to take a turn by telling him Aunt Polly is very particular about this fence, lying that he had to turn away his half-brother, Sid, and the enslaved Jim, who wanted to try. Soon the boys pour out all their worldly goods at Tom’s feet, essentially paying him for their own labor and putting three fine coats of paint on the entire fence. Twain calls this a “slaughter of innocents,” in which Tom discovers “it’s not such a hollow world after all.” He learns, writes Twain, that “Work consists of whatever a body is obliged to do and that Play consists of whatever a body is not obliged to do.” He resolves Karl Marx’s problem of the manual worker’s alienation from his labor, yet he still makes a good capitalist profit. It’s a win-win. Harry V. Jaffa, in his definitive 1972 essay on the novel, “Tom Sawyer: Hero of Middle America” (collected in The Conditions of Freedom: Essays in Political Philosophy , 1975), captures the enormity of Tom’s ruse: “What he realizes is pure profit, purer profit indeed than Karl Marx ever imagined in his wildest polemics, against the iniquity of surplus value.” The whitewashing episode is just the first of Tom’s many successful bids to jolt his quiet town into levity. He is at his impish best in church. As Alexis de Tocqueville recognized, Americans’ religious zeal can sometimes be “so methodical, so calculated that it would seem that the head rather than the heart leads them to the foot of the altar.” St. Petersburg’s congregants labor under the weight of sermons that “[deal] in limitless fire and brimstone and [thin] the predestined elect down to a company so small as to be hardly worth saving.” Tom comes to the rescue, however, and finds a way to relieve the ceaseless fretting over predestination. He uses the loot he got from the whitewashing incident to buy Bible verse tickets, given to children in exchange for memorizing verses. Tom, who rattles off dialogue from The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood by heart, goes to church “snarling” and struggles to recite so much as a sentence from the Beatitudes. So, what a surprise—“the most stunning surprise of the decade”—when he presents enough tickets to claim the coveted prize of an illustrated Doré Bible, awarded to the pupil for memorizing 2,000 verses. The revered local celebrity, Judge Thatcher, gives a predictably moralistic lecture forecasting that when Tom becomes a great man he’ll owe it all to the lessons of his Sunday School days.

title: Alphabet heads for a $500B drop in market value, biggest in its history
abstract:
Alphabet loses $475 billion in market value, the biggest drop in its history Jared Blikre Fri, October 30, 2026 at 11:17 AM CDT 3 min read GOOG SPCX NVDA Alphabet ( GOOGL ) had its worst day ever on Thursday. The stock fell nearly 13% after its third quarter results , steeper than any session since it went public in 2004, including its drops of more than 10% in March 2020 and September 2008. Alphabet lost $475 billion in stock market value, the second-biggest one-day loss ever for a US-listed company, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Only Nvidia ( NVDA ) has lost more, about $593 billion on Jan. 27, 2025, the day China's DeepSeek rattled AI investors. Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance That blew past the $400 billion SpaceX ( SPCX ) lost on June 22, the previous No. 2. In dollars, it was Alphabet's worst day by far. Its previous worst was about $275 billion on July 23. It was also the stock's steepest drop after an earnings report since the company went public, according to Bespoke Investment Group . The previous low was a slide of nearly 10% in July 2008. Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance The quarter gave both sides plenty to argue over. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to about $31 billion, and the Gemini app passed 1 billion users. But search revenue grew 12% to about $63 billion, short of Wall Street's roughly $65 billion estimate. Free cash flow — the cash left after paying for things like data centers — swung to a loss of about $9 billion as AI spending climbed. The company's stakes in AI labs cost it too. "The bears will argue this is the first quarter that AI is starting to seriously hurt their search business," Pivotal Research CEO Jeffrey Wlodarczak said in a rundown of why investors hated the quarter . CFRA's Angelo Zino was more patient, telling Yahoo Finance the pullback "probably represents a buying opportunity." Losses this size used to be unheard of. US-listed stocks have shed $200 billion or more in a single session 18 times this year through Wednesday. That's up from 13 in all of 2025 and none before 2022, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bloomberg data. Alphabet alone has lost about $1.4 trillion since its record in May. Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance Amazon ( AMZN ), the last of the big three cloud providers to report this week, posted faster growth and a record cash burn after Thursday's close. Amazon Web Services grew 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, while its 12-month free cash flow sank to a record outflow of more than $42 billion. Its stock fell after hours, a sign the pressure on AI spenders reaches well beyond Google. Correction: A previous version of this article misstated Alphabet's one-day loss in market value on Oct. 29. India United States Vietnam Netherlands New Zealand Morocco Taiwan Sweden Australia Japan Portugal Spain Hong Kong Oman Lithuania Brazil Nigeria Germany Türkiye United Kingdom Russia France Pakistan Colombia Italy Belgium South Africa Egypt El Salvador Argentina Philippines Dominican Republic Israel Austria Mexico Tajikistan South Korea Algeria Jordan Nepal Iraq Tanzania Singapore Saudi Arabia Ethiopia Costa Rica Armenia Kazakhstan Malta Tunisia Afghanistan Palestine Malaysia Belize United Arab Emirates Poland Bangladesh Seychelles Madagascar Slovakia Paraguay Kenya Finland and 1 more Most of the early accounts are in India. Read how the map filled in Featured on Product Hunt Featured on FoundrList Questions, answered. Something else? Ask us What is Arsaze? Arsaze is Cursor for video editing: an AI-native video editor for agents and humans. It is a real multi-track timeline that you edit by hand, or that an AI agent edits for you while you watch. It is built for video editors, creators and the teams they cut for. Can I try it without an account? Yes. The demos on arsaze.com are the real editor, Agent view, Rewrite and client review page running on sample footage. The AI in the demo plays four sample edits; exporting, adding your own footage and AI generation need an account, and nothing you do in a demo is saved. What can Arsaze do? Everything a cut needs, by hand or by asking. Captions are transcribed with word timing and styled with reusable presets. Silences and filler words come out of a talking head in one pass, and Tab suggests your next edit as you work. Colour has wheels, curves, HSL secondaries, LUTs and shot matching. Audio has voice isolation, noise reduction, loudness and automatic ducking under speech. Images, video, voiceover, music and sound effects are generated straight onto the timeline. Export an MP4 with no watermark, or hand off to DaVinci Resolve and Premiere Pro as FCPXML. Arsaze also has background removal, motion tracking, Animate Studio motion graphics, a node editor for AI generation, an After Effects panel (beta), a free portfolio page and free in-browser tools. Every tool works by hand on the timeline, and every one is also a tool your AI can call. Why “Cursor for video editing”? Cursor works because code is text an AI can read and change, and you can check every change. Arsaze does the same for video: the timeline and the transcript are structured data an AI agent can read and edit through the same tools you click, every edit plays back live, and every edit is versioned so you can review it or undo it. What is Tab in Arsaze? Tab is autocomplete for video editing. After you make an edit, Arsaze shows the next one on the timeline as a preview: cut one pause and it offers the other pauses like it, grade one clip and it offers the same grade on the shots that match, trim speech and it offers to move the captions with it. Press Tab to take it, Shift+Tab to take one part at a time, or Esc to leave it. Nothing changes until you press Tab, and each accepted suggestion is one undo step. Tab is in the editor on every plan, including Free, in the browser, the desktop app and on your phone. Does Tab learn how I edit? Yes. Tab picks up how much air you leave in a pause, which filler words you cut, and which kinds of suggestion you take or turn down, and its next suggestions follow that. Turn one down and it is not offered there again. You can turn off “Learn from my edits” at any time in Settings, under Privacy. How does Rewrite work? Rewrite turns your footage into a transcript on a page. Delete words and they are cut from the video, or cut every um and shorten every long pause in one click. Cuts show as tracked changes, and clicking one puts it back. Reviewer notes sit in the margin, and you can download the script as a Word document. How do clients review a cut? Send a review link, with no export needed. Clients watch, draw on the frame and leave notes at the exact moment they mean. Click a note and the player jumps there, and your AI can read the notes and make the fixes. How do I start using Arsaze? Create a free account at arsaze.com/login with Google or a SidhiLynx ID. No credit card is needed. Open a project, add a video, and edit by hand or connect your AI from the guide at arsaze.com/video-editor-for-ai-agents. Do I have to use an AI agent? No. It's a full manual NLE: a multi-track timeline for video, text, overlays and audio, trim modes, color wheels and keyframes. Undo anything, yours or the AI's, and save versions to compare two cuts. The agent is an operator you can hand the controls to, not a requirement. What happens if the agent makes a bad edit? Every edit is versioned automatically as it happens, so you can step back to any earlier state or try an idea on a branch. Nothing the agent does is one-way. Which AI tools can I connect? Any client that connects to remote MCP servers over Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1, including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Codex, Cursor, Copilot and Windsurf. The MCP guide has step-by-step setup for Claude, ChatGPT and Grok; other clients use the same server URL. Once connected, pick a project and the agent's edits play back live in your editor. Is my footage used to train models? Not without your consent. Your uploads, generated video and voice models stay tied to your account — see the privacy policy for the full detail. Can I edit without uploading my footage? Yes. A local project in the desktop app keeps your video, audio and images on your computer, and they are never uploaded. The AI can still edit it with you, and you can switch that off for any project. The timeline and its version history are saved in your account, so you need to be online while you edit. You can have unlimited local projects on any plan and convert one to the cloud in one click. What do I need to run it? Any modern browser. Exports render on our servers by default, so you don't need a fast machine. The desktop app for Windows, Mac and Linux adds on-device transcription, background removal, local projects and free local exports with no watermark. Can I get my video out? Yes.

title: Claude Duet is the first personal-assistant-type harness that feels useful
abstract:
Written by a human. Not affiliated with Anthropic. Look, I really didn’t want to like Duet. I don’t want to be an Anthropic fanboy and it annoys me when they do things better than the competition. But they have done it again. I have given serious effort to Muse, Dot, NanoClaw, and a host of other personal-assistant-type harnesses. Duet is the first one that felt more useful than tedious, and it feels like a serious evolution of the chat experience rather than another “give me all your credentials to be useful” agent. Here’s why I like it so far. 1. It’s fast Other assistant apps are always doing who-the-hell-knows-what in the background while I wait for a response. Duet clearly prioritizes getting a snappy response to the user even if background work is needed. It’s supposedly powered by Opus 5.5, but I’ve never seen Opus move this fast in other Claude UIs. Clearly some tuning went on here. This is critical to be a useful assistant: If you want to be my shell to the world, I am not going to sit and twiddle my thumbs between commands. 2. Channels are neat Maybe I’m just Slack-brained, but I really like Duet channels. In particular: I like that Duet can create and manage channels for me. One tedious aspect of working with LLMs is trying to keep track of chat sessions: workstreams get lost, context must be carefully maintained, sessions get misnamed, etc. Duet does the tedious session organizing for me. A natural hierarchy has emerged for my work, and I suspect I will have fewer lost threads with Duet. Cmd-k was already reflex for me: it pulls up the list of channels and lets me rapidly swap between them. Channels can also see and reference each other so Duet can help me keep work in the right lane. 3. Access policies are meaningful Access to Github repos is restricted per channel. I can add a few related repos to a specific channel, and not worry that the channel might commingle work from my other projects. It also never tries to get my credentials. This is my pet peeve with most assistant apps: they won’t do much until you hand them the keys. Muse has a credential store, which at least makes the agent blind to the values, but it could still enter those in something untrusted. Duet stores no credentials and actively discourages being given them. At best it might let you login via a Chrome session on its behalf. But it has never asked me to do that: it prefers to use the connector ecosystem Claude already has, and seems content to stay in its lane otherwise. 4. Responses are short This isn’t unique to Duet, Dot and Muse seem to get this too: Nobody wants to read a full page response to a simple question, which has been the de facto chatbot experience for years. I have always had to add a bunch of instructions trying to persuade my agents to give succinct responses. They all can also add emoji “reactions” to messages, though I find that personality makes a difference here: Muse tended to thumbs up everything, whereas Duet uses it to give me an okay without elaborating further, and I find that delightful. THAT BEING SAID It’s in beta, and definitely has some glitches. Sometimes threads are running but not visible. I’ve seen delegated repo access fail to attach correctly (race condition between agent start and access attachment?). I also acknowledge my use-cases likely make Duet a better fit for me in particular. Muse might be a better fit for others. YMMV. And Dot still reigns on voice interaction. Anthropic doesn’t even seem to care about having a conversational voice mode, it’s still just glorified speech-to-text. Duet is already replacing most of my AI workflows I don’t really enjoy the management side of managing agents: remembering who is running and with what context where. There is always some agent somewhere waiting on me to make a decision or follow up on some task. I’m sure some agent did brilliant work for me on a box somewhere that I’ve neglected and will be forgotten forever. The innovation that matters to me most is the hierarchy of concerns: The top level of Duet has a bird’s eye view of all my workstreams, but no low-level access. The channels carry more access, but under more constrained context. Sub-threads spun up by the channels can be even further constrained as they work in specific code sandboxes. The Desktop app can reach local hosts where I let it, and that’s usually only for the QA or deployment edge after the coding is done in the cloud. Most of this is how I already preferred to arrange my agents, and similar flows could be hacked together with some ducttape and API credits. Duet just makes this hierarchy a natural part of the core product, and it works so well that I suspect it’s going to be the default experience for all chatbot UIs in the near future.

title: SUN’IY INTELLEKT VOSITALARI DAVRIDA TALABANING AKADEMIK HALOLLIGI: PEDAGOGIK JAVOB CHORALARI
abstract: Purpose – to substantiate, on the basis of international experience, the pedagogical mechanisms for safeguarding academic integrity under generative artificial intelligence and to adapt them to higher education in Uzbekistan. Methods: a systematic review of 2023–2026 studies indexed in Scopus and Web of Science and of policy documents issued by international organisations; existing responses were compared by point of impact and implementation cost; modelling was then applied. Results: the limits of the detection-and-sanction approach are demonstrated – AI-text detectors show high error rates and a systematic bias against non-native English writers. A three-level model of pedagogical responses is proposed – institutional, course and task level – together with a five-step scale of permitted AI use and a set of cheating-resistant task types. Conclusion: the most effective and least costly measure is assessment redesign combined with transparent declaration of AI use; a detector result cannot serve as evidence in a disciplinary decision.

title: AI-Driven Software Testing for a Test Center of Excellence: A Systematic Mapping and Evidence Synthesis
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to automate and optimize software testing, but the evidence is distributed across heterogeneous testing activities, AI techniques, and evaluation measures. This study maps AI-driven software-testing research and translates the evidence into capabilities relevant to a Test Center of Excellence (TCoE). A systematic evidence workflow was applied to a unified audit corpus of 2,072 records, followed by focused eligibility reconciliation and full-text verification. The final focused evidence workset contains 29 records: 15 primary empirical studies, 9 secondary studies, 1 scope exclusion, and 4 full-text/access exclusions. The primary evidence covers machine learning, reinforcement learning, evolutionary and search-based methods, deep learning, explainable AI, and large language models. The supported testing activities include test generation, selection and prioritization, minimization and optimization, fuzzing, validation, adaptive automation, and maintenance. The synthesis shows that AI should be treated in a TCoE as a governed capability layer rather than as a single automation tool. The proposed capability model links AI techniques to testing activities, measurable outcomes, reusable TCoE capabilities, and governance with human oversight. The study also identifies gaps in reliability, context awareness, test-oracle support, long-term maintenance, CI/CD integration, reproducibility, and standardized evaluation.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Narrative Framing Classification: A TF-IDF-Based Study of Frankenstein
abstract: This study evaluates interpretable supervised machine learning for three-class narrative framing classification of literary text, using Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) as a case study; narrative framing is the evaluative position a passage assigns to the Creature: Threat, Victim, or Ambivalent. The methodology comprised five stages: (1) extraction of passages narrated by Victor Frankenstein, the Creature, and Robert Walton from the 1818 Project Gutenberg text; (2) annotation of 195 passages, with a blinded second annotator re-labeling 68 passages (Cohen's κ = 0.6926); (3) sublinear TF-IDF unigram and bigram representation; (4) classification with Multinomial Naive Bayes, Linear SVM, and Logistic Regression against Majority and VADER baselines under stratified 5-fold cross-validation; and (5) a designation-masking ablation and coefficient analysis. The results show that Logistic Regression obtained the highest mean scores (66.67% accuracy; 47.75% Macro-F1), although its margin over Linear SVM (46.18%) and VADER (44.85%) lies within fold-level variability. Pooled F1 reached 69.0% for Threat and 74.3% for Victim, whereas none of the 29 Ambivalent passages was correctly identified. Masking explicit designations reduced Macro-F1 only to 45.20%, indicating partial robustness to this procedure rather than discourse-level modeling. It is concluded that interpretable classical classifiers can separate Threat from Victim framing using transparent lexical evidence but cannot yet detect ambiguous framing; given the single-novel, small, and imbalanced dataset, the findings are a preliminary proof of concept. Future work should enlarge and balance the corpus, apply group-based and repeated cross-validation, and compare context-aware models, including large language models, on the Ambivalent class.

title: AI-Assisted Business Ideation as a Technology–Cognition–Institutional Pathway to Entrepreneurial Intention: A Serial Mediation Model of Perceived Feasibility and Entrepreneurial Consultancy Services
abstract: Generative AI has significantly reduced the effort and expense of developing and refining venture ideas, without eliminating the uncertainty and resource limitations of executing a venture. This research examines the potential of AI-assisted business ideation (AIBI) to drive behavioral change in accessing entrepreneurial support infrastructure. The study uses technology-cognition-institutional framework to examine the relationship between AIBI and perceived feasibility (PF) and entrepreneurial consultancy services engagement (ECS) and how these two variables mediate the relationship between AIBI and entrepreneurial intentions (EI). The study analyzed data from 319 university students in Pakistan using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). It evaluated the reliability and validity of the measurement model and examined structural relationships through bootstrapping with bias-corrected confidence intervals. Findings indicate that AI-based business ideation positively affects perceived feasibility, which in turn enhances engagement with entrepreneurial creative strategies (ECS).Moreover, ECS positively and significantly affect entrepreneurial intention, this in turn has a positive and significant direct effect on AIBI. The pathway from AIBI to perceived feasibility to engagement in entrepreneurial consultancy services to entrepreneurial intention is significant, emphasizing that AIBI affects entrepreneurial intention both cognitively and institutionally. This study extends AI entrepreneurship research by showing that AI's effects on entrepreneurial intention go beyond boosting entrepreneurial cognition. This study also contributes to existing intention models by conceptualizing entrepreneurial consultancy services as an endogenous behavioral mediator rather than a contextual condition, offering a more complete explanation of AI-enabled ideation's role in entrepreneurial readiness.

title: School principals’ perceptions of generative AI as a decision-support tool: implications for decisional capital
abstract:
This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is perceived as a decision-support mechanism in school principals’ decision-making, focusing on its perceived implications for decisional capital within a centralized education system.
 
 
 
 Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 17 public school principals across different school levels in Türkiye. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify how GenAI is interpreted and positioned within principals’ decision-making processes.
 
 
 
 Principals reported decision-making challenges driven by bureaucratic procedures, restricted autonomy and competing stakeholder demands. Within these constraints, GenAI was seen not as a substitute for professional judgment but as cognitive support that may improve access to information, facilitate scenario-based reasoning and inform evidence-based judgments. Principals reported varying levels of readiness to integrate GenAI into organizational decision-making, with this variation associated with digital competence, institutional support and ethical awareness.
 
 
 
 The study extends discussions of principals’ decision-making by linking GenAI-enabled decision support to the exercise of decisional capital under centralized governance constraints, highlighting conditions under which GenAI may contribute to human-centered and ethically grounded organizational decision-making processes.

title: When Does Mixing Models Pay? Open Fusion, a Bounded Mixture-of-Agents Runtime, and Registered Evidence from Local Coding Benchmarks
abstract: Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) methods combine the outputs of several large language models (LLMs) at inference time and have reported gains on conversational benchmarks. Whether those gains survive deployment constraints — fixed call budgets, local hardware, objective grading and fair same-model baselines — is less clear. I present OpenFusion, an open-source, OpenAI-compatible runtime that implements fourteen bounded multi-model strategies, from fallback and Self-MoA to semantic voting, rank-then-fuse, layered refinement and uncertainty cascades, under a hard per-request call ceiling. It ships with an evaluation laboratory that reports Wilson intervals, paired tests, order-balanced judging and panel-complementarity diagnostics.Using the project's published artifacts, I report a series of local studies on two NVIDIA GB10 workstations with 4B-parameter open models. In a registered prospective study on 500 previously unused MBPP tasks, a fixed test-guided mixed-model workflow passed 78.1% of all-test evaluations versus 72.5% for repeated same-model repair (+5.6 points, 95% CI [3.6, 7.7]), with 17.2% lower mean latency and 29.2% fewer tokens. A confidence-gated escalation policy raised held-out accuracy on a 70-item programmatic benchmark from 75.7% to 91.4% while calling a stronger model on 40% of items.Five later controls, however, did not show that model diversity itself causes the gains. Against fresh sampling from the same model, mixed panels tied or underperformed: −0.57 points on 1,500 tasks, and −5.0 points after a 32-policy development search. I conclude that, in this setting, the measurable benefit of MoA-style systems comes from verification, bounded retries and selective escalation rather than from mixing similarly sized models. I close with a five-step selection rule and a reporting checklist for practitioners.

title: AI-Enabled Intelligent Energy Optimisation for Smart Commercial Infrastructure Using IoT and Digital Twin Technologies
abstract: Intelligent, sustainable management systems are needed to address rapid urbanisation and rising energy consumption in commercial facilities. Traditional Building Management Systems (BMS) are reactive, non-predictive, and non-automated, and they lack AI support for decision-making. This paper introduces EcoMind, an Internet of Things (IoT)- based intelligent energy optimisation framework for smart commercial infrastructures, supported by artificial intelligence. It is implemented in a cloud-native system that incorporates IoT telemetry simulation, predictive analytics, Digital Twin monitoring, sustainability assessment, and a telemetry-based conversational AI module. Anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, occupancy-aware intelligence, and rule-based optimisation mechanisms provide real-time analysis of HVAC, lighting, elevator, escalator, parking, and environmental sensor data. The definitions used for this study are as follows: occupancy utilisation: ratio of actual occupancy over maximum occupancy; total energy consumption: total energy consumed by HVAC, lighting, elevator, escalator and parking systems; anomaly deviation: dif erence between the current sensor reading and the historical normal behaviour; optimisation efficiency: ratio of reduction in energy consumption after applying optimisation strategies to the total energy consumption. The major innovation is using the Gemini APIs large language model to integrate live infrastructure telemetry data into a pipeline, enabling real-time reasoning without relying on static datasets. Experimental results show a decrease in total energy consumption of 18–22 parcent, improved response to anomaly detection and improved operational decision making. The results confirm that Digital Twin intelligence and Telemetry AI is a powerful complement that enhances scalability, adaptability, and sustainability in smart commercial infrastructure systems.

title: INTELLIGENT CAD/CAM INTEGRATION FOR ADAPTIVE MANUFACTURING: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF AI AND IOT FRAMEWORKS IN INDUSTRY 4.0
abstract: The union of Artificial Intelligence and the Internet of Things (IoT) is transforming the way Computer-Aided Design (CAD) and Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) systems are used in the Industry 4.0 production process. Based on the PRISMA 2020 reporting framework (Page et al., 2021), this report is a systematic literature review on the intelligent integration of CAD and CAM technologies in adaptive manufacturing. Based on a structured search of major scientific databases, a curated list of peer-reviewed studies was analysed thematically to address five research questions related to designing with AI, toolpath optimisation using AI, IoT/IIoT architectures for real-time adaptive control, interoperability standards and barriers to AI adoption in specific sectors. AI models, especially deep learning, graph neural networks and reinforcement learning, have led the way in recent research and development on automatic feature recognition and toolpath generation, while digital twins, edge computing and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) sensor networks are more and more being used to implement predictive maintenance and closed-loop adaptive control in the shop floor. The design phase is also starting to change with Generative AI to enable manufacturability constraints to be built in earlier in the CAD process. The literature, however, shows that there are still significant gaps that need to be addressed: AI models deployed outside of the simulation environment are not adaptable in real-time, training datasets are not standardized and openly shared, and there are interoperability protocols that are still quite disjointed, and resources for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) looking to use these technologies are still limited. To situate these gaps in a particular developing-economy context, this review is also supplemented by a series of recently published empirical studies. The review suggests that interoperability standards, Human Safety for Industry 5.0 design principles, cybersecurity, and sustainable practice are the key factors that need to be coordinated for the intelligent CAD/CAM-IoT integration to be fully realised, and it presents a roadmap of future research directions for adaptive and connected manufacturing ecosystems.

title: Machine psychology for language models.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a "machine psychology" for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

title: Death of the Author, Birth of the Algorithm? Reimagining Literary Meaning- Making in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced new possibilities for literary interpretation, challenging traditional assumptions about authorship, readership and textual meaning. While Roland Barthes’ concept of the “Death of the Author” displaced authorial intention as the primary source of meaning, contemporary AI technologies raise questions about whether algorithms are becoming active participants in interpretive processes. This study explores how generative AI reshapes literary meaning- making and examines the implications of AI- generated interpretations for literary studies in the digital age. This qualitative exploratory study was conducted among 20 undergraduate students enrolled in a BA English programme at a private university in Sri Lanka. Drawing on Barthes’ notion of the Death of the Author, Michael Foucault’s concept of the author function, and reader- response theories advanced by Wolfgang Iser and Stanley Fish, the study critically examines the role of generative AI in the production and mediation of literary interpretations. Relevant scholarly literature on AI- assisted reading and digital textuality is analysed to develop a theoretical framework for understanding algorithmic participation in literary meaning- making. The analysis suggest that generative AI complicates traditional distinctions between author, reader, and text. Rather than functioning as an author in the conventional sense, AI appears to operate as an interpretive agent capable of generating multiple readings based on patterns derived from vast textual corpora. This development extends reader- centred approaches to literary interpretation while simultaneously raising concerns regarding originality, authority, and the pedagogical use of AI-generated analyses. The study argues that AI- generated interpretations should be viewed not as replacements for human reading but as additional voices within broader interpretive communities. The paper proposes that literary studies must reconsider established theories of authorship and interpretation in response to emerging AI technologies. By positioning AI as a participant in, rather than a determinant of, meaning- making, the study contributes to ongoing discussions in literary theory, semiotics, and digital humanities. The findings offer insights for educators, researchers, and students navigating literary interpretation in increasingly AI- mediated learning environments.

title: The Comforting Machine: Evaluating User Trust and Emotional Relief in Empathetic AI Astrologers vs Blunt Human Practitioners
abstract: Astrological consultations can create anxiety when adverse predictions are communicated through direct or fatalistic language particularly in culturally subjective contexts where users may attach personal meaning to such predictions. This empirical study investigates whether empathetic AI mediated communication can influence user trust, anxiety and emotional relief when compared with conventional blunt communication by human practitioners. The study introduces two complementary contributions. An AI based semantic reframing approach and an emotional Human Computer Interaction interface framework. The AI approach uses a safety constrained large language model to identify catastrophic or deterministic elements in astrological narratives and transform them into constructive, non-deterministic and growth-oriented interpretations. The HCI framework examines how conversational language, reduced textual density, supportive formatting, and non-deterministic interface structures can contribute to a more emotionally supportive user experience while preserving user agency. A multi demographic user survey was conducted in which participants evaluated identical stressful astrological scenarios presented through a traditional blunt human practitioner script and a safety constrained AI generated narrative. Participants assessed perceived trust, anxiety, emotional relief and overall experience across the two conditions. The findings indicate that human practitioner communication retained a perception of authenticity whereas the AI mediated condition was associated with lower reported anxiety and greater emotional relief. The combination of empathetic linguistic reframing and supportive HCI presentation also showed a positive relationship with experiential trust and perceived user agency. These findings suggest that the emotional impact of AI-mediated communication depends not only on the content generated but also on how that content is structured and presented to users. The study contributes to research on empathetic AI, emotional HCI and responsible conversational design by demonstrating how safety constrained language generation and supportive interface design can facilitate less deterministic, emotionally supportive and user centered experiences in culturally sensitive domains. The findings provide a foundation for further investigation of responsible AI communication in emotionally subjective digital environments.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Cross-Modal Alignment for Diffusion-Based IoT Intrusion Detection
abstract: Diffusion models evolve noisy states toward a learned data distribution, so their sampling behavior depends on the geometry of the representation in which denoising occurs. This dependence is especially important for multimodal data: independently trained encoders can map synchronized views to incompatible latent regions, while uniform alignment can let an uncertain view distort the shared geometry. To address this gap, we introduce a novel reliability-guided alignment rule that uses normalized VAE posterior variance to control directional cross-modal influence before diffusion training. We study this issue in minority-attack generation for imbalanced Internet-of-Things intrusion detection. Tabular flow attributes, a DeepInsight image, and a packet sequence are encoded by modality-specific variational autoencoders. Per-modality normalized VAE posterior variances provide bounded, sample-specific weighting signals in an asymmetric stop-gradient alignment objective. We use these quantities as heuristic encoder-derived reliability proxies rather than calibrated probabilistic uncertainties. The full modality-specific latent means obtained after alignment fine-tuning are standardized and modeled jointly by a class-conditional EDM; a second-order sampler then generates paired attack-conditioned latent blocks for the three decoders. In controlled experiments on TON-IoT, uncertainty-aware alignment obtains the highest mean precision, recall, density, and coverage among three diffusion variants. Augmenting only the training split yields ROC-AUC 0.9515, PR-AUC 0.8954, balanced accuracy 0.8395, and attack-class F1 0.7940 on an untouched real test set. Among the two variants with matched alignment fine-tuning, posterior-variance-based weighting improves both tabular generative fidelity and downstream detection relative to uniform weighting.

title: Regional Anchor Routing for Multi-Object Motion Transfer
abstract: Compositional motion transfer requires a model to extract motions from multiple reference videos, and apply each motion to a user-specified object in one target scene. Existing methods normally struggle to reliably assign different reference motions to the correct target objects, thus a motion intended for one object may affect another. Meanwhile, some motion-specific tuning approaches are still facing another issue: they must run a new optimization whenever the reference video changes, making repeated transfers inefficient. To address these limitations, we propose RART, a framework that unifies object-wise motion extraction, target-region anchoring, and frame-aligned injection into a frozen video Diffusion Transformer for multi-object motion transfer. For each reference motion, RART extracts temporally ordered features from the masked reference video, and then conditions them on the target first-frame mask to form mask-anchored motion tokens. Frame-aligned motion cross-attention allows each generated frame to read only the motion tokens at the corresponding time slots, composing all object motions in one denoising process. During training, a motion-attention routing loss encourages each target region to attend to its corresponding motion tokens and reduces interference between objects. Therefore, RART can handle novel reference-target combinations without per-video optimization. Experiments show that RART achieves accurate motion preservation, efficient inference, and strong compositional generalization.

title: REALM: Identifying Minimal Task Assets for LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often receive access to more files, accounts, and services than a task requires. Prompt injection turns this excess access into an opportunity to redirect execution toward unrelated resources. Applying least privilege therefore requires identifying the assets needed by a task, including assets whose identities emerge only during execution. We present REALM (Required Execution Assets Linked to a Mission), an approach to identifying and maintaining a task's required assets and their permitted uses. The approach represents required assets as Dependency Graph nodes, resolves prerequisite relationships, and admits newly discovered assets through source-scoped selection. It separates discovering an asset from authorizing its use, while preserving the agent's freedom to choose its computation. The REALM Builder maintains the selected grants and projects Asset Files; the Partial API Manager exposes resource-bound Partial APIs to the Agent inside a Task Container. Across 60 clean tasks and 560 injected cases in AgentDyn, it completes 40.0% and 36.4% of tasks and decreases ASR from 16.6% to 0.2% with qwen3.5-flash as the base model.

title: LLM eBay: A Simple and Truthful Marketplace for Fine-Tuned LLMs Trading
abstract: Personalized fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) enhances user experience but incurs substantial computational costs. Recent studies show that initializing training from a style-similar fine-tuned model reduces adaptation overhead, turning such checkpoints into reusable, tradable assets. A marketplace for these checkpoints, however, faces information asymmetry: sellers may misreport a checkpoint's style, while buyers cannot verify its usefulness before purchase, which invites adverse selection. We introduce LLM eBay, a simple single-round marketplace for trading fine-tuned LLMs. Sellers are paid per purchase at a posted price, and a truncated quadratic proper scoring rule adjusts each payment according to how well the seller's style report agrees with a style signal that the platform measures by generating text on hidden prompts. We show that the score elicits the verifier's expected signal, characterize exactly when truthful reporting is a seller best response under per-purchase demand, and bound the downside risk from noisy verification. In an end-to-end study with real LoRA checkpoints on two base models and three buyer tasks, LLM eBay reduces measured convergence steps by 8.5\% relative to retrieval over self-reported style (95\% CI [1.0\%, 15.9\%]). In model-based market simulations built on a measured style-to-cost relationship, it cuts style-claim error by 96.5\% (from 0.424 to 0.015), recovers 96.3\% of Oracle welfare, saves 72.4\% of the cost of fine-tuning from the base model, and keeps all providers profitable in the default setting.

title: Composing and Steering Diffusion Models with Generalized Feynman-Kac Correctors
abstract: Diffusion models have become the leading paradigm in generative modeling, yet many applications require sampling from distributions that are not those of any single pretrained model, but are instead defined through combinations of several models, possibly tilted toward high values of a downstream reward. Naively combining the scores of the models yields incorrect samples, while existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets. In this work, we introduce the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC), a principled framework for sampling from an arbitrary target function of several pretrained diffusion models. We show that the geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function of the models satisfies a Feynman--Kac partial differential equation, and derive its potential in closed form. To evaluate this potential during generation, we further generalize the log-probability ODE to track the density of each model along trajectories driven by a different velocity field. The resulting algorithm operates entirely in the log domain, incorporates reward-based steering at no additional conceptual cost, and corrects the generation on the fly, without retraining or fine-tuning the models. We validate the method on analytic Gaussian models, where it closely matches the ground-truth targets, and on diffusion models trained on MNIST, where it samples from non-trivial combinations of the models and enables effective steering.

title: Attention, Dynamic Wave and Hybrid Sequence Mixers in Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.

title: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
abstract: When one AI agent tells another that"the tests passed"or"a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs, signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Receivers check messages offline and give each claim a three-valued result: proven, unproven or failed. A claim that rests only on the agent's own report is never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval, and the chains can only narrow. We specify four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, and we prove the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all of them stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols (A2A with signed Agent Cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.

title: HALO: Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents
abstract: Proactive agents must decide whether, when, and how far to assist without an explicit request. Existing evaluations often rely on automated scores or binary verdicts, offering limited human diagnosis of evidence use and intervention quality. To address these gaps, we introduce HALO, Human-Grounded GrAnular EvaLuation of PrOactive Agents. HALO-Arena covers 4 proactive need types, Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity, across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments. Scenarios require agents to retrieve evidence from structured databases or unstructured documents before judging whether assistance is warranted and choosing its scope. On HALO-Arena, we construct HALO-8K, a dataset of 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts, and human diagnosis. For rejected responses, human diagnosis covers timing, intensity, and other issues. Recorded reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds measure the effort behind these responses. The best proprietary and open-source models achieve 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, respectively. Our central finding is that over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode, with Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounting for 61.20% of rejected responses. Further analyses yield complementary findings on the balance between intervention and restraint, evidence acquisition, and the calibration of timing and intensity.

title: Radiology Guideline-derived Decision Graph for Efficient Clinical Decision Support
abstract: Radiological risk stratification and management planning are essential downstream tasks in medical imaging. Automating these tasks is challenging because clinical guideline criteria are distributed across prose, tables, and cross-referenced definitions. We present Guideline-derived Decision Graph (GDGraph), a framework that decouples guideline compilation from case evaluation. During compilation, a large language model partitions guidelines into section-based chunks, extracts local decision subgraphs with linked definitions, and aggregates related branches into an executable decision graph. During inference, a fast System One model answers localized clinical questions while deterministic traversal resolves Boolean logic, turning opaque single-pass predictions into a traceable decision path without task-specific training. Across 347 cases spanning renal cyst, adnexal mass, and thyroid nodule guidelines, GDGraph improves System One accuracy from 57.3% to 90.8%, outperforming retrieval-augmented GPT-4o (80.1%) and graph-guided GPT-4o with chain-of-thought (82.7%) at substantially lower latency and cost. The source code will be available.

title: TokWatt: an open, boundary-annotated database of AI inference energy, from chat answers to agents
abstract: Electricity supply is becoming a binding constraint on the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI), yet public evidence on the energy used by a single AI task is scattered and hard to compare. Published figures for one chatbot answer differ by two orders of magnitude, largely because studies count different parts of the system and measure different units of work. We present TokWatt, an open database of 134 published estimates of AI inference energy drawn from 13 sources (2023-2026) and covering 20 tasks, from classic machine-learning inferences to chat answers, reasoning answers, long-document queries, image and video generation, and coding agents. Each estimate records its functional unit, five measurement-boundary components, method, reported interval, and the location of the value in its source. A reproducible procedure scales estimates to a common server-plus-facility boundary and derives per-task reference values with ranges. The reference values span six orders of magnitude: 0.34 Wh for a short chat answer (range 0.16-0.99 Wh), 4.7 Wh for a reasoning answer, 124 Wh for a short video clip, and 150 Wh for one task delegated to a coding agent. Five independent estimates for default production chat systems agree within a factor of 1.8, and the reference values shift by at most 12% under alternative harmonization parameters. A simple identity links personal use to grid load: E watt-hours per person per day across one billion people corresponds to an average draw of E/24 gigawatts. Data and code are released at https://github.com/AraoufBh/tokwatt, and an online calculator at https://araoufbh.github.io/tokwatt/.

title: Can AI Agents Interface Clinicians and Complex Models?
abstract: Background: Contemporary healthcare institutions generate daily very large amounts of data, which contain highly useful information for the improvement of work organization, planning and overall efficiency. While models and techniques to extract these insights are well known and constantly developed in mathematical biology, complex systems physics and data science, the adoption of these techniques among Clinicians and Hospital Administrators remains limited, mainly due to language and methodological divides. Objective: In this article we implement an AI Multi Agent System (MAS) that allows Users to use predictive models and make statistical analyses via natural language conversations. Methods: We developed EpidemIA, a training-free MAS endowed with a modular suite of epidemiological models written by human experts, executable on a single-GPU workstation. To avoid relaying sensitive data to third parties, the system uses locally an open-weights LLM as backbone for its two subagents. Results: Using a dataset of Emergency Department visits provided to us by IRCCS Sant'Orsola (Bologna) we test the model on a few typical use cases, demonstrating the possibility of performing both simpler statistical analyses and visualizations as well as more complicated epidemiological predictions based on dynamical models, through simple queries made in natural language. Conclusions: While still being a proof-of-concept implementation, EpidemIA showcases the transformative capabilities of LLM based technologies as an enabling factor in the widespread adoption of complex dynamical models, which is at present hindered by their steep learning curve.
